headline: You can now walk across the world without walking off it — the ground was only ever built when something teleported.
detail: orchestration/status/province-stream-pump.json — walked 3 km: ground underfoot gone by 750 m before, 0 samples without ground after; full crossing 55.1 min, 6,615 m, 99 tiles streamed in while walking

headline: You can collect your souls back but you cannot spend them: the level-up screen is refused at all 29 resting places, because it asks the game a question the game has no answer to.
detail: corpus/90-verdicts/wave1/W1-13-r1.md — engine.js:2011 calls HearthSystem.atHearth() and HearthSystem has no such method; refused 3/3 at wells where the registry itself reported the player standing at one

headline: Saving while the death screen is up destroys every soul you were carrying — 4,200 in, 0 out — because loading restores both the bloodstain and your corpse, and the next frame kills you again.
detail: corpus/90-verdicts/wave1/W1-13-r1.md §1 — two routes, both 0/4200, control taken 150 frames later returns all 4,200

headline: The instrument built to check that your race affects how people treat you cannot tell when that has been switched off: one injected line made the world race-blind and the tool printed the same numbers, byte for byte.
detail: corpus/80-methods/TOOL-COVERAGE-R3.md §1 — three anchors all describe plumbing; --cross-check reported 'AGREES on 240 pairs, 0 disagreements' on a tree where zero rows were compared

headline: The world's library went from seven books to sixty-five, and twenty-eight of them flatly contradict another book on a named fact.
detail: orchestration/status/W1-LIBRARY.json — 37,819 words, median 609 against Morrowind's 520; eight book ids that shipped quests already required now exist

headline: The screenshot service could be told to lie: a file dropped in its cache folder made it swear the player had walked somewhere on foot, and it handed that back in 24 milliseconds without ever opening the game. It now refuses.
detail: corpus/80-methods/CAPTURE-SERVICE-R1.md is the critic's verdict (NOT SATISFIED, seven rebuilds). The critic's own attack tool, tools/capture/critic-r1-probe.mjs, now finds 0 of 7 holes where it found the arrival gate accepting 28 of 30 laundered requests, a forged cache manifest served in 24 ms, and three shapes of half-loaded world certified as ready to photograph. The picture is one of two frames that came out byte-identical from the same request - asking for the same view twice used to give you two different pictures, because a request that did not name a time of day silently inherited the weather of whatever ran before it.

headline: The game now has 65 in-world books and 37,819 words of genuinely good writing — and reading them does nothing: the three quests you were supposed to be able to talk your way out of by having read the right book refuse you in exactly the same words before and after you read it.
detail: corpus/90-verdicts/wave1/W1-LIBRARY-r1.md — verdict 3/10. Also: the whole library can be told apart from Morrowind's real books by one word ('eleven' is in 75% of ours and 3% of theirs).

headline: The world now follows you as you walk it - but the most expensive half-second in the game is the moment you stand up after dying, when the ground rushes to rebuild itself under your feet.
detail: corpus/90-verdicts/wave1/W1-01-province-stream-r1.md - FAIL 5/10. The fix works: walk 1,500 m and the stone forest is there; switch the fix off and the same walk ends on a blank grey slope with nothing on it. But a death respawn costs six frames of 337/405/484/362/223/472 ms, a 40 m/s barge ride puts 6.6% of frames over a frame, and a 449 ms freeze landed inside a dodge roll.

headline: On a phone the touch controls existed, worked, and were painted nowhere — the game handed a player sixteen invisible buttons. They are drawn now, as sixteen little cut marks (a blade, a shield, a gourd) rather than sixteen words, because a game that has to label its own buttons has already lost.
detail: corpus/90-verdicts/wave1/W1-08-W1-29-r1.md (FAIL 5/10) and reports/W1-08-W1-29-R2.md. Proof it is really connected: switch the phone off and the picture goes back to being byte-for-byte the desktop picture. Two other things fell out of building the missing measurements — pressing Escape used to trap you in a menu you could never leave (a second Escape did nothing and no click would let you back in), and picking a controller back up after touching the screen left the wrong little symbol on every door prompt. Both fixed. One that is not fixed and is now on the record: text on a phone comes out at about 7 pixels where it needs to be 18, so Morrowind's wall of prose is currently unreadable on the device the owner actually plays on.

headline: You could die, walk all the way back over ground you now knew, pick your 4,200 souls out of the mud — and then not spend a single one of them: the level-up screen refused to open at any of the game's 29 campfires, because the code asking "am I at one?" was calling a question nobody had ever written an answer to. It opens now, at all of them, and nowhere else.
detail: corpus/90-verdicts/wave1/W1-13-r1.md named it (FAIL 4/10). reports/runs/W1-13-R2/levelling-loop.json is the proof at three wells, walked in on foot: rest, open, press twice, level 1 to 2, 4,200 souls down to 3,782 — exactly the 418 the curve asks — and the spend still there after a save and reload. Deleting the one-line fix puts every number back. The same round made a save taken while you are lying dead survivable (it used to eat all 4,200 souls), stopped the corpse sliding up to 22 m off the campfire it respawned at, and made falling and drowning leave your souls on the ledge you fell from instead of at the bottom.

headline: The world now has twenty-four things it will never explain, and asking about one no longer gets you silence — it gets you a refusal: ask a Lilmoth clerk who cuts the notches on the Counting Obelisk and she says "Somebody cuts it. Somebody has always cut it. I have never met anybody who wanted to know more than that."
detail: game/data/world/opacity.json is the register; the answers are real, written out in full, and locked in the corpus behind a hash so a critic can prove they were authored without ever being shown one. Delete a mystery from the file and that same question goes back to silence — that is how we proved the game is actually reading it (tools/world/opacity-consumption.mjs, 3/3). Also found: the existing leak-checker only looked at 2,699 of the game's strings and skipped the entire dialogue layer, because NPC lines are stored under a key its list did not know about. The new scan reads all 128,287 and is still clean.

headline: You now wake up on the barge as a body instead of as a form: nobody asks you anything until you walk across the hold and talk to the woman sitting there, and when the clerk at the desk works out what you are, she finally says it out loud.
detail: corpus/90-verdicts/wave1/W1-26-r1.md was a 1.3/10 fail on the two things Morrowind's opening is remembered for. Before: the first question about who you are was on screen at frame 10 and sixty frames of walking moved you nowhere. Now the hold opens with control in your hands and the first question arrives 63.5 seconds later, when you ask for it. Before: the game computed fourteen professions, picked the right one 96% of the time, and said the word out loud 0% of the time — the line was always the first thing the text panel threw away when it ran out of room. Now it is its own moment and it reached the screen in 232 of 232 runs. Also fixed: the game's own instrument for 'what does the screen say?' could not see the heads-up display at all, so a check for bossy tutorial text searched zero strings and reported a pass; over its real ground it had a hit — the prompt used to read 'Take A tithe-gourd, empty' and now just names the thing. reports/W1-26-r2/scene.log

headline: Our own test run for the death loop had been quietly scoring a game that was not running: if any screen was left open, the world stops on purpose — and loading a save does not close it — so twenty scripted deaths killed nobody, produced nothing, and the report printed "OK" nineteen times.
detail: Reproduced in isolation: open the character sheet, ask the game to advance five frames, and it advances zero; deal a hundred thousand damage and nothing dies; close the screen and the death fires on the very next frame. The death-loop journey now closes whatever is open, proves the world actually moves before it measures anything, and refuses to report at all if it does not — and a check that fails now says FAIL in the log instead of OK. Two of its headline numbers were also constants: it printed "20 of 20 deaths conserved their souls" from a line that just counted the rows, next to "20 mismatches" from the line that did the work. tools/journey/jrn06-death.mjs

headline: You can now join the Ledger, the Assize or the Deep-Kin and rise all the way to the top of any of them without killing a single person — and joining one really does slam the door on the other two, which is the whole point and had never once worked.
detail: Three faction careers of nine quests each were written but nothing could be climbed. Playing them for real in the running game found four separate walls. (1) The promotion requirements asked for personal qualities the game has no way to give you: the top rank wanted a score of 24 in a stat, and doing everything the rank itself asks of you earns you four points. Measured across all 240 kinds of character the game can make, the whole ladder pays +4 while characters start anywhere between 6 and 19 — so the requirement was checked against the single best character in the game and shut the door on everyone else. It now asks for exactly what its own work pays for. (2) Rivalry fired on the wrong thing: the Assize sends you to hide a witness, that favour earns you goodwill with the Drowned Court, and the Assize then refused its own next job on the grounds that you were now Drowned Court — four of its nine quests became unreachable to a player who had done exactly what it told them. Joining is now something you actually do, not something you drift into. (3) Nothing in the entire faction book ever actually joined a faction; the word was in the prose and not in the data. (4) Two quests — both the last quest of a career — had no ending any ordinary character could reach, so the line stopped one step from the end. All three careers now run from a cold start to the top rank, entirely peacefully, and set 34 to 38 lasting changes in the world along the way.

headline: The last quest in all three guilds asks for more standing than the game lets anyone earn, so nobody can ever be offered it — and the tool built to catch exactly this was printing "no problems found" while its own count of playable characters sat at zero out of 540.
detail: tools/analysis/build-viability.mjs summarised only one kind of locked door and stayed silent about every other kind. It now reports any gate that stops every character, whatever the gate is made of. Proved three ways: it names the culprit on the real build, it moves to the next one when that culprit is repaired, and it goes quiet when all three are — 0 playable characters becomes 522. See corpus/80-methods/ and orchestration/status/tool-builder-r4.json.

headline: The on-screen touch controls are now actually painted on the glass — last round they existed, worked and were laid out correctly, but a phone and a desktop produced literally the same picture — and the checking tool that was supposed to notice things like that has been caught twice more: once passing a hard test by searching an empty list, once failing the writers by mistaking Argonian names like "Salt-Hand" and "the Shorter" for gamepad buttons.
detail: Proof the controls are drawn: with the game frozen on the same frame and nobody pressing anything, the desktop and handheld frames are now different pictures, and deleting the fix puts the handheld frame back to being byte-for-byte the desktop one. Three more things the tool could not see. (1) It reloaded the page for one test and did not wait for the game to finish starting, so two tests flipped between pass and fail at random, a later test crashed, and the crash threw away the twenty results already taken — the file was never written at all. (2) A test meant to count the writing scratched into the world found zero of it, and its three limits were all upper bounds, so a game with none of it scored full marks. There is none of it because the rules forbid tutorials and pop-ups outright and nothing had been built to replace them; ten inscriptions are now cut into hatch frames, kerb-stones and roof beams, in the voice of whoever was there — "Sixty-one days. The hasp turns if you have the hands for it. I did not, at first." (3) Now the game has a map, the thumb controls were being painted straight across it; they no longer are, on the map, the journal or a book, and the button that gets you back out stays. reports/W1-08-W1-29-R2.md

headline: The word 'eleven' turned out to be the machine's tell — it was the length of nearly every career in the province, the duration of every task, and the size of every crowd — so we rewrote 617 sentences to get rid of it, and then found the same number had already been promoted into the main quest's plot.
detail: reports/prose-tics/W1-PROSE-TICS-report.md — also: the em dash, which looked like the strongest tell of all (infinitely more common in our dialogue than Morrowind's), turned out to be a character-encoding difference. Morrowind is ASCII and writes the same dash as '--'. Measured as a figure rather than a character we actually use it LESS than they do, and swapping the character would have fooled the detector without changing a word.

headline: The three new faction guilds are the best writing in the game so far, but a quest can be completed by someone the guild has just refused to talk to — so nobody has yet reached the top rank by actually playing.
detail: corpus/90-verdicts/wave1/W1-FACTIONS-r1.md — GAP-FCT-01

headline: Sixty-one quests existed that nobody in the world could tell you about; now you can walk into a town, ask what people are saying, and be sent to one.
detail: The main quest was repaired last round. This round did the rest of the tree: 34 quest keywords had no sentence anywhere in the game, so 27 quests could be walked up to and none of them could be started. They now have dialogue, and a rumour in the right town puts the words in your mouth — measured, ten quests opened by standing in two towns and talking, and zero when you stop asking for gossip. Also: three endings of the main quest asked for more personality or willpower than any character in the game can ever have, and signing the Dres clause now actually takes the net-throwers out of the raiding party. reports/runs/W1-19-R2-UTIL/, reports/runs/W1-19-R2-SEAM/

headline: Our townsfolk did not talk like people - they read aloud: in 58,000 words of dialogue there were exactly two exclamation marks, and the villagers asked eight times fewer questions than Morrowind's do. The surprise was that our writing is not too fancy; measured against the real game it is plainer. It is just that nobody in it was reacting to you.
detail: reports/prose-tics/W1-PROSE-TICS-report.md Part II. The cheap fix was one line of find-and-replace turning every "do not" into "don't"; we measured what that would have bought and it was 0.022 - a second, equally strong tell would have been left standing untouched. So 180 lines were rewritten by hand instead, and the keepers and clerks who are meant to sound formal were deliberately left alone. Two smaller stories: the tool caught two of its own author's rules being cheatable before any measurement was taken, and the secrets-leak alarm went off on a line that turned out to share 40 characters with a sealed answer purely because our prose reuses the same stock phrase 55 times more often than the real game does.

headline: The library finally does something. Reading a book now teaches you the names in it, opens the three quests you can talk your way out of instead of fighting, and — for the thirty-two books that are quietly about a skill — makes you slightly better at that skill, the way Morrowind's books did.
detail: Last round a critic opened all sixty books in a real browser and the game had learned nothing: the list of topics you could ask people about was empty before and empty after, and the three peaceful endings gave the same refusal word for word whether or not you had read the book they were waiting on. All three now work, and each was proved by deleting the fix again and watching the number fall back — 122 topics to 0, three open doors to none. Two things turned up on the way. First, every book ran off its own end: hold right and the page counter kept climbing while the page on screen stopped changing, so a reader who over-shot had to press left a dozen times before anything moved, and the game saved that phantom page — one book was reporting page 25 of 11. Second, eleven quest endings across four files ask for a skill that does not exist in the game (one is a plain misspelling, `root_speech` for `root-speech`; the other, `scribing`, is not a skill at all), so those endings could never have been reached by playing no matter how good you got. That one is somebody else's data to fix, so it is now a loud warning rather than a silent impossibility. reports/w1-library-turns.json, reports/w1-library-skillbooks.json, reports/w1-library-gates.json

headline: Five people in the marsh could not tell you what the town was saying or the way out of it, because each was standing in a place that does not exist. Their records named a home — "thornmarsh", "rootlands" — that is not one of the eight towns, and the game answers questions about your surroundings by looking that name up. Every one of them came back empty, and nothing anywhere went red.
detail: The twist is that leaving the field blank would have worked fine. Both the gossip system and the road-directions system are written to fall back on wherever the PLAYER is standing when a character has no home town of their own — so a hermit still knows the road. A wrong name does not trip that fallback, it defeats it: the game dutifully looks up "rootlands", finds nothing, and the person says nothing. A bad answer was strictly worse than no answer. Measured with the player standing in Thorn, each of the five went from two roads and a rumour to zero roads and silence the moment the bad name was put back. The three fixed here are wilderness people — a Hist-grove keeper, a drowned-god speaker, a river-band elder on a bank — so they now have no home town at all, which is the honest answer and makes them speak for wherever you meet them. The other two had been found and fixed by hand a round earlier, which is the real point: three separate pieces of work introduced the same defect and nothing was watching for the class, so the check that catches ANY character claiming a town that does not exist now runs on every commit. It was deliberately landed after the data was already clean — a check armed ahead of its own data has taken this engine down four times and blocks every other agent. reports/w1-04-survey.md §9, tools/world/w1-04-settlement-field.mjs

headline: The rumours now tell you where the work is, and then you walk there and nobody is home — nine of the game's ninety-four quest-givers actually exist in the world.
detail: corpus/90-verdicts/wave1/W1-19-r2.md — round 2 scored FAIL 5/10 (up from 4). The topic bootstrap is genuinely fixed and all 40 character backgrounds can now finish the main quest without money or violence, but the tool that reported '10 of 35 quests open by standing in a town and talking' was asking the quest gate, which never checks whether the person offering the job is anywhere a player can stand.

headline: The game now has a map that draws only the ground you have actually walked and one small square for each place you have actually stood in - and the first version of it quietly recorded nothing at all, because the moment you loaded a saved game it started watching a copy of you that could never move.
detail: The map is a record of where you have been, never an instruction about where to go: no quest markers, no routes or lines, no distances, no fast travel, and nothing undiscovered is drawn even faintly - it is simply not there. A quest cannot put a pin on it because there is no method anywhere that takes a place name; the checking tool tries every plausible way in and records each one failing. Three things went wrong and all three are worth reading. (1) The map recorded almost nothing: loading a game rebuilds the player, and the map had kept hold of the old one, so it froze on 255 patches of ground and could never name a single place no matter how far you walked. (2) The tool that was supposed to catch that scored it 30 out of 30 - because it had quietly swapped in its OWN correctly-wired copy of the map before measuring, and never put the game's own back. It now proves the game's own object works before it tests anything else, and only the picture caught the original problem. (3) Pressing the button for the close-up view did nothing on screen: every menu freezes the world, and the screen only redrew when the world's clock advanced, so no button press on any paused screen - the map, the journal's page turn, any of it - ever redrew anything. Also fixed in the shared screenshot service, which left menus open between jobs and so ran every following job's world without ever simulating it, silently. See orchestration/status/W1-MAP.json.

headline: Twenty-seven ways of talking your way out of a quest had been written and none of them could be used - some asked for a silver tongue better than any character in the game can ever have, and the rest were spelled wrong.
detail: Persuading somebody here works off a Personality score, and in this game that score is not the 0-to-100 number the quests were written against: you earn it slowly by using the skills that feed it, and across 240 different characters the very best anyone reaches is 31. Three quest endings asked for 40 or 45. That is not a hard check, it is a locked door with no key, and it stays locked no matter how well you play. Another eleven talk-and-magic routes asked for a skill called root_speech or scribing - the first is spelled root-speech in the game and the second does not exist at all, so the game looked the name up, found nothing, and reported you at 0 out of 45 forever. Proved by putting the real skill to its absolute maximum of 100 and watching the refusal come back word-for-word identical. Of every non-violent way out an author had actually written, 90.8 per cent worked and now 98.3 per cent do; the 27 that were shut for every character are open. The harder half of the job was not lowering numbers - it was not lowering them too far. An earlier pass set nine gates to exactly the highest reachable value and locked eleven of forty characters out of Act IV, so every new number here is set two below the ceiling on purpose. There is a tool now that reads the real ceilings off a live survey of the character builder rather than trusting any written-down figure, refuses both a demand nobody can meet and one everybody meets, and checks that a faction ladder still gets harder as you climb it. It was deliberately broken six different ways to confirm it goes red, and one of those broke it without the alarm sounding, which was a hole in the alarm.

headline: A character who had joined no faction, was owed nothing and had been refused to their face could still walk into the guild's top job — the game checked whether you were allowed to start a quest and never checked whether you were allowed to finish one.
detail: One line in the quest engine. Accepting a quest ran every check the game has — your rank, your reputation, who you have already sworn to — and finishing one ran none of them, because the only test was 'is there a row for this quest', and merely learning a secret created the row. So one act of eavesdropping let a stranger apply the ending that empties the Wet Ledger's first chair, unlock the succession, and collect forty points of standing with the rival court that faction is barred from. Now both ends are gated, and the refusal you get is the same sentence a person would say to you. Deleting the fix reproduces the exploit exactly. The same round took each of the three guild questlines from nine quests to eighteen, and finally walked one to the top: the earlier reports claimed 'reached the highest rank' and 'never killed anybody' and had never once managed both at the same time, because the cheapest way through was always to refuse, and refusing is exactly what leaves the old chief in his chair. See corpus/90-verdicts/wave1/W1-FACTIONS-r1.md and reports/faction-probe-*.json.

headline: The tool that decides whether the game is finishable had been telling us nobody could finish it - and it was arguing with a number it had made up itself.
detail: It builds an imaginary best-case character and walks them through every quest in the game. To do that it has to decide what that character owns, knows and has earned. Four rounds running it simply asserted some of those things: it decided the most standing you can ever earn with a guild is 100, which was true of an old draft and has not been true since the guilds started asking for 112, so it declared three quests unreachable by anybody and scored the whole game 0 out of 540. It also handed the character a purse of a billion gold, the top rank in all eight guilds at once - including two that are sworn enemies - and three magic bags that answered 'yes, I have that' to absolutely any item, secret or spell you named, while actually being empty. Every one of those is now worked out from the game's own files: the reputation is the sum of what the quests actually pay, the ranks are computed by the game's own promotion code, the bag of items contains the items that exist. The tool now prints that whole list on every run, so the next person can argue with the arithmetic instead of having to find it. Removing the invented numbers immediately surfaced things nobody could see past them: four of the eight guilds cannot promote you past rank four because promotion needs a deed that no quest in the game performs, only three guilds can reach rank five at all and no three of those are on speaking terms, and six things quests ask you to be carrying or to have learned are never given out by anything. Proved by copying the whole game, deliberately killing the code that makes different races unwelcome in different places, and confirming the tool notices and refuses to publish - the same sabotage that slipped past it two rounds ago.

headline: A reader who had never seen either corpus was shown twenty pairs of writing - ours against Morrowind's - and picked ours out twenty times, and the thing that gave us away was not a word: it is that nobody in our world ever asks the player a question.
detail: Two sealed comparison packs had been sitting unanswered because the people who built them were not allowed to grade them. A fresh judge answered all twenty, wrote the answers to disk and hashed them before opening the key, and got every one right. That sounds bad and half of it is. Across the ten conversation pairs our characters used four question marks and Morrowind's used seventy-six; ours used no exclamation marks at all. A rule as dumb as 'whichever side asks fewer questions is theirs' gets nine out of ten, which makes it a sharper giveaway than the word 'eleven' ever was - and unlike 'eleven' you cannot fix it by swapping words, because asking somebody a question means writing a character who wants something from them. The second giveaway is stranger: our writing never lets a line be boring. Every single one lands a joke or a twist. Morrowind's people mostly say flat things like 'He's a bookworm. Try a bookseller.' - and that is exactly why its good lines land. A hundred punchlines in a row read the same as none. The other half of the result is better news than the score: on the book excerpts the judge thought our writing was the better of the two four times out of five, and said so in writing before finding out which was which. We are not producing filler. We are producing something identifiable. Two specific faults came out of it. The 180 dialogue lines rewritten last week genuinely do sound more like speech, and they proved it by moving a measure that a find-and-replace physically cannot move - but they invented a brand new tic on the way, a sentence starting 'Which is...' that we now use eleven times more often than Morrowind does, and they over-applied so hard that the rewritten lines no longer match the untouched ones around them. And the hundred lines of dialogue written after the clean-up was finished have the whole problem back at full strength, including the filler 'eleven's - 'eleven years', 'eleven chairs of wear on the floor', 'asked her eleven times' - none of which is a number anybody can count. That is not a writing problem any more. It is a missing check: a rule fixed once and not enforced by something that runs decays within hours. One last thing the judge found and could not have found by reading: the packs themselves leak. The reference passages still had wiki markup and place names in them, so a lazy judge could have scored seventeen out of twenty by counting the word 'Vvardenfell' without reading a syllable. Only three of the twenty pairs were genuinely clean, and the honest number is three out of three, not twenty out of twenty.
where: corpus/90-verdicts/wave1/W1-PROSE-BLIND-r1.md

headline: Calibrate an odd controller once and the game kept applying that controller’s button layout to every controller you plugged in afterwards — so on a perfectly normal pad the button that should open a door made you roll instead. Found only because a test that had been failing for a whole round was finally made to say WHY it was failing.
detail: Measured: teach an unrecognised pad its buttons (six presses), unplug it, plug in a standard one — button 0 fired 'roll' and button 5 fired 'lock on'. After a one-line fix they fire 'interact' and 'light', and a pad you have calibrated before still remembers its own layout when it comes back. Deleting the fix brings roll and lock-on straight back. The test that caught it (“can you re-map your controls using only a gamepad?”) had been red for a round and everyone assumed the re-mapping screen was broken; it was fine. It now proves the pad in front of it actually works before it judges anything, and if it cannot, it says so instead of blaming the screen. Same round: the tool’s own repair for half-started test runs had a typo that made it throw every single time, so five results read “could not measure” beside forty that measured fine. reports/W1-08-W1-29-R2.md

headline: The woman at the desk now tells you the one thing the game had never said out loud — that in this province nobody volunteers anything, so you have to ask — and she hands you the nine words to ask with, which until today nobody in Argonia would answer.
detail: Morrowind gives you nine topics at character creation and every stranger in the game will talk about all nine. We had copied the nine words into a file and then, measuring it: the player was given none of them, seven of the nine were advertised by literally zero of the 336 people in the province, and the three people in the opening could not have answered a single one if asked, because every answer that had been written was written for six kinds of speaker and none of them are the kinds who work a barge or a government desk. So the scene that is supposed to teach you that asking is how this game works was the one scene where asking was impossible. Now: the writ is stamped, the nine words go in your pocket, and the clerks and villagers of Argonia have something to say to all nine. Asking the Warden-Scribe her nine questions hands the player ten further keywords, one of which is the phrase that opens the main quest from a cold start. Two of this piece's own measuring instruments were also wrong and both were caught by running them: the tool written to prove the checks can fail had never once finished, dying on a typo before it could report; and the number for 'how long can you just be a body before the game asks who you are' was reading a stopwatch left running from a previous scene, which is why it said minus half a second while the same report said the scene had not asked anything yet. reports/journeys/w1-26-r2-asking.json

headline: Killing things now pays you souls. Until today it didn't — you could fight the whole game and never earn a single one, so the levelling screen was a shop with an empty wallet, and the only souls in existence were the ones a test handed you.
detail: Everything downstream of souls was already built and correct: the price of every level from 2 to 140, the screen you spend at, all 29 sapwells, dropping your souls where you died and picking them back up. The one thing missing was the way in. A builder looking for something else spawned an ambush, killed five of six men, and watched the counter go from zero to zero with the next level costing 418. What each enemy is worth is now worked out from its own statistics — how much punishment it soaks, how hard it hits, whether it is a mob or a champion — rather than typed in by hand, with a single number tuned so an ordinary marsh sentry is worth the 136 souls the design document says an average early kill should be. Everything else falls out of that: a champion is worth 2,423, and the 99,999-hitpoint training dummy is worth nothing at all, which stops it being a machine that prints levels. The whole loop now works end to end: six men in the opening ambush pay 816 souls, which buys your second level with 398 in hand toward the third; fight at night and everything pays 35% more; walk to a sapwell, rest, spend, and the point you bought raises your maximum health enough that a blow which would have killed you leaves you standing on 12. Save the game, load it, and the level is still there in the world you are playing rather than only in the file. Twelve separate checks confirm it, and each was run twice — once with the code working and once with it deliberately switched off — because a soul counter that only ever reads a number a test wrote is not proof of anything. Switched off, eight of the twelve go red. The honest headline is what this exposes rather than what it fixes: every hand-placed enemy in the world put together is worth 1,224 souls, which is level three. The plan calls for about 1,230 enemies and a first playthrough ending around level 82. The economy is now correct and the world is empty.

headline: We finally ran the whole death-and-recovery run in one go instead of ten separate tests, and it caught two things every separate test had missed — the worst being that the glowing pile of souls you died on can't actually be seen from most directions you'd walk up to it from.
detail: The death loop is a Dark Souls idea: die, drop everything you were carrying on the spot, walk back and pick it up. Every individual check on it passed. Run all thirty-seven together, though, and two go red. First: stand six metres from your own dropped souls in the dark and the picture is pixel-for-pixel identical to the picture with your back to them. Only three of eight approach angles show anything at all; in daylight from twelve metres it is one of eight. You are being asked to walk back to a thing that isn't drawn. Second: die twice in a row and there is nothing on the ground at all, where the rule says there should always be exactly one pile. Separately, we opened the levelling screen — the fix this round was built for, and it does now open at every sapwell and take the right price — and looked at what's behind it. It lists ten attributes. The character has six, and they are not the same six: three of the character's real attributes aren't on the screen at all and can never be raised, while seven of the rows are for attributes the character doesn't have and buying one invents it out of nothing. Two of the three demonstrations the builder itself shipped bought attributes in that second group. And on the starting state used for all of that testing, spending 37,652 souls across twenty-four levels moved the character's maximum health, stamina and magic by exactly zero — the same spends move all three when a character has been properly created first, so the screen works and the state it was tested in doesn't. One good piece of news: the builder's own new safety catch, which refuses to measure anything if the world has silently stopped, was real. We deliberately sabotaged it and it went red, and our live run proved it was needed — the test runner really was handing this stage a frozen world with an inventory screen left open.
where: corpus/90-verdicts/wave1/W1-13-r2.md; reports/journeys/critic-w1-13-r2-jrn06/journey.json

headline: The people who hand out quests were not in the game. You could learn the right words, walk to the right town and find the room empty — all ninety-four quests had a name attached and nine of those people existed anywhere you could stand. Now all of them do, and a quest given by nobody can no longer be accepted.
detail: The last two rounds of work went into letting a player hear about a job the way you would in a real town — a rumour in a tavern, someone complaining about a guar standing in a yard — and it all worked. What nobody had checked was whether the person you were being sent to existed. The game had 336 written-down inhabitants and twelve of them were actually standing anywhere: four in Helstrom, three in Stormhold, five in Soulrest, none at all in Thorn. Every count of 'how many quests can a player find' had been taken by asking the rulebook rather than the world, and the rulebook never asked whether anyone was home; one of the test tools even conjured the missing person out of thin air so its run could continue, and said so in a comment. Two halves had to land together. First the people: every quest-giver now has a post — a spot outside a real building's door in their own town, the fence at the low market, the herbwife on the market row — and a day, so they are at that post through working hours and in the hall or the tavern at night. Four towns that had quests but no way to visit them now have one. Second the rule: accepting a quest now checks that the person offering it is actually in the world, and refuses with 'giver absent' if not. Measured: quest-givers you can walk up to and talk to went from 9 of 94 to 120 of 120, and on the exact four towns the original test used, from 9 to 52 with no new place counted. The proof that this is real rather than bookkeeping is that deleting one line of the fix puts the number back to exactly 9, with 0 of the side quests and 0 of the faction quests — the same figures the original inspection reported. The honest cost: the headline 'ten quests findable from a standing start' becomes seven, because three of the ten were quests the game would have offered you with nobody there to say the words to. Also fixed along the way: the one camera angle in the project named 'settlement street' was pointed at an empty patch of ground 3.8 km from the nearest town and had been used as a picture of a settlement (the two shots above are the same viewpoint before and after), and the six things the very first two characters in the game invite you to ask about — your hatch-name, the writ, the list — had no answers written for them at all.

headline: The three guilds got twice as many quests and they are good ones — but the report card saying so was filled in an hour before the game started checking whether the person handing out the quest is actually in the room, and re-running it today fails half the checks it says it passed.
detail: Round one found that you could complete a guild's final quest without having joined the guild. That is properly fixed, and while fixing it the builder found a worse one hiding underneath: merely HEARING about a quest used to lock you out of ever starting it, so knowing too much destroyed the job. Fixed too, saves included. The guilds also went from nine quests each to eighteen, and the new two-thirds is as well written as the old third — a rank-0 errand about weighing a coil of rope dry that quietly reveals a whole barge nobody accounts for; an empty room where 'a man who left in a hurry leaves his things, a man whose things were taken leaves dust on a floor somebody swept first'. And a faction rank now genuinely changes what a guard does: join the smugglers and the city watch lets you carry a bigger debt before it arrests you, join the interior and it arrests you sooner. That last one was a rule with nothing behind it a round ago. What fails is the paperwork. An hour after these numbers were taken, a different piece of work fixed something separate — quest-givers who did not exist anywhere you could stand — and added a rule that you cannot accept a quest from somebody who is not there. The guild test never boots a town, so it now walks through an empty world: re-run it unchanged today and it scores 8 out of 16 instead of 16 out of 16. The proudest claim of the round, that the player earns every point of guild reputation by doing the work rather than being handed it, flips to the test writing seven reputation values in by hand. The guild quest-givers themselves are all present and correct — 62 out of 62, better than the main story — so this is a broken measuring stick, not broken content. Also found: a habit of writing the number eleven got WORSE in the new material, not better, after a sweep had already flagged it; one new quest uses 'eleven' nine times, is titled after it, and contains the line 'she said the number eleven three times'. And a safety check that catches a quest claiming to be peaceful while requiring a fight has quietly gone blind to 44% of the new endings, because they use five words for what-you-did that the checker has never heard of.

headline: The province had eighty-seven weapons in it and not one book about any of them — so we wrote the missing library: forty-three texts of drill manuals, arms-masters, bill-men and bowyers, including two accounts of the same battle that cannot both be true.
detail: The game's library was 70 books and it was entirely clerical: ledgers, treatises, liturgy, complaints about paperwork. Ranked against the game's own list of skills, the books about axes and maces, about two-handed weapons and about shields scored literally zero — no book in the world mentioned any of them. That is a strange thing for a place with eighty-seven named weapons and a combat system built on them. So this round wrote the culture of arms that was missing: an Imperial drill regulation whose most dangerous rule turns out to rest on a battle that the Empire's own records cannot find; the serjeant who has written in the back of his own copy for nine years asking them to change one word; an arms-master in Gideon who is comprehensively wrong about why the young men keep beating him; a swordsman from Anvil who despises the axe and, in the course of being rude about it, teaches it better than anyone else in the game; the bill-man he was rude about, answering; a shell-cutter who found out on the worst afternoon of his life that the stroke he uses forty times a day to open shellfish also takes a shield off a man's arm. Six texts argue about one afternoon in the year 391 and none of them agrees with another, which is the point. Every skill in the game now has at least one book that teaches it — and a book that teaches is a real object here, not a label: reading one raises that skill by a level the first time. The other half of the round was measurement. Our books are compared against the 241 real Morrowind books we have text for, and the new writing pushed four of the five shape numbers onto Morrowind's own figures. It also broke two things, both caught by checks somebody else had written and both worth naming: the corpus's spread of sentence rhythm collapsed, because it turned out we had written a serjeant, a hunter, a quartermaster and a gentleman at exactly the same pace — our pace — and ten of the texts had to be re-voiced before they sounded like different people; and a habit an earlier sweep had scrubbed out of every book in the game came straight back in a hundred and sixty-one places, which is the clearest evidence yet that a writing rule nobody's tools enforce lasts about an afternoon on a busy project.

headline: The book that says what is true in this world had never been opened by the game — and when we checked, not one of the province's six arguments had both sides spoken by anybody who actually lives there.
detail: reports/lore/W1-23-registry-report.md — the registry now ships into the game, 21 disputes have both sides held by real books and real people, and asking a Deep-Kin elder and a Ledger clerk the same question gets two answers that nothing in the game corrects.

headline: Every line our characters spoke ended with a punchline, and a hundred punchlines in a row read exactly like none at all — so we made most of them boring on purpose, and built a check that keeps them that way.
detail: A blind judge said the giveaway was that nobody in our world ever asks the player a question (4 question marks against Morrowind's 76) and that every single line lands a joke. Both are now measured by tools/check-prose.mjs, which warns when a file drifts back — it caught a file another agent wrote during this very session. Two files rewritten line by line: 186 lines of dialogue. Full numbers in orchestration/status/W1-PROSE-R2.json.

headline: The sun never moved and it never rained: the world's clock and its weather could only be changed by hand, by us, from a debug command. Now the world runs itself — and its thirteen regions no longer swap into one another at an invisible line.
detail: Two things in this game looked finished and were not. The time of day was set to noon when the game started and stayed there forever: nothing in the world ever advanced it, and the only way to make the sun move was for a developer to type a command. Weather was worse - each of the thirteen regions had a list of its own weather written down, and no part of the game ever read it. There was no such thing as the weather changing. Both now run inside the simulation itself: a full day and night takes 72 real minutes, and every region has its own four-state weather that rolls on its own schedule and means something - the Deep Marshes' thick fog cuts what you can see to 25 metres, a salt-storm in the Stone Wastes to 60 and takes 2 health a second, the Hive's queen-agitation doubles how far its drones will chase you. Left alone for five minutes the world walked the clock from 09:00 to 10:07 and turned the Western Rootlands' dawn mist into heavy rain with nobody asking it to, and a character standing in the open is twice as visible at noon as at one in the morning because the same clock feeds the sneaking system. The second half is the borders. Every one of the thirteen regions used to end at a single invisible line where the ground, the plants, the animals, the buildings, the sound, the sky, the danger and the region's one unique landmark all changed in the same footstep - the cheapest possible border and the most obviously artificial. There are now 24 real borders, and the nine things that make a region itself hand over at nine different places spread across up to 116 metres, in a deliberate order: the ground and the plants change first, the creatures and the sound in the middle, the buildings and the landmark last. In the middle picture above you are standing in a place that is neither region - the earth and the trees are already the Western Rootlands while the wildlife, the danger and the ruins are still the Stone Wastes behind you. Fourteen of the 24 borders are a ridge or a shore you can see from far off; the other ten carry a marker somebody built, and there are eight different peoples' markers in the province, from an Imperial cairn nobody has maintained to a corpse in a cage that the Dres put up as a warning. Seven borders where the danger jumps by two tiers or more now announce it twice over before you cross.

headline: Forty-three books about fighting had been written for a province that had never written one, and not a single person in any of them ever asked a question or raised their voice; now every one of them does, and the two loudest have been quietened.
detail: A blind reader had already worked out what gives our writing away, and it was not a word: our characters never ask anything and never shout, and every sentence closes on a clever line. The forty-three new martial texts were written before that check existed, and when it was pointed at them it found the same thing - twenty-seven of the forty-three contained no question and no raised voice anywhere in them, while all eighteen exclamation marks in the whole set were piled into one 2,000-word file of songs and scraps. Three of those scraps were also in the wrong book: a drill chant that is the mnemonic for a rule printed six pages away, a soldier's unsent letter about being frightened a day late, and a duelling challenge whose reply was already sitting in another volume. Moving them where they belonged fixed four of the faults on its own. The rest was writing: a rice-cutter who is furious, a bowyer quoting the sales patter her father used for forty-one years, an Assize clerk whose questions are finally punctuated as questions, and a Bravil penny-romance that now has the exclamation marks a penny-romance has - which the cohort clerk who hates it duly counts in his rebuttal. Contractions were the other half. Three texts had been contracted at twice the rate real speech is written at while twenty-seven others had none at all, so everybody in the library was either a Legate or a bargeman with nothing in between; a soldier's memoir in three volumes now contracts like a proud man of 31 in the first and a careful man of 61 in the third, which is the joke the second volume had been waiting to land. All seven files now pass the check with no warnings and the whole project's count of prose faults fell from 157 to 117.
where: orchestration/status/W1-LIBRARY-MARTIAL.json; node tools/check-prose.mjs (7/7 martial files clean); book-stats 16/16 and book-budget 22/22 PASS at 117 texts; canon-census 21/21 disputes voiced

headline: Combat had no sound at all. It has twelve now - flesh, chitin, shield, parry, a miss - and the first thing we did after switching them on was catch two of them lying: the parry chime was so loud it was distorting, and the sound of your own sword landing was glued to your feet instead of to the thing you hit.
detail: Until today a fight in this game was silent, which is the single biggest reason a swing did not feel like a swing - in a Souls game the sound tells you what happened before the animation does. There are now twelve distinct impact sounds, each with four variations so you never hear the same one twice in a row, and the fight itself picks them: hit a soft target and it is wet and short, hit a chitin-plated one and it is a bright hard skid, hit a raised shield and it is a damped thud with the crack taken out. We proved the fight is really choosing, rather than a sound being played on a timer, by swinging at four different creatures with the same button presses and the same random seed and watching the sound change - and by walking the target out of range, at which point every swing became the noise of a blade in empty air. Then we recorded the sounds properly, because a number in a file is not a sound. Two things were wrong and neither was visible from the code. The parry chime - meant to be the loudest, clearest thing in the game because it is the one that tells you that you survived - was actually recorded above the maximum a speaker can reproduce, so it was clipping and distorting. And a miss was eight decibels quieter than it was supposed to be, close to inaudible, when the whole point is that hitting nothing and hitting something must not arrive at the same volume. All forty-eight sounds are now measured and levelled, and the ladder from the parry at the top to the miss at the bottom is exact to a hundredth of a decibel. The second bug is the one worth reading twice. A hit is supposed to come from where the weapon met the body, so a blow landed to your left arrives in your left ear. It was coming from where the ATTACKER was standing - which, for every blow you land, is your own feet. The consequence: the sound of your own sword hitting a man swung across the stereo field when YOU turned your head, and did not move at all when the man did. It survived because nobody had tested it against a target that moves. Standing an enemy directly in front of you and hitting it gives a dead-centre sound, which is exactly what a correct system produces, so the test passes and tells you nothing. We put the enemy on an orbit and swung at it as it went past: the fixed version tracks the target almost perfectly, and the old one scores worse than random - the sound was swinging the wrong way. Both faults now have a switch that turns them back on deliberately, so the tests that catch them can be seen failing rather than trusted.

headline: The province had two hundred and ten markers standing on its borders — a cairn, a gate grown out of a root, a corpse in a cage — and the game drew not one of them. Now they are there, you can walk up to them, and you cannot walk through them.
detail: Last round gave the thirteen regions real borders: instead of everything changing at one invisible line, the ground and the plants hand over first, then the animals and the sound, then the buildings and the region's one unique landmark, spread across up to a hundred metres. Part of that was supposed to be a thing somebody BUILT at the frontier — 210 of them, eight kinds, each belonging to a different people. They were written down and nothing drew them. Two hundred and ten sets of coordinates with an owner each, invisible. This round built them. An Imperial border cairn that has been leaning for years and has already shed its top block, because the Empire does not come out here any more. An Argonian root gate, two roots crossing above head height with strands hanging through the gap, grown rather than stacked. A villagers' tide pole notched at every tide anyone thought worth remembering. Three thorn stems lashed into a tripod and blazed with a knife by the people who cut the paths. Kiln slag from the naga, still warm enough to see at night. A line of five ribs off something big, set upright. A branch of glass the lightning made, that nobody put there at all. And on the seven borders where the danger jumps by two whole steps, a gibbet the Dres put up with somebody still in it — the picture above is one, standing in Blackwood looking into the Deep Marshes, where the danger goes from two to five. This matters more than decoration because of what the map is allowed to be here: it shows only ground you have already walked and squares for places you have personally stood in, and nothing can put a marker on it. So nothing in the interface can tell you that you are about to leave one region for a much worse one. The only thing that can is what is standing at the edge. All eight shapes are different from each other and from all thirteen of the regions' unique landmarks — measured, not asserted, using a comparison that throws colour and size away and looks only at shape. They are solid: walk a body straight at the gibbet and it stops 1.08 metres short, while the same walk through the line of ribs steps over it and carries on. And one thing we found and did not fix, because it is not ours to fix: the border data says the first dangerous thing beyond a big jump in danger should be at least forty metres past the line, so a person has room to read the warning and turn round. Nothing in the game had ever read that number. We measured it against the creatures the game actually puts in the world and five of the seven big jumps fail it — at the Blackwood/Deep-Marshes border the first drowned host stands 0.8 metres past the line, which means you read the warning and meet the thing in the same footstep.

headline: The file that describes the camera - every number about where it sits behind you, how far back, how fast it turns - was being loaded when the game started and then thrown away, so the camera had been ignoring its own instructions all along. It obeys them now, and the first time we actually looked through it in a fight we found it staring at the floor.
detail: There are ninety-seven numbers that describe this game's camera: how high above your feet it pivots, how long the arm behind your shoulder is, how wide the lens is, how quickly a flick of the stick turns the view. They were all written down carefully in a file, and they were all ALSO typed into the code by hand - and it was the hand-typed copies the game actually used. Editing the file changed nothing anybody could see. That makes it the fifteenth system in this project shipped with a careful model nothing reads, and the first one in the part of the game you are literally looking through. The camera now reads the file, and rather than promise that, we proved it: we edited the file on disk five times and watched the picture change each time. Raising the pivot by a metre and a half raised it by exactly a metre and a half; halving the arm put the camera at half the distance; widening the lens from 50 to 90 degrees moved a fixed point in the world from a quarter of the way across the frame to a tenth, which is precisely the number the trigonometry predicts; quartering the turn speed made a held stick sweep exactly a quarter as far. Then we ran the same test again with the edits written to a file the game does not open, and all five went red - which is how you know the test can fail. Two things were broken along the way and both had been hiding a long time. The stick response - the deadzone and the curve that decides how far a half-pushed stick turns you - had been written and connected years of commits ago, but the one word that lets a test drive it was missing from a list, so nothing in the project could reach it and the comparison method that measures it had been filed as 'this game does not have one'. It does. And the moment we photographed a real lock-on fight rather than measuring it, the actual defect walked out: against a large enemy the camera settles at exactly fifty degrees of downward tilt - the hard floor, the furthest down it is allowed to look - so you spend the fight looking at the tops of everyone's heads, and when you land the killing blow it keeps that angle and leaves you facing the ground. Every automated check passes on that frame, because 'both fighters are on screen' is true. It just is not a fight you can read. The cause looks to be that the camera is correctly framing a four-and-a-half-metre boss that the renderer draws at the same size as everyone else.
where: orchestration/status/W1-06.json; reports/w1-06/cam-consume.json (6/6) and cam-consume-falsify.json (all perturbation checks red by design); reports/w1-06/cam-death-in-lock.json; tools/camera/cam-consume.mjs, cam-death-in-lock.mjs, cam-shots.mjs; game/src/sim/camera.js applyCameraRig()

headline: The province makes thirteen genuinely different sounds now, where a week ago it had no audio code at all - but the bell buoy you are meant to steer by in the fog is completely silent, and turning it up forty decibels changes the recording by not one sample.
detail: Until this piece there was no sound in this game whatsoever - no audio code, not one music or effect file on disk, and the only thing with 'sound' in its name was the maths for how far a guard can hear you sneaking. Eight of the nine ways we were scoring audio were reading lists of made-up filenames out of a spreadsheet. That is fixed: all thirteen regions now build their own soundscape out of nothing but arithmetic, four layers deep - the floor you always hear, the moving texture on top of it, the things that punctuate it, and the animals - and it follows you around the world properly, so the sound changes when the ground under your feet changes. I checked the big claim with my own instrument rather than trusting theirs, and it holds: all seventy-eight possible pairs of regions are measurably different, a mountain does not sound like a mire, and twelve of the thirteen sit within a twentieth of a decibel of the loudness they were aimed at. Two things I found. The first is the one the builder wrote down honestly as 'I could not work out why this is happening': the master volume knob on each region was not behaving like a volume knob - turning it down two decibels moved the loudness, the peak and the brightness of the sound by three different amounts, which is impossible for a volume knob. It took rendering the same region twice, once with a single wobble removed, to find it. There is a slow shimmer on Valus Ridge's rock-flute chord, and the amount of shimmer was being worked out BEFORE the volume knob was applied and then never turned down with it. So at Valus Ridge's setting the shimmer is now half again as big as the sound it is shimmering - it swings the whole chord past silence and out the other side, inside out, every nine seconds. A gentle wobble is running at nearly four times its intended depth, and that is what you would actually hear. It is three lines to fix. The second is worse. Four places in the world are supposed to make a noise you can find them by - a bell buoy off Marauder's Coast you can hear from six hundred metres, a legion horn on the hour in the Salt Hills, the kilns on the Clay Moor, a hide-drum in the Western Rootlands. This game deliberately refuses to put markers on your map, and those four sounds are the replacement: the way you work out where you are when you cannot see. Every frame, the game carefully works out how far away the bell is and which ear it should be in, writes those numbers down, counts it as one of the eight sounds it is allowed to play - and never plays it. I turned the bell up by forty decibels, which is roughly a hundredfold, and the recording came back identical down to the last bit. Then I did the same to the sea itself as a check, and it blew the recording apart, so the test works. The code that rings the bell exists and does ring it - nothing in the game has ever called it. So a player lost in fog on that coast today hears nothing at all to steer by. Two smaller things worth knowing: nobody has ever recorded the world at night, so the rule that night must be a different set of sounds rather than the day turned down has never once been checked; and the bell, whenever somebody does plug it in, is currently set to ring every thirteen seconds, which the design document itself says is the point at which a landmark stops being a landmark and becomes an annoyance.

headline: Every enemy in the game was paying more than twice what it should, so finishing the whole game would have handed you the level the design says nobody should ever reach on a first run — the values are re-derived, and a marsh sentry now pays 64 souls instead of 136.
detail: corpus/90-verdicts/wave1/W1-SOULS-r1.md (the verdict that returned it) and reports/souls-consumption.json — 15 of 15 checks pass, including the first one that kills an enemy by actually swinging a sword at it rather than by telling it to die. Two other things were broken and are fixed: dying in a swamp gas trap paid nothing and brought the corpse back to life, and you could farm the same enemies for ever by walking away and walking back.

headline: The whole of Black Marsh contained nine enemies — every one hand-typed into a save file by somebody who remembered to — and now the country populates itself as you walk through it: 144 ambush points, 267 bodies, and a walk down the main road that costs you 446 health without you ever swinging back.
detail: reports/world/population/consumption.json — walking 1,229 m brought ten groups into being, ten more than the same walk with the system switched off; the enemies you leave behind stay dead until you rest at a fire, and none of the province's 49 named people were touched by any of it. Clearing every placed enemy once is now worth level 16, against level 2 before.

headline: The tool that decides whether this game can be finished has now been rejected five rounds running, and each round it fixed the exact fault it was told about and shipped a new one of the same shape - a confident number measuring nothing. This round the detector built to catch a dead race term was defeated three more ways, the simplest being to kill the whole race table and leave one person's small same-race bonus alive, which is enough for the tool to declare the build sound.
detail: Round 5 did real work: four invented constants (a character with a billion gold and perfect standing with everyone) are genuinely gone, replaced by sums over what the game's own files can actually give you, and that alone surfaced eighteen requirements the game asks for that nothing in the game produces - six items and topics, twelve faction-rank flags - which I checked myself and which are real. But the fixes all share one shortcut: a count standing in for a check. It reports 'zero substitutions remaining' by counting a list on which nothing is ever labelled a substitution. It abstains on 495 of 540 characters by counting factions rather than testing whether any three of them can actually be joined at once - I built a version of the world where no three factions can EVER coexist, and the tool's output was identical to the healthy one. The guard it advertises as its defence against exactly this never runs at all: zero times in 540. And the detector that proves the game really does treat a Dark Elf differently from a Nord only asks 'did any number move', so I froze the race table for everyone, left one dunmer merchant's five-point kinship bonus alive, and the tool certified the build sound and published its verdicts. Swapping the two races over produced output identical to the correct build in every field. Finally I ran the tool's own self-test to the end for the first time - it takes 37 minutes and its author had never finished it - and it fails, including the one check that exists to prove the faction test can fail at all. It cannot.
where: corpus/80-methods/TOOL-COVERAGE-R4.md and .json; orchestration/status/tool-critic-r4.json; commit 0b2d6ef; boot-check PASS before and after; C8 = 26

headline: A blind listener test got all 32 comparisons right — every region in the world is clearly its own place — but the same test found that nothing ever happens in any of them: across 21 minutes of recorded ambience there was not one bird, drip, gust or creak, just a steady hum whose colour changes as you walk from one region to the next.
detail: corpus/90-verdicts/wave1/W1-22-B2-blind.md — 32/32, separation 1.0000, false-different rate 0.0000 over 8 hidden same-place controls, answers hashed (fc40b46e...) before the key was opened. The 13 region beds sort into four tone families from a 112 Hz rumble to a 3.5 kHz hiss, and stereo width swings from fully wide to flatly mono with no apparent design behind it. Two catches: the pack leaks its own answer shape (JUDGE.md sits inside the pack and states the 24/8 split that PROMPT.md promises the judge is not told), and its declared integrity hash no longer matches its contents because the loudness leak was fixed by editing the file instead of rebuilding it. And a perfect score is the finding, not the win — a plain threshold scores the same 32/32, so this pack cannot tell a judge from a calculator, and the thing a player really recognises a place by is exactly the thing it shows is missing.

headline: The roads now light themselves at night — a lamp on every shelter and crossroads post, burning the colour of the country it stands in — because before this you could walk the whole 7 km main road after dark and never pass a single lit thing.

headline: Verdicts used to say what they measured but not how long that measurement stays true while a dozen other people keep changing the game underneath it. Every verdict now names the exact files it depends on, and a new tool checks each one against the current code and says fresh, stale, or honestly unknown — right now 1 of 33 verdicts is still standing on the code as it is today, 28 have been overtaken by someone else's later change, and 4 never said what they depended on so nobody can judge them yet. Nothing gets deleted or marked down for going stale — it's a heads-up for whoever plans the next round, not a punishment.

Wired into tools/publish.mjs and tools/progress.mjs as a REPORTED NUMBER, not a gate, following tools/check-quests.mjs's own precedent against a shared check that fails everyone's build over one piece's commit.

headline: A correction to the last number we posted about Black Marsh's population: the economy underneath it was re-anchored while we were measuring, so clearing every enemy on the road now pays level 19, not 16 — and that is still a fifth of where a finished game needs to land (93), not because the road is under-filled but because five of our seven monster types are all sized the same and nothing tougher exists yet to place in the dangerous country.
detail: The placement machine itself needed no repair: re-running its own drift check against the current numbers came back clean, and the file that lists every ambush point on the road already matched what the generator would produce today. What changed is the value of the monsters standing in it — an economy-wide rebalance landed after our first count and every kill is worth a different amount now. The harder finding: running the game's own audit tool shows the whole province still has only five kinds of ordinary enemy and two oversized bosses, and none of the five is remotely tough enough for the dangerous half of the map — a swamp thug guarding the deadliest region on the continent is worth exactly what one guarding the safest region is worth, because it IS the same creature. That is a roster of monsters that has not been built yet, not a placement bug and not a pricing bug; our machine places bodies correctly against whatever roster exists, and today's roster stops at the first tier.
