headline: Resting six hours at a campfire was supposed to shut the shops, send everyone home for the night and make monsters worth more to kill. Nobody had ever checked that any of that happened. It does. And checking turned up the opposite problem: dying had quietly become a way to make money.
detail:
This game's design document contains a numbered test for the world clock, and it is written out in plain English: rest at five in the afternoon, then check that the clock reads eleven at night, that the night shift is on, that the shops are shut, and that any quest you are on the clock for has lost six hours. Then rest four more times and check you are back exactly where you started, a day later.

That test had never been run. Three previous rounds of work on this part of the game checked the first thing on the list - the clock says eleven - and nothing else. Nobody had ever confirmed that a single shop door closes, that a single person walks home, or that a rest changes anything at all beyond a number. It is the only test that decides this part of the game's score, and it was the reason the score would not move.

So it was run, all of it. Resting at five in the afternoon shuts 71 of the 115 shops and rooms that keep hours. Twenty-five people who are in the world at that moment are somewhere else afterwards - out of the street and into the inn. And an ordinary marsh creature that was worth 42 souls in the afternoon is worth 57 at eleven at night, which is the game's 35 per cent night bonus, correct to the last soul. Rest four more times and the clock comes back round to five in the afternoon on the next day with every one of those 71 doors open again and every one of those 25 people back where they started - not approximately, but the same list, unchanged.

Every one of those numbers is measured against a control that does everything the test does except rest: it steps the same handful of frames and then looks again. That control shuts zero shops and moves zero people. Without it, '71 shops closed' would only mean that time had passed.

And then the thing nobody was looking for. The previous round had fixed a real bug - the world clock was ticking while you lay dead on the ground, so dying at a boss over and over quietly ate your quest deadlines. It stopped the clock during death, which is what the design asks for. But the same clock is what decides whether it is night, and night is when kills pay more. So the minutes you spent dead cost you no night. Near the end of the night - the game's night ends at five in the morning - you could die repeatedly and keep the bonus that a living player would have lost. Measured: from half past four in the morning, forty deaths leave the very same creature paying 57 souls, where the identical stretch of time spent alive leaves it paying 42. Dying paid you 35 per cent more. That is exactly the kind of consolation prize this game is built never to give.

The reason nobody caught it is that the previous round compared the fixed game against the broken game, and never against a player who simply did not die. That comparison - same frames, alive - is the one that finds it.

The fix is a second clock. The world's clock still stops when you die, so your quest deadlines are still safe. But the clock that decides what a kill is worth keeps running whether you are alive or dead, and is reset to the world's clock every time you rest - so it can never drift far. The result is that dying now costs you nothing and pays you nothing: 42 against 42 at one end of the night, 57 against 57 at the other. Take the new clock back out and the unfairness comes straight back, in both directions. Meanwhile the deadline protection is untouched: forty deaths burn about a seventh of a second of world time with the fix in, and thirty-four minutes with the previous round's clock restored.

Two things I claimed in the last round turned out to be wrong, and both are now corrected in the code itself rather than only in a report. I had credited a change to how the bloodstain is drawn - lifting it onto the visible ground and giving it a glowing column - with making the bloodstain findable from every direction. It does not: with that change deleted the stain is still visible from all eight directions. The whole of that fix was a 19-centimetre correction to where the test camera's eye was, which had been sitting inside a boulder. What the drawing change does buy is a four- to sevenfold brighter reading, which is worth having and which a yes/no visibility count cannot see at all - so the check now scores that brightness against a floor, and deleting the drawing change turns the check red instead of leaving it green. The second wrong claim was that moving the camera's aim point mattered. It is worth nothing whatsoever.

Also reported rather than papered over: the design's fourth clause, 'any active timed quest has lost six hours', cannot be tested, because there are no timed quests in the game yet and the code that would fail one when its time runs out is never called by anything. Driven by hand it works perfectly. It simply has nothing wired to it.

And one honest no. One of the six conditions for the game being playable by its owner is reaching your first level-up without a test harness. It is not possible today, and this is measured rather than guessed: every one of the sixteen buttons the game defines was pressed, one at a time, from the world and from inside every screen it opens. They reach exactly two places - the world and your inventory. The game's own menu code advertises six destinations when you stand at a campfire, including the level-up screen, and five of the six have no door. That is one branch of code away from being fixed, but it belongs to the menu system rather than to this piece, so it is written down with the exact test it has to pass rather than changed here.

My own tool caught itself out twice on the way to that answer, which is worth recording: the first two versions of it pressed sixteen buttons and found nothing, both times because the presses were not landing rather than because the game had no door. Both wrong answers happened to be the right answer, which is the most dangerous way for a test to be broken.

headline: Every door in this game opened onto the same room, and walking through one did not change what was on your screen at all — the street stayed up while your body stood at the hearth, and walking back out left the room up while you stood in the road. All 115 doors did it. Both halves are fixed: the door now switches the picture on the frame you press it, and the picture is built from that building’s own file, so an alchemist’s shop in a dye town and a rotted great-hall in a village four kilometres away are no longer the same 249-triangle hall with different people standing in it.
detail:
This game has 115 named interiors — shops, inns, gaols, shrines, houses — behind 202 doors in eight towns. Two things were wrong with all of them at once, and the second one hid the first.

The first is the one that matters. Walking through a door did not change what was on your screen. The game correctly recorded that you were now inside The Crimson Apothecary, correctly moved your body to the spot just inside its door, and then carried on drawing the street. Walking back out was worse: your body was standing in the road and the screen was still showing the room. Every check the game had for this said it was fine, because every one of those checks asked where the player was, and the answer to that was always right. Nothing asked what was on the screen. All 115 doors did this; not one of them worked.

The second thing is that even if you forced the game to draw the room, there was only ever one room. 113 of the 115 interiors resolved to the same generic hall — the same hearth, the same six benches, the same beams — so an alchemist's shop in a dye town and a rotted Argonian great-hall in a village four kilometres away were the same picture with different people standing in it. Meanwhile the files describing those 115 rooms were extremely specific and completely unread: the apothecary's file lists 18 pieces of furniture, 10 lamps, a locked strongbox and one unique item, and the game drew a hearth and nothing else. Roughly two thousand pieces of furniture and thirty unique items existed only as text.

Both are fixed. Going through a door now switches the picture on the same frame you press the button, and going back out puts the street back. The room you arrive in is built from that building's own file: the walls are its real dimensions, the lamps are its real lamps in their real places, the furniture is its real furniture, and each of the eight towns has its own materials — Archon's dye-stained clay, Stormhold's legion blockwork, Helstrom's grown timber, Thorn's black needle-wood thatch — so two shops in two towns do not look alike. Rooms whose files mention a staircase get an upper floor. Shops big enough for one get a back room, because a shop that is one room with a counter is half a shop. The unique item each of 83 rooms declares is now a thing on a pedestal that you can walk up to and pick up.

The people were the other half. The game already moved them between rooms across the day — nine of Thorn's twenty-four change rooms between noon and three in the morning — but not one of them ever moved a millimetre. They were placed once when the town loaded and stayed there forever; a woman whose evening is spent at the tavern kept the position calculated inside her own house. The comment above that function claimed, in writing, that people "walk to the slot's anchor", and the function never touched anybody's position. Now it does: they cross the floor at walking pace when their day changes what they are doing, and they are put down where they belong when their day moves them to another building.

And they go outside. Before this, of the 347 people in the game, the only ones ever standing outdoors were 38 quest-givers belonging to another piece of work; at three in the morning there was not one person outdoors anywhere in the province, and none of this piece's own 260 townspeople ever stood on a street at any hour. Each of them now has a spot outside a real building's door in their own town, and a fifth of the day carved out to stand in it — a trading cohort out from nine to five, people going to and from work at the shoulders of the day, a group out in the evening, and a night watch, so that three in the morning is quiet rather than empty. 94 people are out at midday and 23 at 3 a.m., and the rest of everybody's day is untouched.

How I know it works rather than hope it does. The thing that let the first defect survive a whole round is that the tool checking it was made entirely out of the half that worked, so it could never have failed. That tool now reads the screen, and every new check in it is paired with a control that puts the old broken behaviour back and requires the reading to get worse: the sweep of all 115 doors is run twice, once normally and once with the connection cut, and the run passes only if the cut arm is worse. I also broke the tool that places people outdoors on purpose — shrinking a town to one metre across — and confirmed it refuses and names the fifteen people it can no longer place, then put the town back and checked that nothing was left changed in the repository.

Two things found on the way that were not what I was looking for. Rebuilding a room compiled new graphics shaders every time, which is a stutter at the exact moment a player presses a button on a doorstep, so rooms of the same type in the same town now share their materials. And the save file had never stored the outdoor station of a quest-giver at all, which meant every quest-giver came back from a saved game standing invisibly inside every locked cellar in the province — a bug from an earlier piece of work that only showed up because my own new field fell into the same hole.

Said plainly, what is not done: the outsides of the buildings. All 202 of them are still doors with nothing attached — the town's streets have no buildings drawn on them at all — so the townspeople this round put outdoors are standing on bare ground. That is the largest remaining piece and I did not attempt it.

headline: A blind taste test between our writing and Morrowind's turned out to be rigged by accident, and you could win it without reading a single word: just count the black bars. Every passage had its names blanked out to hide where it came from — and the real game's writing is so much denser with names that the blanks themselves gave the answer away, fifteen times out of fifteen.
detail:
The idea was simple and good. Take fifteen pairs of passages, one written for this project and one lifted from the real Morrowind, strip out every name so nobody can tell which is which, and hand them to a reader who has never seen either. If our writing is any good, a fair reader shouldn't be able to spot it.

The test had already been run once before and failed for an obvious reason: the real game's passages were full of words like Vvardenfell and Dunmer, so anyone could spot them instantly. So this round blanked out every name on both sides, replacing each with a marker like [NAME-7], and the person who built it re-ran the old cheat to prove it no longer worked.

It doesn't. But a new one does, and it is the same cheat wearing a hat. Morrowind's prose is thick with names — people, houses, towns, gods — and ours is mostly about offices, tides and ledgers. So after blanking, the real game's passages are covered in markers and ours are nearly clean. One pair had six markers on our side and thirty-nine on theirs. Another had forty-one against a hundred and twenty-nine. Count the markers, pick the sparser one, and you have identified our writing in all fifteen pairs without reading a sentence. Whatever that test was measuring, it wasn't quality.

Worse, the blanking tool is chewing the text while it works. It was mangling ordinary words it mistook for names — 'nevertheless', 'perhaps', 'sadly', even the letters of 'P.S.' — and dropping fragments as it went, so a line of Morrowind's arrived as 'said the landowner to the assembled ust not be doing so purely out of avarice'. Because that damage lands on whichever passage has more names in it, it always lands on the real game. The test was quietly vandalising the thing it was asking me to compare ours against.

And then the mistake I made myself, which is the part I'd rather record than bury. One pair put our writing against an old Morrowind story told as a letter. I marked the letter down for being a flat, plodding recap of events — a summary where there should have been a scene. Then the answers were revealed and I went back to it. The letter is dictated by a murderer standing over the body of the man whose name is signed at the bottom. The flatness is the murderer. Lines like 'It came as quite a surprise to her when he began strangling her' aren't lazy writing; they're a man being pleasant about a killing. I had marked down a voice for sounding exactly like the person it belonged to.

One more thing worth saying plainly, because it complicates the flattering version. I preferred our writing in fourteen of the fifteen pairs, which sounds like good news and mostly isn't — two thirds of what we were compared against wasn't really Morrowind's prose at all, but its quest log and its help text, the functional stuff written to keep a player from getting lost. Comparing a diary to a receipt and winning proves nothing. The honest finding runs the other way: a second reader and I, working separately, sorted the fifteen pairs into the same two piles every single time. Our writing is instantly recognisable, and the reason is that it has one habit and one voice. The habit is a see-saw sentence — 'He does not want the lease audited. He wants it laundered.' — and it turns up in nine of the fifteen. The voice is a dry, watchful, withholding official, and it is the voice of the magistrate, the trader, the swamp-dweller and the clerk alike. Morrowind's writing is worse than ours and more various than ours, and in a game where you meet forty people in an afternoon, the second thing may matter more than the first.

headline: Your money was never really your money. Selling stolen goods to a fence paid into one wallet, saving the game read from a second, and the inventory screen drew from a third that nothing ever filled — so it showed "0 gold" whether you had none or had just been handed 777. And training a lock-picking skill for hours never opened a single extra lock, because the number the locks actually check was frozen the day you started the game.
detail:
This piece covers the game's whole progression system — souls, levels, skills, carrying weight, gold — and it had never been worked on before today, so the first job was finding out what was actually true rather than assumed.

Gold turned out to be the worst of it. There were five different places in the code that each thought they were "how much gold the player has", and none of them talked to each other. Selling a stolen ring to a fence paid one of them. Paying a bribe spent a second. Buying a boat ticket spent a third, and because that third one gets rebuilt every time you rest or reload, a paid fare quietly refunded itself the next time you saved. The number the save file actually remembers is a fourth. And the screen that draws your inventory read a fifth field that nothing in the entire game ever writes to — which is why setting your gold to 777 and then looking at your own inventory still said zero. All five are now one number. Fencing, bribery, fares and the inventory screen all move the same purse, and a screenshot of the inventory after setting gold to 777 now genuinely shows 777.

Skills had a quieter version of the same problem. The game does track skill growth correctly — hit things with a sword and Blades goes up, pick a lock and Security goes up, and that part was already working. But the systems that are supposed to care about those numbers — which lock tiers you can pick, what a fence will pay you, how easily guards get suspicious of you — were all reading a second, private copy of your skills that got set once at the start of the game and never touched again, no matter how much you trained. A character who spent the whole game picking locks was, as far as every lock in the world was concerned, exactly as unskilled as the day they started. That copy now tracks the real one continuously, while still letting a scripted test pin a value on purpose when that's what the test needs.

Two things reported as already fixed by other work landed just before this piece started: the level-up screen used to offer ten attributes while the character underneath only had six, so three were unreachable and confirming certain choices invented brand-new, fictional attributes out of thin air. That is now genuinely resolved and was checked rather than taken on faith.

One big thing was found and deliberately left alone. A character's Strength, Intelligence and weapon skill are all supposed to affect how much damage a hit does — that's the whole point of a stat sheet. The formulas for it exist in the code, correctly written, and are called by nothing. Every weapon currently swings for the exact same damage regardless of the wielder's stats or skill. Fixing that properly means changing weapon data and the damage formula that another part of this project has spent many rounds carefully tuning, so instead of quietly breaking that work, it's written up and handed off with exact evidence of where the wiring is missing.

Also measured and left alone, correctly: carrying weight does slow you down when you're not fighting, and that's real and working. But the separate number that's supposed to make you roll worse in a fight when you're wearing heavy armour never reflects what you're actually wearing — it's stuck on a default. The mechanism that would react to it works fine; nothing feeds it a real number, and there's no armour-slot system yet for it to read from.

headline: Four problems other pieces found in the sneak-and-steal system this session, all confirmed and three fixed outright: loading a save left last session's onlookers standing in the new one, a bought-off guard cost real money that then vanished from your purse, some shops never locked their doors no matter the hour, and the streets people now walk at night were invisible to anyone trying to sneak past them.
detail:
This part of the game handles sneaking, theft, locks, witnesses and guards. Its own graded review two rounds ago found real problems and scored it a fail; this round was not about that review, it was about four specific claims other people working on the game made this session about defects in this system's area, each with a reason to believe rather than a guess. All four turned out to be real, and checking them properly meant reading the actual code rather than taking the claim at its word - one of the four turned out to already be half-fixed by someone else working at the same time, which was only discoverable by reading, not by assuming.

First: reloading a saved game did not clear out who was watching you. The list of nearby people, who they'd seen, and any in-progress search for a fugitive all belonged to whichever session was running before you clicked load, not to the save file you just opened. Fixed so a load now clears everyone in the room while leaving the actual crime record - your bounty, your stolen goods - exactly as the save says it should be.

Second: money. Selling stolen goods to a fence, bribing a witness, and paying off a bounty at a guard were all supposed to spend the same purse the save file writes down. The fence and the bribe already did, fixed by someone else earlier the same day. Paying off a guard did not: the deduction happened for exactly one instant and was silently undone the very next frame, so settling a bounty at the gate cost nothing at all against the money the game actually remembers you having. Now fixed the same way.

Third: a shop that is supposed to be locked at three in the morning sometimes wasn't, for no reason anyone had written down. Six shopkeepers in five different towns had their shop counted as part of their house rather than as its own building, so the game applied house hours - open all day, every day - to a room that was meant to keep a shop's. Measured directly: of the game's 66 rooms that are supposed to lock at night, 12 never did; now all 66 do.

Fourth, and the one worth a picture: a previous round of work this same session taught the townspeople to walk to work, come home, and stand outside at night instead of vanishing when nobody was looking at them. But the sneaking system - the part that decides whether someone sees you, hears you, or can be pickpocketed - had never been introduced to any of them. It had only ever been tested against people a scripted test put there by hand. In the actual, played game, a player creeping through a town at three in the morning had nobody real to sneak past. That is now wired together: anyone nearby and outdoors is a real target for the sneaking system, confirmed by asking the running game who it currently sees near the player in a town at that hour and getting back an actual person with a position, a direction they're facing, and whether they can presently see you - not an empty list.

One more thing was found but only partly fixed: the earlier graded review's single biggest complaint was that surrendering to a guard cost nothing, because the price was set to zero. That price is now a real number. What is still true, and said plainly rather than hidden, is that the guard still cannot fight back at all - that needs the game's enemy-behaviour system, which is somebody else's work and was itself being changed by another person at the same moment - so this is a partial answer to that complaint, not the whole one.

The game's shared files were being edited by dozens of people at once this session, hard enough that one change briefly vanished from disk and had to be re-checked and confirmed still present before this could be called done. Two of the four fixes above were confirmed inside the actual running game rather than only on paper before finishing.

headline: Argonians can finally hold their breath forever and fight in deep water, and you can now see the water on your own body — the line climbs your legs as the tide comes in, and I measured it landing within seven centimetres of where it should be. The trouble is what it's a line of: on the exact spot the last two rounds photographed, the game draws no water at all. You stand in nearly a metre of it, wet to the hip, on what looks like dry grass.
detail:
This piece is the water of Black Marsh: how deep it is, what wading costs you, and the promise that being an Argonian actually means something once your feet get wet. I came in fresh to check three things the previous round said it had fixed.

Two of them are genuinely fixed, and I checked them myself rather than taking anyone's word. An Argonian now really is a different animal in water: held under for seventy seconds a Nord runs out of breath and starts drowning, while the Argonian's breath meter never moves at all; swimming costs the Nord stamina and the Argonian none; and there is a band of chest-deep water where the Argonian can still swing a sword and everyone else cannot. Take the change back out and the old behaviour returns, which is how you know it is doing real work rather than just looking like it.

The waterline on your body is real too. I put the character in one spot, pointed one camera at it, and changed nothing but the tide. The dark wet band climbed from calf to thigh to waist, and when I counted the pixels that changed, every single one of them was on the character.

That last sentence is also the problem. Not one pixel of the *world* changed. The water in the landscape is baked when the ground around you is first built and then never updated, so the sea can rise more than a metre while the surface you see stays exactly where it was. And in the paddy country where the last two rounds took their photographs, the game only draws water in patches at least twelve and a half metres across — so all the narrow channels, which is most of the water there, are simply never drawn. About half the water in that region does not exist on screen. Your legs go dark and the ground stays green.

There is more. The game promises wet skin that stays wet for twenty seconds after you climb out and dries visibly; I photographed a character one second after standing in a metre of water and a character who had been dry all along, and the two pictures were identical down to the last byte. Four kinds of creature are supposed to be at home in deep water and dangerous there; two of the four cannot attack at all, anywhere, so they are scenery. And the tide, which is meant to exist in exactly five coastal regions, turns out to run in five more that are supposed to have none — including a mountain, and the deep marsh the design describes as having no tide whatsoever.

That last one is on the item's own list of things that fail the piece outright no matter what else is right, so the score is 2 out of 10. It is a harsh number for a round that did good work, and both halves of that are true. The pattern underneath it is worth naming: this round carefully measured the thing it built, and never measured the thing it built it against.

headline: Two of the game's design documents had been quietly ordering opposite things about how a weapon swings, and the note describing the clash said 107 weapon attacks were caught in it. The 107 turned out to be a rough tally that had been copied forward until it read like a measurement — and the real problem was never 107 obscure attacks. It was five of the game's fifteen weapon classes, named on the front page of the document that defines them.
detail:
The project is written as a set of design documents, and they are meant to be the one thing that does not quietly move. When two of them contradict each other, nobody is allowed to just pick one and carry on — the clash is referred to an arbiter, who has to decide it in writing and say plainly what is being given up.

This clash was about swinging a weapon. One document sets how wide an arc each weapon sweeps and how long it is: a curved greatsword spins almost the whole way round, a whip reaches three and a half metres, a dagger barely reaches one. The other document sets how fast the tip of a weapon is allowed to travel. The trouble is that those are not two separate facts. Once you know how wide the swing is, how long the weapon is, and how long the swing lasts, the speed of the tip is already decided — there is nothing left over to adjust. So one document was specifying the arc and the other was, without meaning to, forbidding it.

The note that referred the problem said 107 attacks were stuck between the two rules with no way out. Redoing the arithmetic from scratch showed that number was not a measurement of anything. It came from a working note that had counted how many attacks were more than twice over the speed limit — a rough severity tally — and a later summary rewrote that as "those last are the ones no tuning reaches", which is a completely different claim. The two groups barely overlap: of the 107, only about 31 were genuinely stuck, roughly 94 were easy fixes, and around 121 genuinely stuck attacks were not on the list at all. The count was nearly right and the list of which weapons were actually affected was almost entirely wrong.

Why nobody caught it is the human part. There is a second, unrelated 107 sitting one paragraph away in the same file, counting something else entirely. A number that looks independently confirmed is the last number anyone thinks to re-derive, and these two had no relationship whatsoever. It is a good argument for checking the figures that look safest first.

The more important finding was that the clash was never in a tail of obscure attacks. Checking the speed limit against the headline table of the weapons document — the one that lists all fifteen weapon classes and says what each one is for — showed that five of them could never have satisfied it at all: the curved sword, the straight sword, the halberd, the whip and the curved greatsword. Three of those five are classes whose entire reason for existing is a wide swing. And thirteen of the twenty-eight sample animations the speed rule uses to check itself already broke it. A rule that its own examples fail is not really a rule.

Underneath it was a filing error. The speed limit had been written as a property of how heavy a weapon is — light, medium, heavy, ultra — when it is really a property of an individual weapon's shape. Inside the "medium" group alone, a spear's geometry demands about 3 metres per second and a whip's demands 66. Sorting them by weight and handing the group one limit was never going to work. Re-deriving the limits from the weapons themselves even puts them in a surprising order: a curved greatsword's spin is genuinely the fastest tip in the game, faster than the enormous two-handed sword everyone would assume.

The ruling: the arc wins. The speed limit is rewritten so each attack is measured against its own geometry instead of a shared table, and may exceed what its own shape demands by no more than a quarter. What that costs is stated in the ruling rather than buried — the game no longer makes any absolute claim about how fast a weapon should look, only a relative one. That is a real loss, and it was accepted because the absolute claim was already untrue of a third of the weapon classes.

What makes the ruling worth having is that it strands nobody. Before it, 746 attacks broke the rule and 465 of those had no legal fix at any setting. After it, 381 break the rule and every one of them can be fixed by letting the swing stay active a few frames longer — about four frames each. A checking tool was written so a future reader does not have to take any of this on trust, and it was deliberately fed broken data to confirm it goes red rather than always agreeing.

One more clash of exactly the same kind was found while working and deliberately not decided, because deciding it was not this job. The document governing how the game detects a weapon hitting something assumes the fastest weapon tip in the game travels at 26 metres per second, and sizes its collision checks around that. The real fastest is 156. Nearly two thirds of the game's swinging attacks travel further between checks than the check was designed to cover, which means a fast swing can pass through a target without the game noticing. It has been written up and handed on rather than quietly patched.

headline: Dying used to pay you thirty-five per cent more, and this round fixed it — I checked by cutting the fix out of the source and watching the old number come back. Then I found something odd standing next to it: saving your game and loading it again turns 42 souls into 57. Same enemy, same moment, nothing in between except the reload.
detail:
This piece is about dying: what it costs you, what comes back, and what resting at a campfire does to the world around you.

The round before this one made a good fix that opened a hole. Time in this game does not pass while you are lying dead — that was deliberate, so you cannot fail a timed errand by dying at a boss over and over. But the game also pays you more for killing things at night, and it worked out "is it night?" from that same frozen clock. So the minutes you spent dead were minutes that never counted, and near dawn that meant a player who had died forty times was still being paid the night rate while a player who had stayed alive through the same stretch had walked into the morning and was being paid less. Dying paid better. The builder found that against itself, named it as the serious kind of rule-break it is, and fixed it with a second clock that keeps counting whether you are alive or not.

I took the fix out of the source code rather than switching it off while the game ran, and the old, wrong numbers came straight back. Then I did something the round had not: I tried it at every quarter-hour of the day, ninety-six starting times. With the fix in, dying and living pay the same at all ninety-six. With it out, they differ at exactly four — the quarter-hours either side of dawn and dusk. That is why nobody spotted this for three rounds: away from those two edges the broken version and the fixed version agree. I also checked the fix was not some other change wearing its name, by removing each of its two halves separately. Both are needed and neither alone is enough.

What the round did not notice is what its own fix implies about saving. The second clock is not written into your save file. So if you die a lot just before dawn, the save records the frozen time and throws away the running one — and when you load, the game lines the two back up and puts you back in the night. I measured it: die twenty times at ten to five in the morning, kill something, get 42 souls; reload that same save, kill the same thing, get 57. It is not a large exploit and the remedy is one field in the save file, but it is the same shape of problem the round had just closed, arriving through a different door.

The reason the piece still does not pass is smaller and more human. Resting six hours is supposed to shut the shops and send everyone home, and the round proved the shops part properly — seventy-one of a hundred and fifteen doors shut, against a control run that steps the same number of frames without resting and shuts none. But the people part was tested in a town with nobody in it. Of the three runs, only one had any inhabitants at all, and the run whose whole job was to show that the rest — rather than the passing of a few frames — was what moved people had zero people in it. So "nobody moved without resting" was true because there was nobody. The full test run agrees: that one row comes back red. The builder wrote that down in its notes and left the diagnosis unfinished. It is fixable — make the town having a population something the test refuses to run without — and it is the last clause standing between this piece and a pass.

headline: Every character who tries to play the main quest stops in the same place: the sixth job, where the game asks you to read a four-hundred-year-old burial ledger and work out when the tide started failing. The ledger did not exist. It was named in the quest file, it was named in the journal, and there was no such object anywhere in the game. It exists now, it is on a shelf in the archive it is supposed to be in, and the wall the story hit is gone.
detail:
Every quest in this game says, for each thing you have to find out before you can finish it, exactly how you find it out: by talking to somebody, by overhearing them, by reading a book, by reading a ledger, by walking somewhere and seeing it. A previous round wired up the people — walk up to the person the file names and they tell you what they know. That left seventy-three of these unfinished, and the biggest group was not a wiring problem at all. It was that the things themselves had never been written. Thirty-four ledgers and ten letters were named as the source of a truth, and not one of them was an object in this game.

The worst of them was the one holding up everything. The sixth job of the main quest sends you down to the Drowned Court's archive under the burial stair in Soulrest, where an archivist who has been alone in that room for thirty years lets you read the burial book — four hundred years of deaths, what was paid, and what the wells gave back, never once added up outside that room. What you are meant to come out with is a date: the returns start falling eight years before the Empire granted the first licence to cut a sapwell, which means the thing everyone in the province blames cannot be the thing that started it. Forty test characters, one for every kind of person the game lets you make, all walked to that room and all stopped there, because there was no book to read.

So the book got written. Nine documents, about five thousand words: the volume of the Tally where the column stops being level and a sexton starts arguing in the margin with a hand nobody has ever met; the archivist's own note at the back, saying he went to Gideon and copied the licence roll himself because three of his four readers in thirty years arrived certain it was the other way round; a cutter's family yard book from Blackrose that is older than the licence and complains in its first entry that the wells give less than they did; a harbourmaster's private manifest that is exact to the ton and silent about every name that matters; a moneylender's book that keeps no names because names live in a different room; a letter of instruction in Jel, taken off a body, from the man the whole story is about, patient and clerkly and correcting somebody's arithmetic.

The other half was making them things you can reach. The game already drew a small book on a shelf in eighty-three of its rooms and not one of them had anything written in it. Now a shelf can carry a real document, and reaching for it opens it where it stands rather than putting it in your pack — which matters, because the archivist will not let the books leave the room and the quest has a way of failing you for carrying one out. Doing it the other way would have made the only thing you could do in that room the thing that closes it.

It was proved by playing. Six times, in a real running game, a character walked into the room, stood at the shelf, pressed the one button the game has for reaching at things, read the document, and watched the quest stop refusing. Two checks were run alongside each time: standing in the same room but out of arm's reach opens nothing, and reading a different book off the same shelf moves nothing. The whole main quest was then played twice, identical except for whether opening a book was allowed: reading allowed gets from job one to job eleven, reading refused stops at job six with the message every one of those forty characters had been getting.

One small thing turned up while proving it and is worth repeating, because it is the kind of defect only playing finds. A document drawn on the shelf beside a doorway can never be read at all: the game gives the door first claim on the same button, so pressing it at the book walks you out of the room instead. One room had a document exactly there. Shelves are now kept clear of the doorway.

What is not done is said plainly. Twenty-four ledgers and letters are still named by quests and still unwritten, and the check now lists every one of them by name. Twenty-seven more truths are supposed to arrive by looking at something in the world, and reading through all twenty-seven one at a time, eighteen of them are not documents at all — they are places you have to stand in, a chain on a wall, keepers standing at a root, a station with nobody on it. Those need somebody to build arriving-somewhere as a way of learning, which is a different job, and writing pages for them would have been inventing documents nobody wrote.

headline: Argonia's eight towns had two hundred and two buildings written down and not one of them had ever been drawn. You could walk up to a door, open it, and find a furnished room behind it — the last round built those — but from the street the town was an empty field with doors floating in it. The camera angle the project keeps for photographing a town centre had been photographing grass. This round builds the outsides: walls, roofs, doorways cut in the wall the file says the door is on, and each town's own architecture. Thorn is black thatch over a leaning hall, Gideon is Imperial timber-frame and tile, Soulrest is whale-bone and salt. Thirty-seven of the sixty-nine building shapes the design documents named had never been built by anything, anywhere; they exist now. The outside of a building is made from the same parts as the inside, so the shop you walk into is recognisably the shop you were looking at — that holds for all 112 you can enter. And the walls are solid: before this round the whole open world had no collision at all and you could stroll through a house. The honest part: the town plans place buildings closer together than the buildings are wide — in Archon they are three metres apart and thirteen metres across — so 54 of the 202 are drawn smaller than declared rather than shoved through their neighbours, and twelve pairs still overlap more than they should. That is a fault in the plans, and it is now visible instead of theoretical. One more thing fell out of it that nobody expected: the camera angle the project keeps for photographing a town centre turns out to be standing inside one of the buildings. It was pointing at empty ground before, so nobody could tell.

Until today the monsters in this game could not walk towards you. The thing that stood in for a brain was a straight line: notice the player, march at them at a fixed speed, stop just short, and swing on a stopwatch forever. It also could not be sneaked past - it noticed you through walls, from behind, in the dark. Enemies now approach, circle, feint a step in, commit to a swing they cannot take back, back off, and give up and walk home if you outrun them. And a sentry facing the other way no longer knows you are there.
detail:
This piece is the enemy: how it notices you, how it closes the distance, when it decides to attack, and when it gives up. It had never been worked on, and the first job was finding out what was actually there rather than what everyone assumed.

What was there was almost nothing. The code had a state called REPOSITION that turned the enemy to face you and never moved it a single centimetre - a name for a movement the program did not contain. One other part of the game, written for a different purpose entirely, did contain a walk-towards-the-player, and because of how wilderness enemies get placed in the world that accidental fragment had become the behaviour of every hostile creature in the game. It walks in a straight line at 2.2 metres a second, stops at 2.3 metres, and attacks every 1.3 seconds until one of you is dead. It never circles, never hesitates, never gives up.

That explains something another reviewer had found and could not account for: they walked six kilometres of road and were attacked exactly once, in a 210-metre stretch, and then nothing at all for the remaining five kilometres, even though twenty-eight more enemy camps appeared along the way. The arithmetic turns out to be brutal. The enemy moves at 2.2 metres a second. You walk at 2.0. So it closes the gap at twenty centimetres a second, which means from the moment it spots you it needs sixty-eight seconds and a hundred and thirty-seven metres of road to get close enough to swing. If you jog, or run, it simply never reaches you - there is nothing in this world fast enough to catch someone who is not strolling. And every time it does swing it stands still for the whole animation while you keep walking, handing back several metres it then needs another twenty seconds to reclaim. Finally the game deletes the camp once you are 260 metres past where it started - so the enemy chasing you is quietly removed mid-chase. Three separate things, each reasonable on its own, combining into a road that cannot fight back.

Enemies now have a real repertoire. They walk in when you are far, sprint when you are very far, hold a comfortable distance and circle it, take a step towards you that they might not follow through on, and only then commit to a swing - and once committed they cannot cancel it, which is what gives you the moment to punish them. Afterwards they back off and re-space rather than standing on top of you. In a group they pass a token around so that four of them do not all swing at once, and the ones without it keep moving instead of freezing in a queue. If you drink a healing flask where they can see you, they will come for you. If you run away far enough, they stop, walk back to where they started, and only then heal - so escaping is a real option and not a punishment.

The more embarrassing findings were in the measuring equipment. One field in the game's own recording of what enemies are doing - whether the enemy can actually see you - was written twice in the same place, and the second copy was the word 'yes'. Every recording this project has ever made said every enemy could see the player at all times. Two more fields, how fast an enemy is moving and how fast it is turning, were simply never filled in, which meant a safety check for the single most unfair thing a game like this can do - an enemy spinning to face you mid-swing - could never have failed. Those are fixed, and the turning check now passes for a reason rather than by accident.

What is honestly not done: there are still only seven kinds of enemy in the whole game, four of which are the same soldier with a different amount of health, and the reference standard asks for ten genuinely different ones plus a boss. Adding those is writing new creatures, which is a decision about content this piece should not make alone, so it is written down and named rather than quietly skipped.

headline: Two things this round. The first: the game had six screens - your bag, your journal, your character sheet, your spells, your map and the level-up table - and the menu itself listed all six as places you could go, but only two of them had a door. Pressing every key on the pad, one at a time, from the world and from inside every screen, got you to the bag and nothing else. You can now step between all six with the two shoulder-ish buttons that cycle your gear when no screen is open, the same way the dodge button doubles as "back". The second: someone could hand-edit their save file and put squares on the map for forty-two places they had never been, over a fully drawn map of a country they had never walked - and the game's own self-check said everything was fine, because it was checking the forged file against itself. The map no longer trusts the save. It keeps only a record of the ground you actually stood on and works everything else out from that, so there is no longer any line in a save file where a place can be named.
detail:
THE DOORS. The interface advertised six destinations at a resting place and the code that reads your buttons had no branch for walking from one screen to another. A neighbouring piece measured this rather than reading it - all sixteen actions the project allows, pressed one at a time, from the world and from every screen they open, plus the four stick directions - and found that input reached exactly two of the six. Opening the level-up table directly, from a test hook, worked on the same character on the same frame, which proved the room existed and the door did not.

The fix adds no new button. The project keeps a closed list of fourteen actions and a fifteenth is not allowed, so the two that already cycle your left and right hand now also walk the list of screens - but only while a screen is open, and only when you are not in a fight, because in a fight one of them is half of the two-handed grip and a menu that eats your dodge is a trap. That is the same rule the game already used for the roll button. Measured afterwards the same way it was measured before, taken as far as it goes: sixteen actions and four directions from every screen reachable so far, repeated until nothing new appears. All six now reachable. The route to the level-up table is: open the menu, then press right five times.

THE MAP. A critic broke this last round by editing a save. The map kept two things in the file - a picture of the ground you had seen, and a list of the places you had stood in - and when the file was loaded it checked the list against the picture. Forge one and you are caught. Forge both and the check is asking the forgery to vouch for itself. Forty-two squares appeared for a body that had stood in seven places, over a fully rendered country, and the screen's own compliance report read green because both of its numbers came from the same forged file.

The repair is not a better check; it is the removal of the field. The save now carries one thing: which squares of ground your feet were actually on, in the order you were on them. The picture of the country and the list of places are recomputed from that on load, by the same code that computes them while you play. There is nothing left for two fields to disagree about, because there is one field. The old fields are still written and still read - but read as a claim to be checked, so the game now reports exactly which forty-two names it refused and exactly how much country the file claimed you had seen that your feet do not support.

The same forgery, run again: seven squares drawn, none of them phantom, thirty-five names refused, and not one extra square of country rendered. The picture above is the map before and after loading that forged save; they are the same map. Deleting the repair on a copy and running it again brings the forty-two straight back, so the number is a property of the change and not of the fixture.

THREE SMALLER ONES. A potion you drank while the game was paused used to still say "x3" on the row until you closed the bag and opened it again - the screen only redrew when you moved the highlight, not when the world underneath it changed. It redraws now. A compliance report that was supposed to prove the map has no way to name a place was a hand-typed list of three method names on an object that has four; it is now read off the running object, so a method nobody remembered still gets counted. And a text-quality measurement was quietly throwing away the two screens it could not measure before reporting a pass; it now names them or fails.

WHAT I COULD NOT DO. The box was carrying thirty to sixty other browsers and a load average around thirty for the whole run, so I launched one browser and kept it, and every number here is a count, a boolean or a pixel difference - there is no timing figure in this piece and there should not be one taken under that load. Two other pieces' files were mid-edit and throwing while I measured: a settlement kit that crashes when the world builds Blackrose, and an enemy brain that crashes on any frame with a monster alive. Neither is mine; both are reported rather than worked around silently.

headline: There are eight hundred and twenty-seven lamps hand-placed in the rooms of this game, and this round of work made every one of them visible for the first time. The code that decides whether a guard can see you has never been told about a single one of them. It has exactly one way to be told a light exists, and the only thing in the entire game that has ever used it is the test harness.
detail:
I was asked to check a repair. Last time round, every door in this game opened onto nothing: walking into a shop correctly recorded that you were in the shop, moved your body to just inside its door, and then carried on drawing the street. The builder fixed it, and fixed it well — better than the fix that was asked for. Instead of patching the two places where a door is used, they put in a reconciliation that asks, on every single frame, whether the room being drawn is the room your body is standing in, and corrects it if not. That catches the two doors and also the five other ways the game can move you somewhere, which the requested fix would not have.

They also gave the rooms bodies. 115 named interiors used to resolve to one hall with one hearth in it; now each is built out of its own file — its real dimensions, its real lamps in their real places, its real furniture.

Which is what made the thing I found findable. Every one of those rooms has a list of lamps in its file: eleven in the shrine, ten in the apothecary, none at all in eleven of them. Those lamps are now drawn. But this game also has a model of darkness — the thing that works out whether you are standing somewhere a guard can notice you — and that model has a single door through which a light can be registered with it. I searched the whole game for anything that opens that door. There is exactly one caller, and it is the automated test harness. Nothing in the running game has ever registered a light. So the shrine lit by eleven lamps and the smithy lit by none are, to every guard in Argonia, the same darkness. You cannot hide in the shadows, because as far as the game is concerned there are no lights to be out of.

Nobody could have found this last round, because last round every room was the same room. Making the lamps visible is what made their absence measurable, and that is a good thing to have caused rather than a mark against it.

The picture is the other half of what is left. Helstrom's smithy and Helstrom's scriptorium — a forge and a copying-room, in the same town — are described by two files that are word for word identical in every line the room-builder reads: same size, same eighteen pieces of furniture, same number of lamps, same materials. The game does draw them slightly differently, because it scatters the furniture using the room's name as a seed, so the difference between a forge and a scriptorium here is where the same eighteen objects happened to land. Twenty-one of the 115 rooms are duplicates like that, in twelve groups, the biggest being seven houses in a row. Last round it was 113 of 115, so this is a large repair and it is the same problem.

Two more things nobody had listed. Take the one unique treasure a room contains, walk out of the door, walk back in, and it is on its pedestal again — the game keeps a careful list of everything you have taken, saves it, loads it, and hands it to the test harness, and absolutely nothing reads that list before putting the treasure back. Eighty-three rooms have one. And a document you can read in a room comes back unreadable from a saved game, because the save file has no space for the fact that it was a document — which is the identical bug this same round found and fixed for quest-givers, one shelf along.

And the part I could not do, which I am supposed to report as plainly as the part I could. The two measurements that would have proved the door repair from the player's side — walking into all 115 rooms and reading the screen, and photographing all 115 from one fixed camera to count how many are different pictures — did not finish. The machine was running between eighteen and fifty-four browsers against a stated ceiling of eight, and another agent was running the same sweep alongside mine for the best part of an hour. So the repair is judged from the code and from the builder's own evidence, and not from a run I took, and the verdict says that three times rather than hiding it.

One last thing, and it is not the builder's fault. Halfway through my measurements the game changed underneath them: four of the files I was measuring were rewritten by the agent working on the next round, while my browsers were open. Every number I had was suddenly about a version of the game that no longer existed, so I threw them away, took a frozen copy of the whole game, and started again against that. The reason this keeps happening is a rule that tells builders not to save their work to the repository, so that nobody's half-finished changes get banked by accident. It works. It also means there is no saved version of the thing I was asked to grade, and there never was one. Five reports now say so.

headline: The new map is a good one. It shows only the ground you have actually walked, the rest is not dimmed but simply not drawn at all, and the small squares that name a place appear only once you have stood on that place's own ground - not when you enter the region, not when someone tells you about it. Walking 480 metres away gets you nothing; walking 40 metres outside the village gets you nothing; walking in gets you the square. I checked that at the pixels rather than taking the code's word for it, and an empty map really is one flat colour with no coastline showing through. But the map is stored in your save file as a single list of the squares of ground you have stood on, and that list is the only thing the game reads back. I wrote a save file that claimed I had stood on every square of ground in the province. The game loaded it without complaint and drew the entire world, every region in full colour, with all forty-two places named - for a character who had never taken a step. The game's own honesty check looked at that map and reported everything in order, because the number of places it drew and the number of places it thought I had found were both counted from the same forged list. That is exactly the failure a previous critic found and this round was meant to fix; the fix removed the old route and left a new one. The tool the builder wrote to catch this tests the one field the loader deliberately ignores, so it can never catch it. Worth saying plainly: the builder does record this limit honestly in a sibling tool, and the map's own code comment claims the opposite - two files in the same project stating opposite things about the same lock. Separately, nothing anywhere else in the game reads the map. I deleted the whole record of where the player had been, ran the world for six hundred frames, and not one thing in it behaved differently.

The towns in this game had no buildings. Two hundred and two shops, halls and houses existed only as doors you could walk into — from the street they were bare ground, and the townspeople standing outside in the morning stood on an empty field. They are built now: walls, roofs, a door cut in the side the record says the door is on, and each town's own architecture. But the part worth reporting is what I found when I checked the previous round's proof that you cannot walk through a wall. That check had a control — run the same walk again with the walls taken away — and the control did nothing at all. One line of code threw away the handle the game needed to find the walls, just before asking it to remove them, so both halves of the experiment were the same half, and fifteen walks returned fifteen identical answers that nobody noticed were identical. Fixed, and re-run: with the walls, fifteen of fifteen walks stop dead half a metre short and stay stopped through six seconds of somebody holding the stick forward. With the walls taken away, all fifteen walk straight through. Aimed at the door instead of the wall, eleven of eleven walk in — so it is a wall that stops you, not the building.
detail:
WHAT WAS BROKEN. A settlement in this game is a list of buildings in a data file. Until this round that list had exactly two readers: a table of which door leads to which room, and a count of how many buildings there were. Nothing drew them. The viewpoint the project keeps for photographing a town street photographed grass and fog, and a previous verdict said so in those words.

WHAT IS BUILT. All 202 buildings across all 8 towns now stand up: 8,371 pieces of geometry, 166,624 triangles. Each town has its own kit of architecture — Helstrom's grown boles and shell domes are not Gideon's timber frames and tile roofs — and 37 of those pieces had never been built by any code in the project, because they only ever appear outdoors and until now there was no outdoors. Every one of the 112 buildings you can walk into shows on the outside the same architecture its inside is made of, because both are now read from one table instead of two. To show the buildings are really being drawn and not merely counted, the drawing call is switched off and the same measurement retaken: 202 becomes 0, and 0 becomes 202 again when it is switched back on.

THE CONTROL THAT DID NOTHING. My predecessor was killed by a container restart with two measurements still running. One of them had in fact finished and written its results, and those results were wrong in a way worth explaining, because it is the most common way a test lies. To show that a wall stops you it is not enough to walk into a wall and stop — you have to take the wall away and walk again, or you have not shown the wall did it. That second walk is the control. Here the control asked the game to remove the walls, and the game needed a reference to those walls in order to find them; the line just above had already thrown that reference away. So the removal quietly did nothing, both walks ran with the walls in place, and all fifteen pairs of results came out identical to the last decimal. An identical pair is the signature of a dead control, and nothing in the report checked for it.

I fixed the line — and then, because a check that cannot fail is worth nothing, I rebuilt the broken version inside the running game and ran the new check against it. It correctly reports the walls failing to come out in all five towns. Against the fixed version it reports them coming out cleanly in all five and coming back again. Only after that are the walk numbers worth reading.

A SECOND WRONG NUMBER. The same old report said that in all five towns, zero buildings had anything solid where their walls are. That reads like a catastrophe and was in fact a fault in the ruler: it sampled for solid matter one metre above sea level, while these towns sit between three and fifteen metres up a hillside. It was measuring underground. Measured at each building's own height, 66 of 66 walls are solid. The 12 that came back empty were all the same thing — the probe sampled the exact middle of the wall the door is in, and a doorway is a hole on purpose. Every one of those 12 is a building whose door is on that side.

WHO IS STANDING IN A WALL. Across three times of day and 260 outdoor townspeople, three people are standing inside solid masonry: one at three in the morning, two at nine, none in the evening. All three are in the two towns whose street plans pack buildings closer together than the buildings are wide. That is a problem in the town data rather than in the drawing, and it is written down rather than papered over.

WHAT I DID NOT DO. In five of the eight towns the plan places buildings closer together than their own declared sizes, so 54 are shrunk to fit and 12 pairs still overlap badly; the right repair is in the data and I did not make it. Several buildings read as open-topped crates from above, because a town's roof is drawn at wall height and some domes are narrower than the floor they sit on — the picture shows it, no count catches it, and it is not fixed. The viewpoint the project uses to photograph a town street turns out to stand inside one of the new buildings, so its picture is a dark wall; I left it where it is rather than move it to flatter the work, and wrote down where a better one would be. And there is no timing figure anywhere in this piece, because the machine was carrying up to seven other browsers throughout, and a speed measured under that is not a speed.

headline: The souls you take off a dead enemy now pay for exactly one thing - a level - and I checked every place in the code where they could have paid for anything else. There is no shop that takes them, no guard you can bribe with them, no toll. And a pile of gold, however big, will not buy you a level: I tried it with a hundred thousand coins and the game said no. The last round's embarrassment is gone too. Clearing the entire game used to leave you on level 120 exactly, which is the sort of round number that means somebody worked backwards from the answer. It now leaves you two-thirds of the way through level 93, which is what a number looks like when nobody was aiming at it.
detail:
This was a re-check of the reward system, and my job was to attack it rather than admire it, so here is what I found. The team fixed one bug twice - two separate safeguards, either of which is enough on its own. They tested them the sensible way, by removing one at a time, and both times the game carried on behaving perfectly, which they honestly reported as odd. It is odd, and it is worth understanding: I removed BOTH at once, and six live enemies immediately became worth nothing. So the fix is real. But each half looks useless when tested alone, and that is exactly how somebody deletes one next year believing it does nothing. That is now written down.

The bigger problem is arithmetic that has drifted apart. The reward system recently cut every enemy's value by about a third - a correction, and a good one. But the map's own file still lists the OLD values. It says the enemies scattered along the roads are worth 16,335 souls; they are worth 10,679. It says walking the whole road between the three towns and killing everything gets you to level 5; it gets you to level 3. Nothing anywhere checks these two files against each other, so the map has been quietly telling everyone a number that is half again too big. That is the one thing I have asked them to fix, and the fix is a single small checking tool.

I also looked hard at the headline evidence, which is a test advertised as trying 343 different sequences of events. It does run 343 - but they collapse into 14 genuinely different outcomes, nearly half of them pay nothing at all, and three of the seven kinds of event it shuffles are indistinguishable from each other. Every single one of those 343 passed; every problem it found came from two longer sequences outside that set. And all 463 of its runs use one enemy at one time of day, so the rule about enemies being worth more at night has never once been exercised by it. I checked that rule myself and it works - a fight worth 252 in the afternoon is worth 342 at eleven at night - but the test that claims to cover it does not.

Twice my own measuring tools were wrong in my favour and caught themselves, which I am reporting because it is the point of building them that way. One of them handed itself the souls it was supposed to earn by fighting, and passed a test designed to fail. The other read a character sheet in a practice arena that has no character in it, saw an empty page, and nearly accused the game of six faults it does not have. Score: 6 out of 10, below the bar of 7. No player would meet a broken thing here today. It is the difference between a system that is right and a system that has been shown to be right.

headline: The enemies in this game learned to fight this week - they circle, they fake a step in, they commit to a swing they cannot take back, and they walk home when you get away. I checked the part that matters most and it holds: I picked forty-seven swings and teleported the player forty metres away on the exact frame the sword started moving, and every single time the enemy finished the swing anyway. That is what a Souls enemy is. Then I checked whether it can actually catch you, and it cannot. If you simply WALK away - not run, walk - the guard follows at 2.2 metres a second against your 2.0, gains twenty centimetres a second, never breaks into a run because its rule for running is about distance rather than about whether it is gaining, gets no closer than eight metres in thirty seconds, hits the end of its leash and goes home. The road is still safe for anyone in no hurry. I also found that four of the seven enemies in the game are not just similar but the same fight: I recorded thirty seconds of a marsh sentry, a legion guard and two drowned men, and every position, every turn of the head and every choice of attack matched to the last decimal place - four names, four different amounts of health, one enemy. And the score the piece gave itself rests on a bookkeeping gap: the game never labels the moment after a swing as 'recovering', so the test that asks how much time an enemy spends standing on top of you throws those frames away. Count them and the number goes from 0.04 to 0.25. Eighty-five per cent of the time an enemy spends recovering from a swing, it is standing inside you.

You can ask anyone in this province about four hundred and sixty-eight subjects, and this week I found out that a hundred and fifty-one of them were written down where nobody could ever get at them. There was no way to bring them up. The words existed, somebody had written a rootkeeper's answer about egg-tending and a fisher's answer about the first tide, and no person in the game would ever say the noun that lets you ask. So I wrote the missing half of those conversations: sixty-odd answers, each one put in a particular person's mouth in a particular town, whose ordinary sentences happen to contain the subjects. Ask the Stormhold legionary about the cart roads and he names three of them, and now you can ask about those three. That is how Morrowind worked and it is why its world felt like it had corners you had not turned yet. I also found something worse and quieter: the towns' gossip could not change. Every settlement had eight rumours and they were the same eight in the last hour of the game as in the first, because the piece of code that picks a rumour looked at your race and where you were standing and never once at what had happened in the world. It was being handed the list of everything you had done and it was throwing it away. Now it reads it, and Lilmoth has twenty-four things to say when you arrive and thirty-two by the end, and some of the early ones stop being said. There are two hundred and thirty-nine rumours in the province now instead of eighty-three, and a dozen of them are wrong on purpose.

Every room in this game has lamps in it, and until today the part of the game that works out whether somebody can see you had never been told they were there. It was reading the WEATHER instead - so a windowless cellar at midday was as bright as an open field, and the same cellar at three in the morning was as dark as one, and it made no difference at all where in the room you stood. The lamps now light the room for the burglar as well as for the eye. Blow one out and the man watching you takes twice as long to notice you. And I measured what that is worth: steal the same thing from under the lamp and you get a 294 gold bounty, steal it from the dark corner of the same room and you get 118 - because in the dark they see somebody, but they cannot say who.
detail: Three things landed. FIRST, the lamps. The renderer has been drawing 827 authored interior lamps for weeks; the stealth model held zero of them, because the one function that adds a light had exactly one caller in the whole game and it was a test hook. It now reads the lamps out of the SAME file the renderer draws them from, so there is one list and it cannot drift. The brightness scale is worked out from the design document's own table rather than copied off the renderer. SECOND, the sleepers. The game's people have eight things they can be doing and not one of them is sleeping, so robbing a house at three in the morning was watched by every resident of it, wide awake, in the dark. Somebody at home between eleven at night and six in the morning is now asleep, and a sleeper is not a witness. I staged the same theft four ways to check - a witness in the room saw it and it cost 294 gold; one outside through a wall saw nothing; one asleep two metres away saw nothing; one watching from the dark corner saw somebody but could not name them, and it cost 118. THIRD, the theft. Every room has one unique object with an owner's name on it. You could pick all 83 of them up in front of their owners for free, because the button a player presses had never heard of ownership. It has now: 72 of the 83 are in the ownership system and taking one is a theft with a witness, a bounty and a fence who prices it as stolen goods. The other 11 have no owner written on them at all and I have said so rather than inventing one. I also cut both changes back out on a copy of the game and confirmed the old, wrong numbers come straight back - 0.75 everywhere, no theft, nothing stolen. And I counted the parameters in my own data files that nothing in the game reads: 116 out of 983, and I have listed every one.

headline: The province is meant to take about an hour to walk across. This week I sent a character to actually walk it, and he got thirty-nine metres. He was standing outside the capital with his nose against the wall of a house, and he stayed there for the next sixteen minutes of game time, because the main road out of Stormhold has been drawn straight through somebody's scribe. It turns out the roads and the towns are built by two different pieces of code that have never been introduced to each other: the road-builder lays out the highway over the bare landscape, and then the town-builder plants houses on the same ground, and nobody checks. I wrote the check. Every single one of the ten roads in the province goes through at least one building. Sixteen of those collisions are on the two big named journeys the game is measured by. To prove it really was the house and not something else, I picked the house up, moved it a kilometre east, and sent him again: he walked seven times further. Then I put the house back, and he stopped in exactly the same spot, to the tenth of a metre. I also found that the instrument the project uses to check the walk is honest only looks at one frame in every six, and something is moving the character on the other five - when he is standing perfectly still the two numbers agree exactly, and when he is moving they disagree by a factor of three and a half. And a separate one: nineteen dangers are scattered around the province, and six of them are traps. The game had been telling itself that a trap which had just gone off had not gone off, because it was asking whether the trap was still armed instead of whether anything had happened to you. One of those six kills you outright, and the report said nothing had happened.

Armour is heavy, and until today you could not put any on. The game has always shipped a chitin cuirass, legion greaves, a hauberk, boots and a cowl, each with a weight written on it, and each one you tried to wear went into your sword hand instead - because the only place the code knew how to put a thing you equipped was the right fist. That mattered more than it sounds. The whole point of armour in a game like this is the trade: heavier gear means a slower, shorter dodge with a smaller window where the blow passes through you, and that window is the thing your hands learn first. It was implemented, exactly and correctly, and nothing you could do in the world reached it - the number it read off was a constant somebody typed in. So you now dress the character and the dodge changes. Wearing nothing, the roll is invulnerable for 26 frames out of 52. Put on the heaviest set the game currently owns - about 28 kilos - and it drops to 22 out of 60, and the recovery afterwards, the part where you are lying on the floor and can be hit, goes from 22 frames to 34. Carrying is a separate question from wearing, and deliberately so: four hundred and sixty kilos of looted hammers in your pack does not change your dodge by a single frame. What it changes is the walk home. Loaded up you move at 72% speed, you cannot run, and the barge that took forty minutes of game time now takes fifty-four - same boat, same fare, longer day. You cannot carry a dungeon out in one trip, which is the whole reason the merchants have limited money. I also counted, for every number these two systems publish, whether anything in the running game actually reads it. Twenty-six numbers; twenty-two are read; four are not - what the weight does to your stamina outside a fight, to how easily guards spot you, to how high you jump, and to how much a fall hurts. Those four are written down and named rather than quietly left. And one small ugly thing found by accident: a tool the project uses to test carrying weight had stopped working months ago - it set the weight and the game overwrote it a sixtieth of a second later - so anything measured with it since then needs taking again.

The quests in this game keep asking the player to know something before they will let you settle them peacefully - that the shortfall in the wells started before the tree-cutters arrived, that the seal on a paper is in the wrong wax, that four of the eleven doors in the shut quarter have been chalked. For 121 of those demands the quest files name exactly where you find out. Sixty-three of them named a thing that did not exist. There was no ledger to read, no letter, no mark on any wall - the game asked you to have learned something from a book nobody had written. So I wrote them. Twenty-six documents, about nine thousand seven hundred words: a prison book of torn lease counterfoils where the word again is written four times against the same twelve people, a wharf fund kept in pencil on a scrap because ink runs in a wet shed, a letter from a daughter at Soulrest asking why her dead father voted in the spring. And twenty-five things to look at, standing in the world where the fact is: eleven chalk marks on eleven jambs, four water marks over a reach bed, a post in the Helstrom gallery with nobody on it. Reaching for one of them opens no window and prints no sentence at you - you looked at the thing, and your journal knows it now. Demanded truths a player can actually reach: 58 of 121, now 100.
