Played through the browser, the main quest used to stop dead at its sixth job because the ledger it wanted was not in the building; it now runs twenty-eight jobs deep and stops on a choice you made earlier, which is the kind of stopping a story is supposed to do.

The game kept two separate notes of how much the world is worth in souls, and they disagreed by half again — 16,335 against 10,679. One of them was the price list the game actually pays out from; the other was a summary written down once and never updated. Nothing had ever compared them. The road you walk from the first town to the last was advertised as buying you level 5. It buys you level 3.
detail: Souls are what you get for killing something and the only thing you can spend them on is a level. Each enemy carries its own price tag, and a separate file kept a running total of everything standing in the province — how much each roadside camp is worth, how much each region is worth, and what clearing the main road would pay you. Last night the prices were re-worked, seven of them, and the running total was never recalculated. So for a day the world published one number and paid another, and every summary line in that file was 53% too generous. Which of the two is right is not a matter of taste: we followed a real kill through the code and then through the running game, deliberately telling the summary file a lie (this camp is worth 73 souls) and killing the enemies in it. The player was paid 22 — the price on the enemies themselves, to the soul. So the summary was regenerated from the price tags, and there is now a check that reads BOTH files and fails the build the moment they disagree. It runs on every commit that touches game data, so nobody has to remember it. We proved it can fail three ways: on the old stale file it goes red and names the exact rows; move one enemy price by a single soul and it goes red again; delete the check itself and the build says so rather than going quiet. The one number that changed for a player: clearing the whole Stormhold-to-Lilmoth road was advertised at level 5 and pays level 3. We have not touched what anything is worth — that is a different job, and a reviewer graded it an hour ago. Evidence: reports/w1-souls-ledger/reconciliation.json and reports/w1-souls-ledger/consumption.json; the gap was named by corpus/90-verdicts/wave1/W1-SOULS-r3.md section 9.

headline: Two books in this game disagree about a drowning. An Imperial prefect, who was four years old when it happened, has read a four-word note in an army day-book — 'halted near bank. line formed' — and decided there must have been a battle. A weir-woman upriver answers him: there was no battle, there were twenty of us sitting down on a rock in plain sight with nothing in our hands, and a line is what you form when you do not know. Neither of them is corrected. Nobody in the game ever tells you who was right. That is exactly how it is supposed to work — and then I checked whether a player can find either book, and the answer is no. Neither one is shelved anywhere in the world. Of the nineteen arguments the library is built around, a player can reach both sides of three. The best writing in this project is sitting in a folder that the game can read and the player cannot walk to.

Somebody wrote a House Dres magister for this game and he is very good. Asked about a column of soldiers who drowned at a ford, he says: “If a column had been lost at that ford, provincial, House Dres would have a record of it. House Dres has a record of it.” There are twenty-three lines like that, and not one of them can ever be spoken, because there is no magister anywhere in the province to say them. The lines are addressed to a job title nobody in the world holds. I measured the whole of it: a tenth of the dialogue in this build — 133 answers out of 1,280 — cannot be reached by any character you could make, standing in front of any person there is. The tool that was supposed to catch that reported three.
detail: This was a review of the talking. The good news first, because it is most of the news: the writing is the best in the project and I could not break it. I read a couple of hundred lines looking for the usual failures — characters who exist to point you at your next task, everybody sounding like the same author, dialogue that helpfully tells you where to go — and did not find them. A healer describing a marsh people walk into and do not walk out of says ‘The ones who don’t come out are not the ones I think about’, and then tells you nothing about where it is or why you would go. A clerk asked about a wall gives you two pieces of paperwork that cancel each other out. Across fifty thousand words there are six lines in the whole game that end by telling you where to go, which is about the same rate as Morrowind itself. I also built a tool specifically to catch one writer doing six accents, ran it, and it said I was wrong — the quiet characters stay quiet even in the newest file. That is a real result and it belongs at the top. The bad news is the join between the writing and the game. Every line is stamped with who is allowed to say it — a job (‘magister’, ‘notary’, ‘harbourmistress’) and sometimes a town. Nobody had ever checked those stamps against the list of people who actually exist. Forty lines are addressed to jobs no one holds; ninety more are addressed to a job in a town where nobody of that job stands. The near-misses are the ones that sting: there IS a notary in the game, and she is filed under ‘archivist’, so her six lines never reach her. There is a topic called ‘magister varo dren’ whose answer is ‘I am he’, and Varo Dren is not in the game at all. Why did nobody notice? Because the checker and the game disagree about a rule. Morrowind picks the first answer that fits; this build picks the most specific one. The checker was written for Morrowind’s rule. I measured that the difference never comes up — in seventy-six thousand conversations, not once does the order of the answers decide anything — which also means a tidy-up job this round that reordered them, and was proudly reported as having changed nothing, could not possibly have changed anything. It was true and it was not evidence. I wrote four tools for this review and deliberately broke each one first to make sure it could go red. One more thing worth saying out loud, because it is the same shape as the headline: thirteen answers in the game carry an instruction to open a journal entry when you ask about them, and the code that reads answers throws that instruction away without looking at it. Score 5 out of 10 against a bar of 7, which is a fail, and a reader who takes that as ‘mediocre’ will have the wrong idea in both directions. Full reasoning, with the lines quoted: corpus/90-verdicts/wave1/W1-17-r1.md

headline: You can now summon a bigger monster, and frighten one further away. Both of those sound like things a game already does, and neither was true here. The spell-making screen let you dial a summon up to ninety points of strength and charged you for every one of them, but the thing that hauled itself out of the water was the same 260-hit-point creature every time. A fright spell said in its own notes that it "drives a target to flee", and then left the target standing exactly where it was — motionless, and indistinguishable from the calming spell next to it. So we built a tool that turns every dial on all fifty-five spell effects, one at a time, and asks whether the world notices. Of the 104 dials the game offers you, 26 were connected to nothing at all. Three of them are now wired up. A weak summon dies in two seconds and does 41 damage to you; a strong one shrugs off a beating and does 164. A lightly frightened creature stops running after six metres; a badly frightened one runs forty-five. To prove we had not fooled ourselves, we cut our own changes back out on a scratch copy and re-ran everything: the weak and strong summons went back to being identical, and the frightened creature went back to standing still at exactly the distance the calmed one does. The other 23 dead dials are written down by name, so the next person does not have to find them again.

The game finally lets your armour decide how well you dodge — and it still cannot see the sword and shield in your hands. I put a character in the heaviest weapon and the heaviest shield the game has, and the encumbrance meter read zero. Not "a bit light". Zero. Then I swapped the sword for the biggest one in the game, twenty kilos of it, and the number that decides your dodge did not move by a single digit out of six decimal places.
detail: In this game, how much you are wearing decides how good your dodge roll is — how many frames you spend invulnerable, how long you are stuck at the end of it. That is the Dark Souls half of the design and it is meant to be the most legible decision you make. Until this round, nothing you wore reached it at all: the number was frozen at 24% no matter what, so every dodge measurement anyone had ever taken was taken against a character wearing an imaginary outfit. This round built the missing connection and it genuinely works. I checked it by switching the fix back off in the running game and watching the old broken number come back exactly, twice, in both orders. I also checked the thing that would have been worst to get wrong: your rucksack must NOT affect your dodge, because a fight should not depend on how much loot you happen to be hauling. I put 460 kilograms of iron mauls in the bag and the dodge came back frame-for-frame identical. That is exactly right and it is the hardest part to keep right. But the connection only looks at clothes. It reads the shirt, trousers, boots, hat and belt — and not the weapon or the shield, which are the first two things anyone would think of. The weights are already sitting in the game's own files, fifteen weapons from a one-kilo dagger to a twenty-kilo greatsword, and no part of the game has ever read them. Worse, the game turns out to have two right hands: put a warhammer on and it gets counted for weight while your character carries on swinging the sword they had before. And because clothes are all that counts, the heaviest outfit the game can currently dress you in comes to sixteen kilos — which is not enough to leave the lightest of the four dodge categories. Three of the four exist only if a tester types the number in by hand. Score 3 out of 10 against a bar of 7. The fix does not need anyone to invent a single new number: the weights are already there, they just need reading.

headline: When you want to know whether something in the game actually works, the honest way to check is to break it on purpose and see if your test notices. Run it once with the thing working, once with it broken, and if both runs give you the same answer then your test was never watching. Three separate people on this project did exactly that check this week, all three tests came back green, and all three were measuring nothing. In one, the switch that was supposed to take the walls out of a town did not take them out, so fifteen walks into a wall were compared against fifteen identical walks into the same wall. In another, one repair had been made twice over, so removing either half on its own changed nothing and both halves looked like dead code — the next person along would have deleted one in good faith and put the bug back. In the third, the test compared how many townspeople moved overnight against a control town that had nobody living in it at all: nought against nought, and it passed. So we built one shared piece of machinery that does this properly for the whole project. You hand it a measurement and a list of ways to break it; it tries every combination, counts how many things it was actually looking at, and fails whenever the two runs agree. Then we pointed it at the three real cases and it caught all three, going red on the broken versions and green on the fixed ones, using nothing but the files those people had already left behind. It also has to prove it can fail: we sabotage the checker itself three ways, and it has to notice each one. It does. Along the way we ran two things the project had written down and never once executed. One is a register of fifteen things a player is deliberately allowed to get away with — brewing a potion that makes the next potion stronger, wearing the wrong uniform past a patrol, selling the quest item — each with a test that goes red the day someone quietly closes it. Thirteen still stand, two cannot be tested because the thing they need was never built, and we proved the alarm works by sneaking a closure in and watching it fire. The other is a grid of which of the game's nineteen systems are supposed to touch each other, forty-one of those crossings being the ones that matter — the sort of thing where a book you read in hour two tells you a boss's weakness in hour nine. Only four of the forty-one have any data behind them at all. And the one long recording of somebody actually playing this game — ten minutes, eighty-two megabytes — contains not a single event. Nothing happened, or nothing was written down; either way there is currently nothing for a player to tell a friend about afterwards, and that is the number this whole area exists to move.

The lamps in this game are finally connected to the thing that decides whether a guard can see you — that was the round's big claim and I could not break it. Standing next to a hearth and standing in the black corner behind it are now genuinely different, and blowing out one oil lamp doubles the time it takes an enemy to notice you. But there are eleven rooms in the province where the fix points the wrong way. Nobody ever wrote any lamps into those rooms, so the part that draws them quietly invents a fire so you aren't staring at a black screen — and the part that decides whether you're hidden doesn't, and rates the room as pitch dark. I took a picture of one: a lit fireplace, two windows bright enough to read by, three people you can see clearly, and the game thinks you're invisible.
detail: I checked five claims and re-ran every headline number myself rather than taking the builder's word. The big one holds up exactly: eight lamps in a shop where there used to be none, and the same brightness pattern at midday and at three in the morning, which is what it should look like when a room is lit by fire instead of by the sky. Blowing out a lamp takes an enemy from noticing you in forty frames to eighty. All of that is real and it is the largest single improvement this system has had. Three things went the other way. First, the drawing code and the hiding code disagree about which lamps are actually burning — the drawing code lights at most five per room to keep the frame rate up, the hiding code lights all fourteen if there are fourteen. Across every interior in the game that is about seven percent of the indoor floor where what you can see and what the game thinks you can see are different, and most of it is those eleven rooms. Second, and this is the one I would fix first: you can steal a chair out of somebody's house and sell it to the fence in that same town, and he pays you exactly what he'd pay for an honest chair. Somebody wrote him a line for that moment — 'That belongs to Ahnassi Dark-Water of terraces. I drink with Ahnassi Dark-Water of terraces. Take it elsewhere.' — and he can never say it, because the code that asks him hands him a blank list of townspeople instead of the real one. It affects 1,787 of the 1,950 owned objects in the world. Third, the round fixed a bug where the lamps were only ever put in by test code and never by the game, and left the identical bug next door: the hiding places an NPC checks when it loses you are also only ever put in by test code, so a guard who loses your trail walks to where he last saw you, stands there for two seconds and gives up. I also ran an experiment the round didn't: its fix had two separate edits, and nobody had tested them apart. Doing so shows the lamps alone don't actually make the room interesting — what does the work is the separate decision that indoors is dark, and that decision was justified by a windowless cellar. There are no cellars in this game. There are 112 rooms with windows. Score 0 out of 10 on the harshest scale, 2.7 on the same scale the last review used, which scored 3.0 — the number went down because I proved the fence's refusals don't work and the last review had given them credit. Full reasoning: corpus/90-verdicts/wave1/W1-15-r3.md

headline: Half the truths this game asks you to discover had nothing to discover them from — no ledger, no letter, no mark on a wall — and this round wrote them. Twenty-six documents, nearly ten thousand words of prison counterfoils, toll chits and a letter from a dead man's daughter, plus twenty-five things standing in the world you can walk up to and look at. I checked the central claim with my own tools rather than theirs and it holds: a hundred of a hundred and twenty-one now have a route, the main quest gets from five quests deep to twenty-eight, and when I deliberately broke the code that lets you look at a mark, the same four tests went from all passing to all failing. The writing is genuinely good. But it has habits: nineteen of the twenty-six documents end by telling you where the paper is kept and whether the drawer is locked, all eight of the questions in the whole collection are the same short pointed question in eight different mouths, and one ledger does the reader's arithmetic for them in a voice that belongs to nobody in the document. And the list the round left behind of the eleven people still missing from the game names three who aren't blocking anything and leaves out three who are.
detail: Six things were checked. (1) The prose, read end to end. The Blackrose lease stubs — where a clerk has written the word 'again' four times against the same twelve people and a later clerk rules the total at four hundred and eleven and initials it so the next one knows it is a real count — are excellent, and the arithmetic checks to the digit. Against the project's own measured yardstick, though, the word 'four' appears in seventy-seven percent of the twenty-six documents and 'eleven' in thirty-one percent, where the real Morrowind books measured for comparison use 'eleven' in under three percent. The prose checker passes the file because its rule for that was deliberately narrowed years of rounds ago and never covered 'four'. (2) The claim most likely to be wrong: a leftover line in an old measuring tool that hands the game answers it should have to earn. It turns out that tool was never used for the headline number, and I proved with a fresh tool that switching the line off changes nothing anyway. (3) The headline number itself came from the builder's own instrument, so I built a different one that plays the whole main quest through the real game logic with no browser at all — two of the three published figures came back identical, to the same quest and the same missing fact. The third didn't, and the gap turned out to be my tool's, not theirs, which I say so. (4) The proof that the world actually reads any of this: re-run, four of four, and zero of three once I broke it on a copy. (5) The twenty-one truths still unreachable: count confirmed exactly, composition corrected. Seven of the nine that need eavesdropping already have the people; only two need writing. (6) Two bugs the round found in a browser and fixed — one where documents got stacked so close together that pressing the button opened the wrong one, another where every reset left the world with no marks in it at all. Both hold: I checked all eighty-three rooms in the game and six resets in a row rather than one. Along the way I found that the little pixel font nine of this project's chart tools share is broken in a way nobody had noticed: two dots are missing from the middle of every letter and number, which slides everything below them sideways. The round reported it for its own chart and fixed its digits, but it is in nine tools, and in the round's own published picture the word BOOK reads as POOK. Score 6.5 against a bar of 7 — a near miss on a strong round, failing on a hand-off list built from the wrong query and a reporting bug that was found, half-diagnosed and never scoped. Full reasoning: corpus/90-verdicts/wave1/W1-READABLES-r2.md

headline: The rulebook and the game disagreed about how an NPC picks what to say, and nobody had noticed that every tool built to check the dialogue was checking the rulebook's version. Morrowind's rule is simple: the writers put the answers in an order and the game reads down the list and takes the first one that fits the person you are. Ours quietly scored each answer for how specific it was and took the highest. Most of the time those agree — the writers had already put the fussiest answers first — but on eight subjects, from the price of a room in Stormhold to who really witnessed a killing in Gideon, the game overrules the writer and says something else. I measured it properly for the first time: 1.9 million of 1.46 billion possible conversations come out differently, which is 37 places in the world where a specific person gives a specific wrong answer. The ruling is that the game changes, not the rulebook, because dialogue is Morrowind's to own. The bigger discovery is what this made invisible. A tool had been run to tidy the order of every answer file, and it reported that it changed nothing, and that was treated as proof it was safe. It could not have changed anything: under the scoring rule the order only matters in one topic in the whole province. The reassuring zero was guaranteed before the tool ran. Once the game follows the writers' order, shuffling it moves 18% of all conversations — so the same check finally means something. There is a test now that a future writer can run to see whether the game and the rulebook still agree, and I broke it on purpose to prove it goes red. Separately, and worse: thirteen conversations were written to open a journal entry when you ask about them, and nothing in the game reads that instruction. Delete it entirely and not one word changes anywhere. That is the twentieth thing this project has found that was carefully written and plugged into nothing.

I sat down and actually played the opening the way you would — I opened the page with no special settings, pressed the keys, and nothing else. The good news is real: the title screen comes up, you press New, and you are standing in the hold of a prison barge in third person with a woman on the other bench, a knife on the floor, and not one word of explanation anywhere. You can walk around for as long as you like and nobody asks you anything; she only speaks when you go over and reach for her, which is exactly the trick Morrowind's famous opening pulls. Then it falls over twice. When you type your name, fourteen of the twenty-six letters are silently swallowed, because those keys are also the buttons for walking and swinging a sword — so I typed "Silt-Under-Salt" and the game wrote down "il-Un" — and the letter E is the talk button, so typing it ends the conversation in the middle of your own name. And when you walk up to the clerk who is supposed to write you into the province's records, the game stops dead: nothing ever told it what species you are, so the clerk repeats an internal error message at you forever and the door out is locked until she has written you down. Every impressive number this part of the game has ever reported was measured through a back door that fills in that missing detail automatically, so nobody had noticed. Both are small repairs, and the writing they are hiding is genuinely better than the game it is chasing.
detail: W1-26 round 2 verdict: FAIL 1.3/10 (RI-JRN09 2, RI-JRN01 2, RI-EXP01 0), unchanged from round 1 for entirely different reasons. Round 1's biggest gap is closed and O6 — control before definition — is repaired and measures 61.5 s against a 60 s bar. Three new caps: creation cannot be completed from the title (censusBegin({}) never observes a race); text entry is shadowed by the control map; and DTR 0.000 at hold.out, where Jeeh-Ei's reply to your name is drawn in the next room by the wrong speaker.

headline: A tenth of the best writing in this game could not be heard by anybody. Not badly written, not hidden behind a hard quest - simply addressed to people who did not exist. One hundred and thirty-six lines of dialogue were written for a Gideon records-clerk, a Stormhold sap-buyer, a Lilmoth gravedigger and a House Dres magister, and when we went to look, the province had no such people in it. The magister was the worst of it: twenty-three lines, some of the sharpest in the whole script, written for a man the story names out loud - you can ask about Varo Dren and the answer is 'I am he' - and Varo Dren had never been put into the world. Nobody could say it back to you. So this round did not write a single new line. It gave the existing ones mouths. Twenty-two people were added to the towns their lines were already written for, and twenty more lines were handed to somebody who was standing there all along under a different job title - the notary who was filed as an archivist, the harbourmistress filed as a clerk. One hundred and thirty of the hundred and thirty-six can now be heard by a real player standing in front of a real person. We also had to fix the measuring tape twice on the way: the tool that counts unheard lines was quietly confusing unrelated topics with each other, and the tool that checks each character type has its own verbal tic was only reading half of what it was told to read - which had made one archetype look broken when it was fine. And we deleted thirteen lines of machinery that was supposed to open a quest journal when you asked about something, because it pointed at thirteen quests nobody ever wrote.

The main road out of the capital ran straight through a scribe's house, and it had done since the day both were built. Two different pieces of the world-builder were responsible: one drew the roads across the landscape, the other put the towns down afterwards, and neither of them had ever been shown the other's work. Nobody had noticed because each was doing its own job perfectly well - the road was a good road, the house was a good house, and the wall between them only existed for anyone actually trying to walk past. Which is what we finally did: we put a body on the province's headline journey, the hour-long walk from Stormhold to Lilmoth, and it got thirty-nine metres before it stopped dead against somebody's back wall and stood there for sixteen simulated minutes. All ten roads in the province had the same problem somewhere along them. The fix was to decide which side gives way, and we chose the road: a town is where it is for reasons, a road is only ever a way of getting somewhere. So the road-builder now reads the town plans before it lays anything down, and wherever a road comes within fifty-five metres of a building it re-cuts that stretch on a one-metre grid with the houses treated as walls. Crucially it does not swing wide around the town, which would have been a worse world than the bug - it threads between the houses and becomes the street, the way a road does in Morrowind. The whole detour costs ninety-five metres on a seven-kilometre crossing, about forty-eight seconds of walking. Ten roads out of ten are now clear, and the body walks five hundred and fifty metres instead of thirty-nine. It still does not reach Lilmoth: past the capital it climbs the Valus Ridge and slips off the edge of the road onto a fifty-seven-degree hillside it cannot climb back up. That is a separate and older fault - the same steep stretches were on the old road too - and nobody had ever got past the wall to find it.

The province had a hundred and fifty-two books in it and ninety-nine of them were in no room, no shelf, no pocket and no hand. They existed only as files. The best writing in this project is a pair of accounts of the same afternoon at a river crossing - an Imperial prefect who was four years old when it happened, building a battle out of four words in somebody's day-book, and a weir-woman answering him with 'a line is what you form when you do not know' - and a player could not have read either one. Nineteen arguments are formally registered in this game as arguments, two books each, deliberately disagreeing. You could get to both sides of three of them. Now you can get to both sides of all nineteen, because ninety-nine texts have been put into forty rooms that already existed, on the rule that a book lives where its argument is had rather than in a library: the army's standing instruction is in the Stormhold garrison and the sergeant who thinks it is nonsense wrote his answer in the back of his own book in a different town's guardhouse. The Empire's pamphlet about how happy everyone is sits in the customs house that hands it out, and the salt-factor's private ledger, which is the answer to it, sits in another building across the town. We proved it the only way that counts: walk in, stand at the shelf, press the button a player presses, and watch the right book open - then take the placements out again on a copy and watch the shelf be empty. The second thing was the names. More than half the Argonians in this game were called things like Falura Nine-Teeth, which is a Dark Elf first name bolted to an English nickname, and one of them was 'Sedura Nine-Teeth' - sedura is a Dark Elf honorific, so the town roster contained an Argonian called Sir Nine-Teeth. Forty-three names were being worn by more than one person, one of them by six people in five different towns, and eighteen had a bit of the generator's plumbing still showing in them ('of salvage yard', with no 'the'). Argonians in the source material have names in their own language, and the descriptive nicknames are a minority form - eleven percent of the real ones. Ours were fifty-six percent. They are now ten, every coined name built out of the project's own root-list and passed through the project's own phonology checker, and every name that was written by a human being was left exactly alone. And we wrote eleven small things the library did not have: six songs and five children's stories, including a toll clerk's tariff set to forced rhyme, a lullaby out of the plague years that two households end differently, and the story of the girl on the Soulrest steps who carried a full jar up all forty of them for thirty years without spilling and is in none of the Chapter's books.

Magic in this game is supposed to work the way Morrowind's did: you don't pick a spell off a list, you build one. How strong, how long, how wide - three dials, and you turn them yourself. This round finally connected two of those dials to something. Turn the width up and a fireball catches four people in a room instead of one. Turn the strength up on a summoning and the creature that crawls out is genuinely bigger. Both of those hold up: I rebuilt the tests from scratch to try to catch them out and they are real. Three things do not hold up. The first is quiet and expensive: a spell cast by touch fires itself four to seven times instead of once, so the cheapest way to cast is also five times the strongest, and nobody had noticed because the measuring tools all preferred touch. The second is stranger. Casting the same summoning spell six times in a row gives you six different creatures - the sixth hits fifty-four times harder than the first - because the code that makes a summon strong is accidentally editing the master record every monster of that kind is built from. The spell has a permanent side effect on the world. And the third is the big one. All the machinery for building your own spell exists and works: the price, the limits, the sensible refusals, even the way it silently trims a spell you've asked too much of. There is no way into it. No shop, no screen, no person. The game's own notes name four spellwrights and say that walking to one is part of what a spell costs; none of the four is anywhere in the world. A player would finish this game having cast only the seventy-two spells somebody else wrote for them, which is precisely the thing this whole system was built to avoid.

In a game where the weight of your gear decides how well you dodge, the sword and shield in your hands weighed nothing. Not a little - nothing at all. You could be holding the biggest two-handed sword in the game and the heaviest tower shield, and the number that decides how many frames you are untouchable for during a roll read 0.00%. It only counted your clothes. Worse, there were two right hands: picking a maul up off the floor and equipping it made you heavier, while the fight went on swinging the sword you started with. The weight of the maul and the weapon you were actually using were different objects that had never been introduced. Both are one object now. Equipping something puts it in your hand and on the scales at the same time, and taking it off gives you your old weapon back. The numbers were already in the game and nothing had ever read them: fifteen weapon classes each with a declared weight, from a 1 kg dagger to a 20 kg ultra greatsword, and every shield with a weight too. Nothing was invented to make this work. The effect is immediate: the same five pieces of armour that used to leave you in the nimblest roll tier now push you into the middle one, and a full heavy kit reaches the fat-roll tier for the first time. One more thing was in the rulebook and in no code anywhere: being overloaded is supposed to stop you sprinting. It didn't. An overloaded character covered exactly the same ten metres for exactly the same stamina as a featherweight one. Now holding the sprint button while overloaded covers 6.4 metres and costs nothing, which is precisely what happens if you never press it. Reported plainly and not fixed: the heaviest legal outfit in the game still cannot reach the top tier, because the wardrobe tops out at 49.8 kg and you would need 65. That needs armour that does not exist yet, and making some up to hit a number would be cheating.

Every enemy in this game has something like a mind: it knows what it is doing, who it is fighting, how long since it last swung, and where home is, so that if you run far enough it gives up and walks back. Saving the game destroyed all of that in a way nobody could see. The save wrote the mind out as a lifeless list of numbers - it copied down what the guard was thinking but not the ability to think - and when you loaded, the guard got the list back instead of the mind. The very next moment of the game crashed. And this is the part that cost other people real work: the project's standard health check starts the game up and takes one picture, and this failure does not happen until the game actually runs a frame after a load, so the health check said everything was fine for a week. Four other teams hit the crash, could not see where it came from, and lost measurements to it - one set of map results was written up as four map failures when the map was innocent. It is fixed properly: the mind is now saved as what it knows, and rebuilt as what it is. Two things came free. The save file shrank by 42 percent, because copying the guard's mind was accidentally copying the entire rulebook of the game into every guard. And the guard now remembers where home is across a reload, which it did not before - we proved that by writing a false home into a save file, loading it, and watching the guard turn round and walk toward the lie. The health check now loads a save and takes another step, which is the thing it never did; we broke the game on purpose first to make sure it noticed, and it did, twice, in both of the two different ways this can go wrong.

title: The charts have been spelling numbers wrong, and one of them said POOK
body: Every chart this project publishes draws its text with a tiny hand-made letter shape table, and that table was two dots short in every single letter. Because the drawing code counts dots in fixed rows of five, two missing dots do not leave a small gap at the end — they shove every row below them one dot to the left, so the shape shears apart. Nothing crashed, because a sheared letter is still a picture of a letter. It just is not the right one. A 2 came out looking more like an 8, an 8 more like a 6, and in the picture published yesterday the word BOOK came out as POOK. Nine chart tools carried a copy of the same broken table, and two more were written today by copying it again. The table now lives in one place, written as five rows of five you can read at a glance, and the code refuses to load it at all if a row is the wrong width — so this exact mistake can no longer be made quietly. There is a test that renders 28 OF 32 and BOOK and checks them dot by dot, and it has been watched failing on the old table so we know it is capable of failing. Six published pictures have been redrawn; the rest are named in the report so the people who made them can redraw their own.

title: The towns have outsides now, and one inn is a shed with a hall inside it
body: Two rounds of work on Argonia's eight towns came up for judgement together, and both of the big things they set out to fix are genuinely fixed. Walking through a door now shows you the room the file describes - I checked that by reaching behind the game and moving the picture without telling the world, to be sure the check was reading the screen and not just believing the game's own paperwork. And the towns have buildings for the first time: 202 of them, olive walls and shell domes and arched doorways, where three weeks ago there was bare ground with people standing on it. But two things came out of it that nobody had spotted. The first is that to stop the buildings overlapping, this round quietly shrank 54 of them - and left the rooms inside them the original size. So 41 buildings are now smaller on the outside than they are on the inside, and the worst is Blackrose's inn: a shed three metres across whose door opens onto a room four times wider than the whole building. There is a picture. The second is about how the project measures pictures at all. There is a test that walks into all 115 rooms, photographs each one, and counts how many photographs are different - the idea being that if all the rooms look the same, something is wrong. It reported 115 different pictures, which sounds like a pass. Then I ran it again with the room-building code switched off, so every door opened on the same empty hall, and it still reported 115 different pictures. It turns out the game's picture changes very slightly every single frame, so photographs taken at different moments are never identical, and the test was counting the clock rather than the rooms. The test had actually printed a warning about this to itself and nobody had read it. The verdict is still a fail - 4.6 out of 10 against a bar of 7 - but it is a fail with the foundations finally under it.

title: Two people asked the same clerk the same question, and the game and every tool that checks the game disagreed about the answer
body: When you ask somebody in this world a question, the game looks down a list of possible answers and picks one. There were two rules for picking, and they disagreed with each other. The design document says: read the list from the top, use the first answer that fits. The game actually did something cleverer - it scored every answer on how specific it looked, and used the highest score. An arbiter ruled that the document wins, and this piece made the game obey it. The scoring was deleted rather than adjusted, because the point was never which answers come out; it was who decides. Under scoring, the order the writers put their lines in was ignored, so a writer could not be wrong and there was nothing to check. Now the order is the answer, and a checker can catch a line that has been buried. Landing that turned up something worse than the ruling knew about. The answers for one subject are often spread across several files - 92 of 468 subjects, holding 488 of the 1,280 lines - and those files get stacked in some order before anything is read. Nobody had ever chosen that order. It came from whatever order the files happened to be listed in, and it turned out the game and every tool that measures the game were listing them differently. Measured: 5,760 answers came out different in the real game from what every measurement of the game said. A customs clerk in Soulrest genuinely said one thing when you played and a different thing when anybody checked. There is now a file that simply states the order, the game reads it, and adding a new file of dialogue without saying where it goes is refused outright. The two orderings now agree exactly, including when the files are fed in backwards on purpose. The change has a price and it was paid in the open rather than hidden: five lines of writing that used to be reachable no longer are, and all five are named. Every one of them is a specific answer sitting in a later file behind a more general answer in an earlier file, so they are a writing problem with a known fix rather than a fault in the reader. Finally, the tool that sorts these files was re-run and had nothing left to do - but the safety check that was cited in its own notes as proof the sorting changes nothing turned out never to have been written. It exists now, and when deliberately broken it moves 33,030 answers, where under the old rule it could not have moved more than one subject's worth. That is the difference between a measurement and a formality.

headline: Last time round, anyone who opened their save file in a text editor could type the names of forty-two places into it and the game's map would then show all forty-two, including thirty-five the character had never been anywhere near. That is fixed, and it is fixed in the right way: the save no longer has a place-name field at all. It carries only the list of squares of ground your feet have actually been on, and the map is worked out fresh from that every time you load. I wrote a save with eight different forged fields in it, including four the game has never heard of, and the map came back showing the same six places I had genuinely walked to and not one more - and the game listed, by name, all thirty-six places my save had lied about. The other big fix also holds: the game has six screens, and last time five of them had no door. Pressing real keys on a real keyboard, and then a real gamepad, I can now walk through all six and back out again. But two of the three measuring tools this round changed were never actually run, and when I ran them both went red - one of them because the author had written down, in the tool, that the map screen has no readable text on it, when it has two lines of it.
detail: The most interesting concrete fact: the tool that is supposed to catch floating damage numbers over enemies - the only check in this whole piece that looks at the actual picture rather than asking the game to describe itself - had never been run against any version of the game. I ran it. It reported 66 damage numbers hovering over six enemies. I cut those 66 out of the frame and looked at them: every single one is the ridge of an enemy's helmet or the dark line of its jaw. The tool is measuring a 1280-by-720 patch of a 1920-by-1080 picture, so it is not even looking where it thinks it is looking; it graded a frame in which the sword never connected; and its own self-test finds ten digits in a place where three were drawn. Around it, eleven of the fifteen checks in this piece's five measuring tools will report a pass if they happen to measure nothing at all - including two that are written to pass on absence on purpose. That is the gap: the fixes are real, and the instruments that are meant to prove they stay fixed cannot currently tell 'nothing is wrong' from 'nothing was looked at'.

headline: Last round, the sword in your hand weighed nothing. A character holding the heaviest weapon and the heaviest shield in the game was, as far as the dodge was concerned, carrying air. That is genuinely fixed now, and I checked it myself rather than taking anyone's word for it: a garrison sword and a medium shield come to 13% of what the character can carry, an ultra greatsword and a tower shield to 45%, and the dodge really does get shorter because of it. Picking up a maul and equipping it now actually changes the weapon you swing, which it did not before. And the heaviest tier - the one that stops you sprinting - can finally be entered without a debug switch: put on everything the game ships and cast the Burden spell the game ships, and you are there, and the sprint button stops doing anything. But there is a new hole and it is a bad one. Save the game in the middle of a fight, load it back, and your dodge loses four frames of invulnerability. Nothing in the world changed. The save file records how heavy you were and then never reads it back, so on reload the game recalculates - and because the sword now counts, the answer lands on the wrong side of a threshold. In both of the two practice arenas that every combat measurement in this project is taken in.
detail: The round's own safety argument was that the practice arenas state their weight explicitly, so nothing it changed could disturb them. That is true right up until somebody saves. Its own check for exactly this problem loaded all forty-nine of the game's scenes and never saved one of them, so it could not see it. I ran the same scene twice with the round's own break-switch: with the new sword-weight counted, saving and reloading takes you from 26 frames of invulnerability to 22; with it switched off, the same save and the same reload leave all 26 in place. So the new feature is what tips it over. Three smaller things. A spell called Feather, whose whole purpose is to make you lighter, leaves you heavier than you started if it is bigger than your current load - the code floors the number at zero when the spell lands and then adds the whole amount back when it wears off. Measured: you go in at 13%, sit at 0 while it lasts, and come out at 43% in a worse dodge class. Second, the formula the design document gives has four things in it and the game now counts three; the fourth, a talisman, has no weight, no slot and nothing reading it anywhere. Third, there is a bow in the game that cannot be picked up because it names a weapon type that does not exist. Refusing to pick it up is the right call. But nothing tells the player: you press the button and the game does nothing at all, says nothing, and the explanation goes to a log file no player will ever see.

title: You can make a character and walk out of the room now, and you can type your own name while you do it
body: Three things stood between the owner of this project and playing their own game, and all three are fixed. The first: choosing 'New game' from the title screen put you in a barge hold, let you walk around, let a woman on the other bench ask your name - and then, at the desk where a clerk writes you down, the game quietly broke. The clerk's job is to LOOK at you and write down what she sees, and nothing anywhere ever told her what you were. So she failed, and the error message the programmers wrote for themselves - 'race must be observed before the scene reaches the desk' - was printed on screen in her voice, as though it were something she had said, with the door held shut behind you. That is worse than crashing, because it looks like writing. Two repairs, not one: the clerk now looks at the body you are actually standing in, which is a real thing the rest of the world already reads, so changing it changes what she says out loud AND what gets written on your papers - I checked that with four different bodies and got four different sentences and four different documents. And a caught error can never again be printed as dialogue: the programmer's text goes to the log, and what she says instead is a line somebody actually wrote for her. The second defect: you could not type your own name. Fourteen of the twenty-six letters were wired to buttons - W walked, E was 'interact', space was 'dodge' - and the keyboard checked the buttons before it checked the text box, so those letters silently vanished. Worse, typing an E ended the conversation mid-word. A critic predicted, from the settings file alone and before opening a browser, that 'Silt-Under-Salt' would be recorded as 'il-Un'. It was. Now a text box takes the keyboard first while it has your attention, and I typed a name containing every letter of the alphabet plus spaces and a hyphen and got all thirty-one characters back exactly. Movement is untouched everywhere else; the box only claims the keys while it is open. The third: the woman in the hold says your name back to you and remarks on it - the single moment the whole opening is built around, and the thing Morrowind is most remembered for doing. It was being drawn one room later, above a completely different person's head, in a room the first woman is not in. Her own goodbye was never drawn at all. Both are now said where and when she says them. Then I made a whole character using nothing but a keyboard, start to finish, and took a photograph of them standing in the world holding their stamped papers. There is also a ./play.sh at the root now: one command, and it prints a link. One correction to the record while I was in there: the previous round reported that the test walker got physically wedged on a crate in the barge hold and could not reach the way out. It had not. I put a body on the exact spot and pushed it in all eight directions and it moved every time, seven different ways. What had actually happened is that the game had stopped running altogether, and the walker had no way to tell 'stuck against furniture' from 'nothing is moving at all' - both look like zero. It can tell now. I also caught myself making the same mistake inside the test written to catch that mistake, and fixed it before reporting it.

title: The charts that were spelling numbers wrong are all fixed now, and the door is bolted behind them
body: Every chart and diagram this project publishes draws its letters and numbers from a tiny hand-made alphabet - a grid of dots, five across and five down, for each character. That alphabet was written down wrong. Each character was two dots short, and because the drawing code counts along in fives regardless, every row below the missing dots got shoved one dot to the left. Three or four of the five rows came out wrong on most characters. Nothing ever complained, because a squashed letter is still a picture of a letter, and nobody was checking. What makes it worth the fuss is that the damage is not random: a squashed 2 comes out looking more like an 8 than like a 2, and a squashed 8 looks more like a 6. So a published finding could be read as a completely different number. Somebody fixed the alphabet itself last time and repaired eight of the drawing tools. Five were left, four of them because the people who owned them were still mid-job. This round finished all five. The count of tools still carrying the bad alphabet is now zero, down from five. Three of the four affected pictures have been redrawn and now say what they were always meant to say. And the check that spots the bad alphabet, which until now only printed a polite warning, has been turned into a hard stop: nobody can commit it back into the project a third time. That mattered, because two of the five tools I fixed had been written on the day of the original repair, by someone copying the broken alphabet in all over again. It was still spreading while it was being fixed.
detail: The fourth picture I deliberately did not redraw, and that is the interesting part. It belongs to a piece about a road out of the capital that ran straight through somebody's house. Its numbers are still drawn in the broken alphabet. But when I regenerated it, the whole map moved, not just the text - so I chased why rather than shrugging. Another piece had since rerouted the roads to go between the houses instead of through them, which changed the length of that journey from 6,816 to 6,911 metres. I proved that was the only thing that had changed by rebuilding the picture with the old road data and watching it come back identical to the published one. So redrawing it at today's data would have quietly restated somebody else's later finding under the original author's headline - a different false statement, not a fix. It goes back to its owner, whose remaining job is exactly that road join, with the tool now clean so the redraw is one command. I also went looking through all 164 published pictures by reading the actual pixels, rather than trusting the list of filenames the tools say they write, because the previous round had said plainly that it never looked at the images. The first version of that pixel-reader passed its own test and then got all four known-bad pictures wrong, because charts are full of straight lines and a five-by-five window slid over them finds tens of thousands of accidental matches for a hyphen. Fixed by only counting letters and digits, and only in runs of three or more sitting on the same line - which is to say, only counting actual words.

title: The map is the good news; the save file is the bad news
body:
The game now has a map, because the owner overruled an earlier decision that it should not. It is meant to be a Morrowind map and not a modern one: it shows only ground you have actually walked, a small gold square for each place you have personally stood in, and your own position and facing. No quest markers, no arrows, no routes, no 'travel here' button, no distances. I spent this round trying to break it.

First I had to re-check four earlier results. A bug elsewhere in the game meant that whenever you saved and reloaded with an enemy nearby, the next moment of simulation crashed - so a test that walked a character around was really a test of a character who never moved. Somebody fixed that bug and listed my predecessor's map results as possibly worthless. They are not. I re-ran all four twice, once in an empty world and once with three live enemies on the floor, and got identical answers both ways. The previous critic had already spotted the problem and guarded against it, and the guard worked. Nothing false was ever published. That is the system doing what it is supposed to do.

The map itself holds up beautifully. Undiscovered ground is not greyed out or fogged - it is genuinely never drawn, so there is no coastline to squint at. A place only appears once you have physically stood in it: walking past at forty metres gives you nothing, and being TOLD about a place by a quest or a conversation gives you nothing either. I checked. The name that appears when you point at a square is the place's own name and carries no quest information at all. The pictures are worth a look.

And then there is the hole. The map trusts exactly one thing in your save file: a compressed trail of the squares of ground your body has occupied. Everything else on screen is worked out from that one trail, which was a deliberate design decision and a good one. But it means that if you can edit that one field, you own the map. The previous critic showed this. I showed something worse: you do not need any special tools. I asked the game to save a doctored record, and the game politely sealed it for me with its own tamper-check, and then loaded it back without complaint. The result is the fourth picture: the entire province revealed and all forty-two places named, for a character who has walked nowhere at all. It survives being played afterwards, too - I spawned enemies and ran three seconds of real simulation on it and nothing fell over.

The part that troubles me most is not the hole, it is that the game says it is fine. Every self-check the map runs reads clean on that forged screen: places drawn equals places discovered, markers zero, routes zero, nothing rejected. The game's own test suite passes 32 out of 32 on the same build, including the test named 'a forged save is refused' - which passes because it forges a field the loading code no longer reads. Meanwhile the loading code already works out exactly the evidence that would catch this, and then throws it away. Publishing that one number would make the forgery visible immediately. That is the main thing I have asked for.

Two smaller things. There is still a spot in memory where anything inside the game can swap the whole map out for a fake one - one line of code closes it, and it was pointed out a round ago. And I found a mistake in my own method worth admitting: the test everyone has been using to prove undiscovered ground is blank was reading the menu's own drawing surface rather than the picture on screen. On the real screen the parchment is slightly see-through and the world behind it shows faintly through the black. That turns out not to break the rule - what shows through is the room you are standing in, not the province - but the number people were quoting was measuring the wrong thing, so I rebuilt it to measure the screen and to tell those two causes apart.

Score 3 out of 10 against a bar of 7. That reads harsher than the screen deserves: as a piece of design this is one of the best things in the project. The whole distance from the bar is one field the game trusts and one door nobody locked.

title: The road was never too steep. The walker was looking at the wrong thing.
body: For three sessions nobody could walk from Stormhold to Lilmoth. The last report said a 57-degree slope on the Valus Ridge was stopping the body. It wasn't. We measured the actual gradient of every road in the province: the steepest is 24 degrees, and a person can walk 40. The road was fine all along. What the body had actually done was fall off a bridge — the road over the ridge is a viaduct 471 metres long standing fifty metres above the mountainside, and the walker was steering straight at the next milestone rather than following the road, so on every bend it cut the corner and walked off the edge. It now steers at the road itself: if it gets knocked off, its next step is back towards the road. On the ridge it now holds the middle of a six-metre deck to within 1.2 metres. That same defect is almost certainly what has been drowning bodies on the Soulrest road, where the ground is completely innocent and a body was still managing 6.4 kilometres of an 1.8 kilometre walk. And one more thing turned up: the province is dangerous. A body that walks the crossing without ever sheltering or healing is killed by the weather and the rockfalls before the halfway point.

title: You can lie to the map about where you've walked. That was never the rule it was breaking.
body:
The game's map has one rule that everything else hangs off: it only ever shows you ground you have actually walked, and it puts a small square on a place only if you personally stood there. A critic found a way round it. Your save file lives on your own computer, and inside it is the trail of ground your character has covered. Edit that trail and you can claim to have walked the whole province. The map believes you, because there is nothing it could check you against — the save IS the history. The critic said, fairly, that if the rule means what it appears to mean then no game could ever pass it, and handed the question up rather than failing the build for it.

I ruled on it today. The rule is real, but it is not about cheating. Look at what else is on its forbidden list: no quest markers, no arrows, no routes, no 'show me on the map' links, no distances. Every one of those is about the GAME telling the PLAYER something it shouldn't. The clause about squares is the rule that makes the rest of them enforceable — if the only thing that can put a square on the map is your own feet, then no quest, no conversation and no journal entry can put one there, because there is nowhere for them to write it. It was never a promise that you couldn't cheat. The owner's reason for wanting a map in the first place was 'Morrowind has a map, Morrowind doesn't have quest markers' — and Morrowind's map, incidentally, has always been editable in exactly the same way. Nobody has ever thought that was a flaw in Morrowind.

So I drew the line where a design can actually hold it: the game cannot check whether you are telling the truth, and shouldn't pretend to, but it can guarantee that it never shows you anything MORE than what you claimed. I proved that rather than asserting it. The province is 42,846 squares of ground. I fed the game each one of them, one at a time, as a forged claim — with every other lie an attacker could write in the save bolted on alongside — and checked what came back. All 42,846: not one square, and not one patch of ground, that the claim didn't already account for. Because of how the code is written, that's not a spot check, it covers every save file that could ever exist. Run the same test against the version from before the fix and you get 1,798,811 squares drawn with nothing underneath them.

The nicest thing I found was an argument against the obvious fix. You could demand that the claimed trail be joined-up, the way a real walk is — a scattered forgery would then be rejected. I measured it. The cheapest forgery today is 42 numbers, 108 bytes, and it reveals 34% of the province. Force it to be joined up and the forger writes 848 numbers instead and reveals 46%. Making the rule stricter makes the forged map show MORE, because every extra square you claim lights up the countryside around it. That settled it.

And the last piece: the forger has to know which squares to name, and the only place those coordinates exist is a 16-kilobyte plain-text file sitting on the same disk that lists all 42 places by name at full precision. Faking the save is a slower way of reading a file you already have. It isn't a leak.

The ruling ships with a test anyone can run, which I also broke on purpose five different ways to prove it can go red. I also found the check that was supposed to be enforcing all this: it still tests for the old rule, from before the owner changed his mind, and asks whether the map exists at all. It has been impossible to pass for days.

title: The road was fixed. Twenty-four minutes later the houses grew and it was broken again.
body:
Yesterday a builder fixed something bad: the main road out of the capital ran straight through a scribe's house, and it had done since the day both were built. Ten of the ten roads in the province had a building standing on them. The fix was elegant and it worked — the road now threads BETWEEN the houses and becomes the street, instead of detouring round the town, and when it was measured it came back clean: nothing on any road anywhere.

I checked that number, and it was true. It was true for twenty-four minutes.

What happened next is the interesting part, and it is nobody's carelessness. A different agent, working on a different problem, noticed that some buildings were being drawn far too small — an inn shrunk to the size of a shed while the room inside it stayed full size. It fixed that. Fifty-four buildings across the province got bigger; not one got smaller. Nobody touched the roads, and nobody touched the map. But the walls moved, and the road stayed where it was, and today five houses in the town of Blackrose are standing on it again. The main crossing of the province runs into a wall at the five and a half kilometre mark.

The reason this could happen is worth writing down plainly, because it is the shape of mistake this project keeps making in new costumes. The road is worked out once, ahead of time, and written into a file. The buildings are worked out fresh every time the game starts. So the road is an ANSWER to a question that can change afterwards, and nothing was set up to ask the question again. The builder actually saw this coming and wrote it down — but wrote it down as 'someone might edit the town data', when what actually changed was the code that decides how big a building is. It also spotted that the check for this ought to be run automatically before every commit, and then didn't add it, because the list of automatic checks is generated by a tool and it felt like someone else's file.

The repair is one command, and I ran it on a scratch copy to be sure: rebuild the roads and the province goes straight back to clean, exactly and repeatably. So this is a good piece of work sitting one command away from being true.

I also settled two arguments while I was in there. The builder said the OTHER thing still blocking the crossing — a body stuck on a mountainside — wasn't its fault, and it was right, though its reasoning didn't actually show that: I measured the old road and the new road at the exact spot where the body stops, and they are twenty-one centimetres apart. The road didn't move; something else is wrong there, and another agent is already on it. And a finding that three agents have been waiting on — 'the town walls are not what is drowning bodies on the Soulrest road' — turned out to have been proved on a version of the world where the walls had already been cleared away from that road, so switching them off couldn't possibly have changed anything. The conclusion was right. I re-ran it on today's world, where the walls really are back on that road, and it still holds. Those three agents can stop testing walls now — but on the new evidence, not the old.

title: The books are on the shelves now — and then I found four you still cannot open
body: Last time round, this project had a library of a hundred and fifty-two texts that almost nobody could reach. Ninety-nine of them were named nowhere in the game at all. Nineteen pairs of books had been written to deliberately disagree with each other - that is the point of them, two people telling the same story differently and the game never saying who is right - and a player could get to both sides of three of those nineteen. The two books arguing about whether the Empire keeps people as property, which is the biggest moral question in the province, existed only as files on a disk. This round put them all in rooms, and put the two halves of sixteen arguments in two different buildings on purpose, thirteen of them in different towns, because an argument you find on one shelf is a folder and an argument you have to travel between is an argument. The standing order about how soldiers form up is in the Stormhold garrison and the sergeant who thinks it is nonsense wrote his answer in the back of his own book in Blackrose. I did not take that on trust. I opened a browser, walked to twelve of those books in twelve rooms, stood a metre away, pressed the button a player presses, and checked three things each time: the right book opened, words actually appeared on the screen, and they were THAT book's words and not another one's. Twelve out of twelve, and there is now a photograph of one of them open - the first picture anyone in this project has taken of a book in this game. The round's own filed picture was a bar chart of how many books there are. Then, because twelve is a sample and not a census, I went back and walked every single document in the six most crowded rooms - forty-five of them. Four do not open. You can stand in front of them, they are drawn on the wall, and pressing the button does nothing at all. One of the four is half of one of those nineteen arguments. The reason is worth understanding because it will happen again: this game has two separate ways of putting a document in a room, and neither one knows where the other has put things. Books on shelves are spaced out carefully so you can stand at each one. Quest papers are dropped at fixed coordinates by completely different code. When they land within half a metre of each other, the game hands your button press to whichever is nearer, and the book behind it becomes unreadable forever. Every automatic check in the project says this is fine. So do two of the checks I wrote myself. It took walking all forty-five.
detail: The other half of the round was names. Two hundred and seventeen Argonians were carrying English descriptive names like 'Falura Nine-Teeth' - fifty-six per cent of them, against a real Elder Scrolls figure of eleven - with Dark Elf first names bolted on, forty-three names reused across different towns, and eighteen carrying a visible bug where the template leaked into the name ('Llarara the Elder of salvage yard'). Five hundred and twenty-one people have genuinely been renamed. I checked the percentage moved because the names moved and not because somebody redefined which names counted: not one person was reclassified. The share is now nine per cent, the reuse is zero, the template leak is zero, and not a single hand-written character in the story was touched. Then I gave myself the test the design document calls 'the test that actually matters' and which no tool can take: twenty-one names, no context, say which culture each belongs to. I built the pack so it could not be answered by anything except the sound of the word, and it threw out its own first two drafts for accidentally making the answer guessable from name length. Twenty-one out of twenty-one. What holds the score down is almost silly: the design document fails the whole naming system if more than two per cent of names cannot be sorted into a culture, and eight of three hundred and thirty-seven cannot - two point three seven per cent. Five of those eight are not bad names at all. Four are Imperial officers whose rank is stored in one place and whose name is stored in another, so the checker sees 'Sedd' where the rule wants 'Marcus Sedd'. Putting a first name in front of four of them, without changing the existing word, takes the whole system from a hard fail to a pass. I ran that against the project's own checker rather than guessing, twice, and both times it passed. I also found and reported two smaller things against the round: it said a tool that reads text off the screen was blind to the book screen and could not be fixed, and that is not true - the screen only redraws when something changes, and while you are reading a book nothing changes, so ask before you open the book instead of after and fifteen hundred characters come back. And its own naming tool has the same bug it found and fixed in a neighbouring file an hour earlier: load it from another program and it quietly kills that program.

title: The map is sound, the ledger it keeps of its own doubts is not
body:
The game now has a map, because the owner overruled an earlier decision that it should not. It is meant to be a Morrowind map and not a modern one: it shows only ground you have actually walked, a small gold square for each place you have personally stood in, and your own position and facing. No quest markers, no arrows, no routes, no 'travel here' button, no distances. I spent this round trying to break it.

First I had to re-check four earlier results. A bug elsewhere meant that whenever you saved and reloaded with an enemy nearby, the next moment of simulation crashed - so a test that walked a character around was really a test of a character who never moved. Somebody fixed that bug and listed my predecessor's map results as possibly worthless. They are not. I re-ran all four twice, once in an empty world and once with three live enemies on the floor, and got identical answers both ways. The previous critic had already spotted the problem and guarded against it, and the guard worked. Nothing false was ever published. That is the system doing what it is supposed to do.

The map itself holds up beautifully. Undiscovered ground is not greyed out or fogged - it is genuinely never drawn, so there is no coastline to squint at. A place only appears once you have physically stood in it: walking past at forty metres gives you nothing, and being told about a place by a quest or a conversation gives you nothing either. I checked. The name that appears when you point at a square is the place's own name and carries no quest information at all. The pictures are worth a look.

Then I spent most of the round attacking something that turned out not to be a fault. If you edit your save file you can hand the map a fake record of everywhere you have walked, and it will draw you the whole province and name all forty-two places. I pushed this further than anyone had: I got the game to write and seal the forged file itself, using its own tamper-check, and then load it back without complaint. The fourth picture is the result. While I was doing that, somebody else in this project was writing a formal ruling on exactly that question, and it landed in the tree underneath me. Their argument is better than mine: Morrowind's own map has always been editable in a save file and nobody has ever called that a flaw in Morrowind. Asking our map to prove you really took the walk is a bar no design can pass, and it was never what the rule was protecting. The rule exists to stop the GAME volunteering where to go - a quest dropping a pin - and that part is airtight here. So I withdrew the finding instead of arguing with the ruling, and re-ran their check myself rather than take it on trust. It proves the map is honest for every one of the 42,846 pieces of ground the province is made of - not a sample, all of them.

I should say plainly that I missed that ruling for most of the round. I searched the rulebook for the row I was told to read and never noticed the row directly beneath it, which changed the answer. Had I filed my first draft I would have failed this build for something the project had already decided was not its problem.

What did survive is smaller and sharper. The new ruling keeps one promise: if a loaded save's own claims disagree with what the game works out from it, the game must itemise the disagreement rather than quietly swallow it. The loading code does compute that itemisation - seven separate figures - and then every one of them is thrown away before anything can read it. Worse, the new check for that promise only tests the noisy kind of forgery, the one that writes claims for the game to contradict. The quiet kind writes nothing to contradict, and on that one the two figures the check looks at are both zero, while a third figure reads 42,846 and nobody can see it. So the promise reads green and is not being kept.

Two smaller things. There is still a spot in memory where anything inside the game can swap the whole map out for a fake one - that is different from editing a save, because it puts squares on the map with no claim to have walked anywhere at all, and one line of code closes it. And I found a mistake in my own method worth admitting: the test everyone has been using to prove undiscovered ground is blank was reading the menu's own drawing surface rather than the picture on screen. On the real screen the parchment is slightly see-through and the world behind it shows faintly through the black. That turns out not to break the rule - what shows through is the room you are standing in, not the province - but the number people were quoting was measuring the wrong thing, so I rebuilt it to measure the screen and to tell those two causes apart.

Score 4 out of 10 against a bar of 7. That still reads harsher than the screen deserves: as a piece of design this is one of the best things in the project. The whole distance from the bar is a ledger nobody publishes and a door nobody locked.
note: Repaired by W1-04-r4: this line was written over W1-04 round 4s line in place, so it carried W1-04s task id and W1-04s two screenshots under W1-MAPs title and body. The title and body are W1-MAPs and are untouched; the task id is corrected and the two screenshots that were not this pieces have been removed rather than guessed at. W1-04 r4s own line is appended below.

title: Forty-one buildings were smaller on the outside than they were on the inside, and the roofs did not cover the houses
body: A town in this game is built twice: once as the outside you walk past, and once as the room you find when you open the door. Last round somebody made the outsides smaller so buildings would stop standing inside one another - and nobody checked the rooms. The result was forty-one buildings you could walk all the way around in a few paces and then step into a hall four times the size. The worst was the inn at Blackrose: a three-and-a-half-metre shed with a fourteen-metre inn behind its door. That is fixed, and not by making every building big, which would have turned eight distinct towns into eight rows of identical boxes. Where a street is too tight a building now gets narrow instead of getting small - it keeps its depth and becomes a terrace, which is what crowded towns actually look like - and the room behind the door is fitted to the building that holds it. None of the hundred and twelve buildings is now smaller than its own room, and there are thirty-four different building sizes among them. The roofs were the other thing. Every building in two of the eight towns was an open-topped tray with a dome sitting loose inside it, corners open to the sky. You could only see it from above, and a critic's photograph is what found it; sixty-two of those are now roofed, and Archon still has its dome. The last part is about measurement rather than about the world. Twice this project has accepted 'we took a hundred and fifteen photographs of a hundred and fifteen rooms and they all came out different' as proof the rooms are different. They came out different because the clock had moved between the shots: photograph one unchanged room eight times and you get eight different pictures. So the photographs have been replaced by a fingerprint of the shapes themselves, and before it is allowed to report anything it has to prove itself twice - read the same room twice and get the same answer, and give a hundred and fifteen doors that all open on one room and get the answer 'one'.

title: Quit in the middle of a boss fight, come back, and your dodge was shorter than when you left
body:
Your character can only carry so much before it starts to cost them. Armour and a weapon decide how well you roll out of the way of a sword; everything in your pack decides how fast you walk home. Two separate ideas on purpose - the whole point is that a bag full of loot must never make you worse at fighting.

The blocking problem this round was found by a critic who was looking for something else entirely. Two of the practice arenas - the ones every combat number in this project is measured in - are set up to state their own weight, so the fight always starts identically. Put on a mail shirt and greaves, save the game, load it back, and the game forgot it had been told. It worked the number out from scratch instead, landed just over the line into the next weight class, and your roll came back four frames shorter. From the chair: pause a boss fight, quit, resume, and you are worse at dodging than you were a minute ago, for no reason you could ever see. That is fixed - the save now records that the weight was declared, not just what it was - and I proved it by switching the fix off again and watching the exact same four frames disappear.

Four other things, each of which reverses something the previous round believed.
