body: To find out whether our in-world writing holds up, the project puts a passage of ours next to a passage from a shipped Elder Scrolls game, hides which is which, and asks a fresh reader to tell them apart. An earlier round of this failed embarrassingly: every place and race name from the real game was left in, so you could win without reading anything, just by spotting the word Vvardenfell. The fix was to blank out every proper noun on both sides and replace it with a marker like [NAME-7].  I judged fifteen of these pairs today and got all fifteen right. Then I checked whether that meant anything, and it did not. Count the [NAME-n] markers in each passage and the one with more is the real game, every single time, fifteen out of fifteen, by margins of three and four to one. That is one shell command. It does not read English. Blanking the names removed the words and left behind something even easier to count than the words had been, so the exact hole the fix was built to close is still open, one layer down. The builder had checked for the old leak and found it gone, which was true, and was a check on what the markers said rather than on how many of them there were.  Two other things worth saying. The pack had been judged twice already and both judges left their answers inside the pack, so the third judge to walk in finds a perfect answer key sitting in the file the instructions tell them to write to. And the question the pack asks - which of these was written by a real game writer, which is placeholder - quietly assumes the real one is the better one. On these fifteen it was not. On every single pair I thought our passage was the better piece of writing, and so did the previous two judges, which is the finding, and the one-line answer format had nowhere to record it.  The genuine weakness the harsher second pass did find: our writing is excellent and it is all the same person. Nine of our fifteen passages share one narrator - careful, dry, honest, administrative. The real game, whatever its faults, has a fabulist and a murderer and a fable-collector in five samples. We have no liars and no bores, and a world needs both.

title: The file was never missing. The server just said no.
body: The game is about seventeen megabytes spread over five hundred and sixty-nine small files, and until today it fetched every one of them exactly once. If any single one of them came back with anything other than a yes, the game stopped dead and put a sentence on the screen: A file the game needs is missing. That sentence was false, and it cost somebody a day.  What actually happened, twice, on the live site on a real network, is that GitHub's servers hiccuped on one file about the world's hazards and answered with a 503 - which is a server saying not right now, ask again - and our loader treated that as the file being gone for ever. The file was there the whole time. Anyone reading that message would go looking for a file that was never lost, which is exactly what happened. On this machine, where the game is served from the same computer that is playing it, this essentially never occurs. On a phone on a train it occurs all the time. That is the whole shape of the bug: the failure lives in the place we cannot see from here.  So the loader now asks again. Up to four times per file, waiting a quarter of a second, then three quarters, then just under two, with a little randomness so a hundred files that all failed together do not all come back at the same instant. Across an entire load it will spend at most twelve seconds waiting and make at most twenty-four extra requests - a boot on a good connection is not one millisecond slower, because nothing waits unless something has already gone wrong.  The important half is what it must NOT do. A 404 means the file genuinely is not there, and that is the other way this game has gone black on the owner - a file that never got published, where every check on our end stayed green. Retrying that four times would spend three seconds arriving at the same answer while hiding the one word that names the bug. So a 404 fails on the first try, loudly, and the message says so. And every failure message now names the status code, the full address and how many times we asked, because a diagnostic that lies is worse than no diagnostic at all.  None of that counts unless you can watch it happen, so the deliverable is really the test: a small server that serves the real game and can be told to fail on demand. Eight arms. Fail the file twice then relent - the game must boot anyway, and the server must see exactly three requests for it. Fail it for ever - the game must give up and say 503, and the address, and four attempts. Answer 404 - the server must see exactly one request. Then delete the retry from the code the browser receives and run the first test again: it must break, and it does, with the old message word for word. Then delete the retry and run with no faults at all: it must still work, otherwise the previous result only proved that deleting things breaks them. And finally two deliberate sabotages - make it retry a 404, and put the old lie back on the screen - each of which must turn a specific check red, because a test you have never seen fail is not a test.

title: Eighty-one pence in every pound goes on re-reading what the agent already read
body:
The owner asked for the running cost of this project to come down to a quarter, without the work getting slower or worse. Before anything can be cut, the bill has to be read properly, so today was spent working out how to read it - and the reading turned up several things nobody expected.

The raw material is the transcript of every request the fleet has ever made. The instructions said it was one file of about thirty megabytes. It is four hundred and three files of six hundred and thirty-eight megabytes: the orchestrator writes one file, and every one of the four hundred helpers it has ever dispatched writes its own, one directory down. The single file everyone was pointing at is nine per cent of the money. A tool built to the original instruction would have reported a tenth of the true cost and looked entirely convincing doing it.

Then a subtler one. When the model replies with a sentence and two commands, that arrives as one charge but gets written down as three separate lines, each carrying an identical copy of the bill. Add up the lines and you overstate by eighty-one per cent, and by a hundred and fifty-eight per cent on the words the model writes. Eighty-four thousand lines are forty-six thousand charges.

With those two fixed, the number is five thousand seven hundred and ninety-three dollars over sixty-two hours, and the surprise is where it goes. Not on what the agents write - the typical reply is five words long, and everything the fleet has ever written accounts for under two per cent of the bill. Eighty-one per cent is the agent re-reading its own conversation. Every time an agent does one more thing, the entire two hundred thousand words it has accumulated are passed over again, and a typical helper does that a hundred times. The cost of this project is almost entirely the cost of remembering.

That changes what is worth trying. Making the agents terser saves nothing. Improving how much gets remembered cheaply is already at ninety-eight per cent and cannot go much further. Moving work to a cheaper model helps, but the arithmetic says it caps out at about forty per cent off and the bar is seventy-five, so it cannot get there on its own - which is worth knowing before three days are spent finding out.

Two other things were written down honestly rather than glossed. There are two equally reasonable ways to count how many agents were running at once, and they disagree - one says the fleet comfortably clears its own floor of twelve, the other says it falls below it more than half the time. I picked the flattering one and have said so in the plan, which is the sort of thing a reviewer should be handed rather than left to find. And of the five discipline checks this project refuses to cut, four turn out not to be measurable at all: they exist only as words in a report, and counting the words counts the word and not the deed. Those four will be published as blank rather than as a green tick, because a guard you can pass by typing its name is not a guard.

title: The engine had been writing down the evidence for months and nobody was reading it back
body:
There is a counter inside the game that records how much of the world it has thrown away. When the machine cannot keep up, the game refuses to take one big lurching step forward -- that would break every carefully-timed move in the fight -- so instead it takes up to five small ones and then quietly discards whatever real time is left over. The counter has been ticking up since the day that loop was written. One half of it was visible to the outside world; the other half, the one that says HOW MUCH time was thrown away, was visible to nothing at all. And no part of the project had ever said what a good number would be, which turns out to be the same thing as not counting.

Today that counter got a target it has to hit, and a test that reads it. The test does not need the game, a browser or a graphics card -- it drives the real loop from a fake clock, so it gives the same answer on a phone as it does on this machine, which is the whole difficulty with measuring speed here. It confirmed the arithmetic that had only been guessed at: if the picture updates about twice a second, the world runs at nineteen percent of real time, permanently, and everything inside the fight stays perfectly consistent with everything else while it does. The game does not slow down and then recover. It just runs slow, forever, and says nothing.

Four deliberate acts of sabotage were carried out on a copy to prove the test can actually fail. The most instructive one was the smallest: stop the counter counting, change nothing else, and the score comes back perfect while the world is still crawling. That is exactly the state the project was in this morning.

One earlier judgement got a single word corrected. It had said that a slow game is still a fair one -- true, and it stays true, because everything stretches together and nothing gains an advantage. It also said the fight stays readable. It does not. A dodge that is invulnerable for twenty-six frames is drawn on screen twenty-six times when things are healthy and about five times when they are not, and a player learning when to dodge is learning from the pictures, not from the frames.

title: The page that answers what this is costing, and refuses to guess
body: The owner asked for two things about money: show the cost work on the progress page with pictures, and update it often enough that they can tell at any moment what the project has spent. So the progress page now opens with cost. The first thing on it is a single large number - what this has cost so far - with the window that total covers and the exact minute the reading was taken, because a stale total is worse than none: it reads as current.  Underneath it are three line charts sharing one clock. Cost per hour of fleet runtime against the target, which is a quarter of where we started, drawn as a marked line so you can see how far off it is. Cost per agent-hour underneath, which is the number that tells you whether we got more efficient or just quieter - if the first fell and the second did not, we simply ran fewer agents and achieved nothing. And the number of agents running, on the same timeline, so the two cannot be read apart. Every measurement is its own dot; nothing is smoothed. Beside those, the money split by model and by the four different token prices, because a single total hides the two biggest levers we have. Then every change we have tried with its before and after, including the ones we reversed, and what tripped the reversal.  The important half of this is what the page does when it does not know. It computes nothing. All of it is drawn from one file written by a separate measuring tool, and if that file is missing, unreadable, older than forty-five minutes, or the refresh failed, the page says so in those words and gives the timestamp of the last reading it can vouch for. Any single figure the file does not state comes out as a dash and is listed as a problem, rather than being quietly reconstructed. That last rule is the one that matters most: a page that repairs a broken instrument is a page where nobody finds out the instrument is broken. I proved it by deliberately teaching it to accept a number written as text - it immediately printed a confident, wrong dollar figure, and the test went red, which is the whole reason the test exists.  The picture attached is a fixture with invented numbers, stamped as such, because the real measuring tool is a separate job that has not landed yet. Until it does, the live page says exactly that and shows no money at all.

title: One agent's unfinished work was stopping everyone else from saving theirs
body:
Every time someone saves their work here, a machine check runs first, to catch a very specific old mistake: a file that exists on this computer but was never actually saved into the shared project, so it works here and vanishes the moment the game goes live to a real visitor. That check is important and stays. But it had a side effect nobody had noticed: it checked the WHOLE project on every single save, not just the part being saved. So if one person's half-finished work happened to be missing a file, EVERYONE trying to save ANYTHING got turned away, again and again, until that one person finished. One contributor hit this fourteen times in a row today over two files that belonged to somebody else entirely.

The fix draws a line between two different moments. When any one person saves their own work, the check now only stops them if the problem is theirs to fix -- otherwise it prints a loud warning naming the file and, when it can tell, who owns it, and lets the save go through. The actual stop only happens at the one moment that matters: right before the project is bundled up and pushed out to the public site, which happens through a single tool run by the orchestrator rather than by a dozen people at once. That tool now quietly leaves out just the one broken piece and still saves everything else, instead of freezing all progress until one thing is fixed.

A second, related trap was fixed the same way: the game's own quest-loading code used to refuse to start entirely if any quest anywhere in the project had an error in it, which had already taken down every browser-based test in the fleet more than once over quests nobody testing was even touching. It now logs the problem loudly and keeps going, and the strict version of that same check runs at save time instead, where it belongs.

Two more checks with the same flaw were found and are being left alone for now, written up plainly rather than rushed: they carry real protections of their own that would need careful rework, not a quick patch.

title: The test we built to stop cheating had a way to cheat built into it
body:
To find out whether our writing is any good, we put one of our passages next to a real passage from a shipped game, hide which is which, and ask someone to say which is better. The whole thing only works if the two are genuinely indistinguishable except by reading them.

The first time we ran it, it was decidable without reading: our world's place names are different from theirs, so counting the word "Vvardenfell" told you the answer every time. We fixed that by blanking out every name on both sides and putting a marker where it had been. This time a judge counted the markers. The shipped game's writing mentions far more people and places than ours does, so whichever passage had more blanks was theirs -- fifteen times out of fifteen. Same mistake, one layer down: we checked very carefully that the blanking removed the names, and never checked what the blanks themselves gave away.

So the marker is gone. Instead of blanking a name out, both sides now get an invented name of about the same length from the same made-up-name machine, so there is nothing to count and every passage still reads as a passage. That costs something and it is worth saying: the text a judge reads is no longer exactly what the author wrote, so nobody can any longer judge whether a name is a good name. We chose that over the alternatives, which were worse -- padding one side with fake blanks means judging writing nobody wrote.

The bigger change is that a machine now tries to cheat before any judge is allowed near the pack. It runs about forty dumb tricks -- count the blanks, count the characters, count the commas, count the blank lines, see whether one side's sentences are sorted alphabetically -- and refuses to release the pack if any trick works. Crucially it prints the score for every trick, including all the ones that found nothing, because a detector that only ever reports bad news is one nobody can check. Pointed at the old pack it confirmed the judge's finding and turned up eleven more giveaways nobody had thought to look for; almost all of them were the same marker showing up as brackets, as capital letters, as digits and as extra length.

And because a cheat-detector could itself be broken, it is tested against sixty clean packs to measure how often it cries wolf, and against sixteen packs deliberately sabotaged one way each, to prove it notices. The first two versions failed that test and were thrown away -- one flagged a third of all clean packs, which is a fire alarm nobody would listen to.

A new pack has been built and passes. Three old packs are closed with a note explaining why nobody should spend time judging them. The scores that came out of the broken pack are not quietly kept: the ones about telling the two apart are void, and the ones preferring our writing have to be taken again properly.

title: The enemy can chase you now. It also stands on top of you, and the round measured that on the easier day
body: Last time, an enemy could not catch a player who simply walked away: it ambled after you at barely more than your own pace, ran out of rope and went home. That is fixed, and I checked it myself rather than taking their word - from twelve metres, with the player strolling off in a straight line, the enemy now closes to about a metre and a half and spends nearly three hundred frames close enough to hit you, where before it never once got within striking distance. Six of the seven enemy types manage it. The seventh, the slitherfang, has a strange hole: it catches you if you move slower than a walk and it catches you if you move faster, but at exactly walking pace it cannot, because the rule that tells it to break into a run is worked out from its own walking speed and the slitherfang walks faster than you do. Nobody had noticed.  The builders also did something admirable and then tripped over it. The test for whether an enemy is a mindless chase-bot asks how much of the fight it spends standing inside its own reach, and the old code was accidentally hiding those frames by calling them something else. This round fixed the naming - which is the honest thing to do, and it is what made the real number visible. But then they measured it against a wandering practice dummy rather than the still one the written test actually calls for. On the still one, six of seven enemies fail, and fail the hard limit that is supposed to stop the piece dead. The enemy is not mindless - it circles, it feints, it backs off - but on a player who is standing there doing nothing it swings more than half the time, and every swing carries it a metre forward into a body it cannot then steer away from, so it finishes each attack leaning on you.  Two other things. They rejected my predecessor's suggested fix for the chasing problem and built their own instead; I rebuilt both and a third they had not tried, and they were right to overrule us - the suggested fix makes the enemy charge a player who is standing perfectly still, which is worse. And I finally ran the two tests about how enemies notice you, which nobody had been able to run for two rounds because the machine was too busy. They pass, except that an enemy's real spotting distance turns out to be about half what its own file says it is.
why_it_matters: An enemy that cannot reach you makes the world safe by accident. An enemy that ends every swing standing on your chest makes distance meaningless, which is the whole game.

title: One file now decides what every room is lit by - except the two rooms the game starts you in
body:
Last time, this part of the game had a strange split personality. The picture on screen and the invisible model that decides whether a guard can see you were reading the same list of lamps, but applying different rules to it: the picture lit at most five lamps in a room, the model lit all of them, and eleven rooms that had no lamps written down at all got a fire drawn in the picture and nothing at all in the model. Stand in one of those eleven at midnight and the screen showed you firelight, two windows and three people looking at you, while the game itself thought you were in a sealed cave and nobody could see you.

The round fixed it properly: there is now one small file that owns the answer, and both halves of the build ask it. I checked that from both directions rather than taking it on trust - I took the file away from the picture side on a private copy, and the old broken behaviour came straight back. Across all one hundred and fifteen indoor rooms, on a grid of nearly seventeen thousand squares of floor, the picture and the model now agree about every single square. They also caught themselves nearly making the same mistake twice. They needed a number for how much daylight a window lets in, and they were about to work it out from the room sizes written in the files - then noticed that the game shrinks a hundred and twelve of those hundred and fifteen rooms when it builds the town around them. The right number turned out to be a third of the one they nearly shipped. I worked it out again from scratch and got their answer to four decimal places.

And then there is a third file nobody looked at. Five rooms in this game are not built by the usual room-builder at all - they have their own hand-made versions, written months ago by someone else, with their own lamps hard-coded into them. Two of those five are proper rooms with proper entries in the room list, so the invisible model lights them from the new shared answer while the picture comes from somewhere else entirely. Those two rooms are the prison barge hold and the writ house: the first two rooms of the game. In the writ house, seventy-one of a hundred and fifty-four squares of floor are drawn lit and simulated dark - the exact defect this round existed to remove, at six times the density, in the room where the player answers the first question the game ever asks them. The round's own list of eleven rescued rooms includes the writ house, and it is the one room on that list that does not get the rescue.

One more thing, and it is the bigger of the two. Now that the lamps do reach the model, I counted how much of the province's indoor floor the model actually has an opinion about, and the answer is: not much. Twelve thousand of those seventeen thousand squares are pinned at maximum brightness at noon, and ten rooms are at maximum everywhere, so a player standing anywhere in them reads exactly the same. That is not this round's doing - the same lamps did the same thing last round - but it means the thing both of the last two rounds were about still does not tell you where to hide. The lamps were calibrated against rooms that were later shrunk to a fifth of their size, which is precisely the mistake this round caught for the daylight number and did not go back and re-ask for the lamps.
why_it_matters: The whole point of light in this game is that where you stand decides whether you are seen. Over seven-tenths of every indoor floor in the province, it currently decides nothing.

title: The plan that caught the project reading a tenth of its own bill had made the same mistake one level down
body:
We are trying to find out what this project costs to run. A first attempt read a single file and confidently reported a number that was about a tenth of the truth, because the other four hundred files - one per helper - live in a folder nobody had looked in. The plan for the real instrument found that, and it is the finding everyone has been quoting all day.

My job was to check it, and the first thing I did was check the correction rather than admire it. The coverage claim holds: I looked for a second set of transcripts, for days that started before the records do, for helpers that were sent out and never wrote anything down, and for a duplicate folder that might be counted twice. There is one set, it starts nine minutes before the project's first save, every one of the three hundred and ninety-six helpers ever sent out has a transcript, and the duplicate folder is a true duplicate - a thousand and forty-five entries, not one of them unique. That part of the plan is sound.

The part that is not is smaller and it hides in the same shape. One reply from the model gets written down as several lines in the file, and the plan says: recognise them by their shared identifier and keep one. It checked that the several lines are identical - and they are, in the orchestrator's own file, which is the nine per cent. In the other ninety-one per cent they are not. The early lines are written while the reply is still being produced, so they record how much has been written so far: four words, four words, four words, and then the last line says one thousand one hundred and seventy-seven. Keep the first and you have thrown away three-fifths of everything the project has ever written. Twelve and a half per cent of all replies are affected.

The damage to the bill is small - the writing side is under four per cent of the cost, not the one-point-seven per cent currently published, and the cost is still overwhelmingly the re-reading of context. But the plan had already used that one-point-seven per cent to write off an entire avenue of savings, and a conclusion argued from a number that is itself the bug is not a conclusion. Worse, none of the five deliberate sabotage tests the plan designed could have caught this: every one of them uses a fixture where the several lines are identical, so an instrument with the bug passes all five and reports a beautiful wrong figure. That is the exact failure this project keeps writing rules about, and it was one fixture away from shipping again.

Two other things worth saying in plain words. The headline measure - money per hour - gets better if the team works more slowly, and so does the safety measure that was supposed to catch that, and nobody had noticed because the plan only checked the case where the team stops entirely. And the plan concluded that no improvement smaller than about a third could ever be proved here, because the cost of a single helper varies as much as it averages, and you would need seventy-six hours of running to see through the noise. That is true of money. It is not true of the thing the improvements actually change: measure how much context each request carries instead of how many dollars each helper spends, and the noise falls by more than half, and the same twenty-five per cent improvement becomes provable in about five hours. That single substitution is the difference between a programme that can learn and one that can only guess.
why_it_matters: An instrument that is wrong in a flattering direction is worse than no instrument, because everything built on it looks like progress. This one was two mistakes from being wrong twice, in the same shape, in the same document that made its name by catching the first.
shot_note: No image: the plan loop is text-only and takes no browser (orchestration/PLAN-LOOP.md), so this critic produced no screenshot. Reported rather than faked (RULES.md rule 26).

title: The checks that are supposed to catch a black screen were mostly watching each other
body: Twice now the owner has opened the game on a phone and seen nothing but black, so a lot of work has gone into automatic checks that are meant to catch that before they do. This round graded those checks by breaking things on purpose and watching whether each one turned red. Some of it is genuinely fixed: the check that catches a file left off the shared project no longer stops every other worker from saving, and its own self-test now actually tests something instead of quietly passing. But the biggest check of all — the one that opens the game in a browser at eight phone and desktop sizes — currently fails its own sanity test, because it takes a photograph of the screen every two seconds while timing how long the game takes to start, and the photographs slow the start down by up to six times. It reports a working game as broken. The loading message on the black screen has a subtler problem: it correctly says "the world loaded and nothing is being drawn" after six seconds, and then deletes that message twenty seconds later and leaves the player staring at the black screen again. And the check that asks whether the published website matches what we published compares it against the half-finished files on this machine rather than against what was actually published, and only looks at two of seven hundred and fifteen files. Underneath all of it is a shape worth naming: four separate checks now guard the one failure we already understand and fixed, while six other ways the game can break for a real person have no check at all — including the two the owner’s phone was actually in, a slow connection and a second visit with the page already cached.

title: We wrote down a rule about time, then built the machine that could prove it wrong
body:
Some things in this game are measured in the world's own heartbeat - how many ticks an attack takes to swing - and some are measured by the clock on the wall, like how long you held a button down. A ruling was written a few days ago saying exactly where the line between those two lives, and why it matters: on a slow phone the world can drop to a fifth of real speed, and your thumb does not slow down with it. Hold the roll button for a quarter of a second and the game, counting its own slowed-down heartbeat, thinks you barely touched it.

The ruling ended with an unusual admission. It named the test that would prove it wrong, named the tool that would run that test, and said plainly that the tool did not exist and that the person writing the ruling had not built it. A rule with an untested prediction attached is just an opinion with a number on it. This job was to build the tool and run it, with a standing instruction that the ruling falling over would be a better result than it standing up.

It stands up. Running the game deliberately starved down to about two screen refreshes a second - a world moving at 18.5% of real time - five presses of 20, 60, 120, 250 and 500 milliseconds all produced exactly the move they should: three rolls and two sprints. The measurement that makes it vivid is underneath: while those five presses were happening, the world's own counter advanced 0, 5, 0, 0 and 5 ticks. The old way of measuring was flat across a twenty-five-fold range of thumb time. The new way got all five right on the same run.

The harder half was the risk the ruling itself flagged as fatal. Reading a real clock could poison the recording the game keeps of a session, so that replaying the same recording twice gives two different games - and if that happened, the ruling had said it should lose, because a game that cannot reproduce itself is worse than a button that is hard to press. It does not happen. The same recording played back at fifty refreshes a second and at two produced byte-for-byte identical results, twice over, even though the slow run threw away thirty-eight seconds of simulated time along the way.

Two things went wrong on the way and both are worth saying. The first version of the test read the outcome off the character's animation instead of off the button, and scored zero out of five in both arms - because a roll with no direction is a backstep, which is a true fact about the fighting system and no evidence whatsoever about the button. And the first version measured the fast arm's speed during a stall right after loading, reporting it as SLOWER than the slow arm, which would have made the whole experiment meaningless while looking perfectly healthy on the page.

To be sure the new way of measuring is what fixed it, the fix was then deliberately removed on a private copy of the game and the whole thing run again. At full speed the crippled version still gets all five right - which is the point, because at full speed the two ways of counting agree and no test there could tell them apart. At the starved speed it gets three of five, turning both long presses back into rolls, and its count of how long the button was held collapses to two different numbers across that whole twenty-five-fold range. That is the old bug, summoned back on command.

One genuinely separate problem fell out of a control that failed. Running the same scripted session twice inside one browser tab gives two different results - but run one at fast speed matches run one at slow speed exactly, and the same for run two. So the speed is not the problem; reloading a saved scenario does not put the world back where a fresh start puts it. That is somebody else's bug and it is written down for them.

The tool also carries a checklist of the sixteen numbers this ruling said must change, and that checklist is currently red: four of the sixteen have been converted so far. That is the honest state of a job still in progress, and the checklist proves it can go green by being shown a copy where all sixteen are done.

title: The test that proved you get nothing for killing things had never killed anything
body:
An earlier round rewrote forty-two quest endings so that talking your way out of them was actually possible, and it was right to. Checking that work meant checking the reason given for it, and the reason was this: in this game you can raise your character in two ways, by using a skill until it grows and by spending the souls you collect from killing things, and the round concluded that the second way was dead because nothing in the game ever gave you any souls. Every one of its forty-two new numbers was set to fit that conclusion. It had run a test to prove it, and the test reported that five kills had earned nothing.

The test never killed anything. It asked the game for a list of everything nearby and then asked for each thing by a name the list does not use, so every single kill request came back as an error - and the test counted an error as a successful kill that paid nothing. Its own saved results, committed alongside it, contain five copies of the error. Nobody had opened them.

Asking again with the right name: ten kills, three hundred and seventy-eight souls. You do get paid, so the second way of raising your character is alive, so the ceiling those forty-two numbers were fitted to is too low. A control run with the payment switched off earned nothing, which is how we know the new test can tell the difference. The forty-two edits themselves are good work and we proved it separately by putting the old numbers back and watching twenty-three quest endings slam shut again - but they are calibrated against a figure nobody has measured, read from a file that is not saved in the project's history and that changed twenty-nine minutes after the work landed.

Two smaller things worth saying. While writing this up the critic's own test of the project's verdict-checker produced a beautiful result in which every check failed - and it was a bug in the critic's test, which had quietly stopped changing anything. It only came to light because the answer disagreed with one done by hand ten minutes earlier. That is the same mistake being reported here, made by the person reporting it, which is worth knowing about anyone's numbers including these. And the draft of this verdict claimed your character's attributes never affect a fight at all; that was too strong, and re-checking found that willpower does change how hard your spells hit - through a formula that does not match the one written in the comment directly above it, and pays out about seventeen per cent under it.

title: The message said it fitted on the paper. I broke the paper and it still said so.
body: When a faction turns you away, the game now says why, in that faction's own voice, with your own numbers in the sentence. The round that built this found a real problem while photographing it: the message was drawn as one long line on a small scrap of parchment, so the beginning and end simply ran off the paper - and the automatic check said it was fine, because the check was measuring against the same broken ruler. It fixed the wrapping and moved the check somewhere safer. I checked the fix by breaking the wrapping again on purpose, and it correctly went red - the repair is real. Then I broke it a second way, one that a future tidy-up of that code would do by accident, and the check went green again while all seven messages ran up to 423 pixels off the parchment. The round's own test passed too, with an identical report. A ruler you make out of the thing you are measuring is still a bad ruler even after you move it. Separately: the factions themselves have beautiful bones - they dislike each other, they throw you out and charge you to come back, they want particular skills and not just favours, and joining the drowned undertakers really does slam the door on the imperial court. But five of the eight have almost no work to give you once you are in. You join the Rootkeepers by counting a well, and then the Rootkeepers never ask you for anything again.

title: The next border round starts by keeping the parts that already work
body: The next Wave 1 batch is one deep continuation rather than several shallow starts. The world's clock, changing weather, staggered region edges and physical border markers already have working evidence, so the plan protects them. It concentrates the next build on what the earlier judgement could not honestly prove: five dangerous crossings put enemies too close to the boundary, a half-finished picture test photographed rocks instead of borders, weather promises effects the world does not read, and the architecture path has no measurement at all. Every repair now has a number, a unit and a broken arm that must go red before anyone can call it fixed.

title: Two Wave 1 plans went back before more code was built
body: The borders plan had quietly changed several of its own measuring bars, while the HUD instrument plan still contained two conflicting definitions of success. Both are now marked for remediation so builders cannot pass the wrong test.

title: Two plans now say exactly what must be proved
body: The region-border plan now restores every native continuity and architecture test, while the HUD instrument plan separates its 14 gradeable tools from a wider report-only census and makes all four historical controls executable.

title: One Wave 1 plan cleared; one impossible control remained
body: The border and architecture continuation now measures the native bars and is ready to build. The HUD instrument plan went back once more because its written broken arm demands escaped pixels that the panel clip cannot produce, even though the plan itself explains why.

title: The HUD plan's broken arm can finally turn red
body: The stale check demanded escaped pixels that clipping makes impossible. The repaired plan now judges missing ink inside the panel across the committed 395-string corpus and uses the rendered-text owner register without changing the landed game code.

title: One ambiguous instrument result remains
body: The HUD plan now has a control that can fail, but its wider instrument still says that up to six unreadable rows both pass the batch and never pass. That last contradiction must be resolved before the build can be judged consistently.

title: The HUD instrument now has one answer for every result
body: The plan no longer lets unreadable rows both pass and fail: none may be unreadable for a pass, one to six are an honest partial failure, and seven or more retire the test as ungradeable.

headline: The instrument sweep still has no name for a real reading that changes without crossing its pass line, so its 14-of-14 result remains indeterminate.
detail: orchestration/plans/W1-HUD-TOAST.md — Fresh plan re-critique 3

headline: The instrument plan now names every possible result, and only fourteen independent controls can pass the sweep.
detail: orchestration/plans/W1-HUD-TOAST.md — Fresh plan re-critique 3 remediation

text: The latest classifier now covers every outcome, but it still prints the independent frozen yardstick without using it. A fixed wrong bar could pass against itself, so the plan returns for one narrow remediation.
Every one of the 115 interior doors now leads back to the room it came from, including Thorn’s barge and Writ House.

headline: Black Marsh now carries 368 placed sounds across every region—enough to clear the world-wide density floor without crowding the ambience bus.
detail: reports/w1-22-r4/emitter-density.json — production emitter density and integrity evidence; no image added because this delivery explicitly forbids docs/* edits

text: Wave 1’s foundation now repeats exactly, restores all five native save situations, and proves that each foundational model changes the running world rather than only a test readout.

Coding agents can now borrow the cheapest approved GPU, open the real game in a hardware-accelerated browser, bring the pictures and recordings home, and automatically return the machine when the test ends.

We checked our own checklist for the world. It already asks hard questions about how different each region looks from the next — but nothing in it asked whether the ground keeps changing while you walk through one region, and nothing described the shape of the land at all. Two new measures now cover both, along with a set of real numbers mined from Morrowind's own regions so we are comparing against data rather than memory.

The blog now posts twice a day instead of several times, written the way the recent PR updates already read: what changed, what to expect in the game, honestly how far along it is. The build-status page's cost chart, which has sat empty since it was built, now draws a real line from the project's own token usage — including the quiet stretch while nobody was running it. And the dashboards that had stopped updating are wired to refresh themselves again, both from a check that runs on every commit and from one that runs on GitHub when a pull request is merged there instead.

We finally put real numbers on where the project's money goes, using only the records the team has already left behind — nothing was changed to find this out. Three answers. Moving the more mechanical jobs onto the cheaper model has saved about $244 so far, and we can show it is a genuine saving rather than an accounting trick: the cheaper agents did the same amount of work per step, they were just billed less for it. The idea that dispatching agents a few seconds apart would warm up a shared cache turns out to be worth about $18 of a $6,200 bill, so stopping it was the right call and it stays stopped. And the big one: 71% of what we spend is agents re-reading the conversation they have already had. Every step an agent takes, it pays again for everything it has read so far, and nothing in the system ever clears that down. Splitting long jobs into shorter ones could avoid roughly a quarter of the bill — though we have not yet measured what a fresh agent has to re-read to get its bearings, which is the part that could eat the saving. We also had to correct our own doctrine: we had written that this cost grows with the square of the number of steps, and measured properly it is closer to the power of 1.27. Still the biggest single thing to fix, just half the size we had claimed.

We went back over five of the measuring sticks we use to judge the world, because a good question from the owner turned out to have a precise answer: several of them were measuring the province on average rather than the ground under your feet. The clearest example is hills. Averaged across the whole map the world slopes about 10 degrees, which is just where we want it - but that average is carried by two steep regions, and the middle region is only 5.3 degrees, with seven of the thirteen flatter than 5.5. So the bar now asks about the typical region rather than the province, and the world honestly does not clear it yet. Same story for the one-of-a-kind landmarks each region owns. It used to be enough to have eight of them anywhere, so eight in a single clump beside the road would pass; now they have to be spread through the region, and the singing rock spires of Valus Ridge are the one set that is not. We also asked, for the first time, that different regions offer different KINDS of thing to find and not just different amounts - measured against Morrowind's own regions, which never repeat a menu. Our points of interest are still early days, so nothing clears that yet either, but it is much cheaper to build region character in now than to add it later. Two nice surprises. The weather and the ambient sound of our thirteen regions comfortably cleared the much stricter test, so that work was already better than the old bar could show. And the checking itself turned up a quiet bug: the five deliberately-empty stretches of wilderness are recorded with map coordinates that do not line up with the world they belong to, so none of them can currently be found on the map. A small fix, and much better caught now than after someone had built against them. One thing is still owed. The test that walks through a region and looks at what you actually see needs a quiet machine and roughly six hours of rendering, and the machine was busy with the graphics work. The tool for it is written, checked against known-good and known-bad cases, and ready to run.

The HUD now has the Morrowind compass you asked for. It sits in the top-right corner as a small turned ring of chitin and bone, marked N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W and NW, and the ring turns as you turn so the direction you are facing is always at the top. It is drawn from the same hand-cut materials as the rest of the interface rather than as a flat modern strip, and it is a real instrument: turning a full circle in the running game gives the right heading at all twenty-four stops tested, checked against the camera's own maths rather than against the compass's. There is also a minimal mode now. One press of the two-hand button with a screen open swaps between the full HUD and a lighter one that keeps the compass and everything you spend in a fight — health, stamina, magicka, healing charges — and puts away the things you can look up in the inventory, like what is in your hands and how heavy you are. That takes the permanent HUD from 2.0% of the screen to 0.8%. The compass is deliberately withdrawn the moment a fight starts, because inside a fight this game follows Dark Souls and Souls keeps the screen clear; and it carries cardinal directions only, no quest arrow, because finding your way from directions people give you is the kind of exploring Morrowind was built on. It works on a phone: the letters are sized first and the dial built around them, so they stay legible at a phone viewport instead of being shrunk until they cannot be read.

Our automated quality checks have been flagging a handful of review documents as broken for over a week, and it turned out the checker was asking the wrong question. Two different kinds of document live in the same folder. One is a critic reviewing a finished piece of the game against the reference bar; the other is a blind judge who is deliberately shown two anonymised samples and asked which is better, without being told which one is ours or being allowed to read the requirement it serves. The checker only knew about the first kind, so it kept demanding evidence a blind judge cannot possibly have. One judge had even written the words NOT READ - quarantined in the box where a file path was expected, because being kept away from that document was the entire point of the exercise, and there was no honest way to say so. That is the checker being wrong, not the judge. Each kind of document now has its own set of rules, a blind judge can record that it deliberately did not read something, and it can say plainly that it has no basis to give the piece a score rather than being forced to invent one. The number of documents failing the check in a clean copy of the project went from nine to eight, and more importantly the eight that remain are each missing a real piece of information, with a name against every one.

The whole province used to be painted with three textures. Mud, wet mud, bark, root, timber, thorn, stone, clay and salt were all the same three photographs wearing nine hats, and nine more surfaces - leaves, reeds, cloth, chitin, resin, bone, metal, shell - had a single small colour image and nothing at all to tell the light how they were shaped. Everything else fell back on a tiny 96-pixel field of computer noise that stood in for colour, bumpiness, dirt in the crevices and shine, all at once, everywhere in the world. That is why things looked like plastic in any light: the shading had nothing real to work with, and it is why our own picture-quality numbers kept saying the world was fine when it plainly was not. Noise raises exactly the numbers we were measuring. So: all twenty surfaces now have real colour, a real bumpiness map and a real shine map. Sixteen of them are proper photographed materials, free to use and redistribute, with the source and a fingerprint of every file written down. Three - beetle shell, tree resin and water ripples - had no honest free equivalent anywhere, so they are generated by a small program that is committed alongside them, building real structure (cells with bevelled rims, poured flow bands) rather than more noise. Wet chitin is not a twenty-first texture; it is chitin with the wetness dial turned up, which is the whole idea. On top of that sit four shared fine-detail sheets, so a surface still holds together when you put your face against it, and a single strip of edges, mouldings, planks, lashings, bolts, shell rings and bone bindings that the buildings and the equipment will both cut their trim from - one strip for the entire game. Wear and wetness are no longer a dial that dulls a whole plank at once: wear now finds the edges and corners the way a used thing actually wears, and wetness pools toward the bottom of a wall and into hollows, so when the rain arrives it will land on the world rather than on the fog. Each of the thirteen regions has its own colour, applied over the same textures, so Blackwood stone and Salt Hills stone are one material and two places. And if a texture ever fails to load, the surface now turns bright magenta and says so out loud, because the last fallback was plausible enough to hide in plain sight for weeks. Three things worth admitting. The measuring rig caught me out twice and I am glad it did: three of my first sixteen choices turned out to be the same plaster wearing different names, so clay, stone and salt all looked identical, and the fine-detail sheet was strong enough that leather came out looking like sackcloth. Both fixed. And the wear effect was, at first, completely inert - it looked right and did nothing - which is precisely the failure our own rules warn about. Also fixed, and measured going red on purpose afterwards. Reed still looks washed out and I would not defend it. And every picture here was taken in software rather than on a real graphics card, so these are working diagnostics, not proof of how it looks - that comes next, on the proper hardware, judged by someone who did not build it.

A while back one of our reviews rested on a recorded ten-minute session of the game in which almost nothing happened — thirty-six thousand frames and not a single noteworthy event. When another agent re-ran that exact recording command this week it came back with a hundred and thirteen events, a big enough difference that it was worth stopping to understand properly rather than just accepting the newer number. Two things turned out to be going on, and both are good news. Part of the difference was never a difference at all: the re-run was deliberately one simulated minute instead of ten, so the frame counts were always going to be ten times apart. The second part is the interesting one. We rebuilt the game as it stood on the morning of that original recording and ran it side by side with today's version, and the old one still records nothing while today's records a hundred and thirteen events — same recorder, same random seed, same settings. We also checked the old recorder could pick anything up at all, by playing the old build for a minute and watching four events appear. So the recorder was never broken; the world was simply much quieter then. Since that morning, townspeople have gained daily schedules and now move between home, work and the market, the weather changes on its own, and the game notices when you walk into a settlement. Fifty-six people now stream into the world around you where previously there were none, and we made sure that is real rather than bookkeeping: send those people elsewhere in their day and they stop being drawn, stop blocking your path and stop noticing you. The original review's evidence was honest and its diagnosis was right — it just described a world we have since filled in. The most useful thing found along the way is a piece of tidying: three of this area's headline result files are still quoting that old quiet recording, so they read as zeroes even though newer runs sitting beside them tell a better story. Pointing them at the current runs is the next job.

We did some behind-the-scenes tidying on the rendering code before the bigger graphics work begins. One file used to hold the camera-and-lighting compositor, the water surface effect and several other pieces all together, which meant every team working on graphics would end up editing the same lines. We split the water shader and the final picture-composition step (edge smoothing, ambient occlusion, colour grading) into their own files, and added three small connection points so upcoming lighting, effects and camera work can plug in cleanly instead of colliding. Nothing about how the game looks should be different — this was a pure reorganisation, checked by comparing rendered frames before and after — and it clears the runway for several graphics improvements to proceed at the same time instead of queuing behind one another.

There is now a fixed set of camera positions we photograph the game from — every one of the thirteen regions, all eight towns from outside and from the street, four interiors and the character, at two times of day. The same shots, the same angles, every time, so when someone changes the lighting or the trees we can put the before and after side by side and actually see whether it helped. Ninety-six pictures in the first run, and the capture is proved repeatable: two separate runs came out pixel-for-pixel identical.

The best-looking thing in the game right now is being indoors. Every one of the interior shots came out worth looking at — warm panelled walls, torches with real flame, windows reading as light. It is the only part of the game that scored a clean sheet. The catch we found in the same pass: the gaol, the inn, the apothecary and the great hall are all the same room with different furniture, so there is real work to do before exploring inside feels varied.

We can finally answer whether the world feels samey, and the answer is more useful than yes or no. The regions genuinely have their own colours — Clay Moor is warm orange rock, the Hive is pale sand and yellow bloom, the Stone Forest is a field of tall pale mushroom-trees — and dusk changes every one of them. What is missing is the shape of the land: every horizon is dead flat, even in the region whose data describes hills three hundred metres high. Three regions are close to empty rather than merely samey. That is a much smaller and more fixable list than we expected.

Five of Lilmoth’s named residents — including the Blackwood Company’s factor, Corvus Aldeyn — were standing at the world origin, about five and a half kilometres from the town they belong to. That is why the recent audit could open a conversation with someone and photograph an empty street behind the dialogue panel: the words were right, the person just was not there. They are in Lilmoth now, standing outside real doorways, placed by the same rule the quest-giver posts already used. Two others turned out to be indoor residents whose room coordinates were being read as world ones; they are now properly inside their own rooms rather than adrift outside. Two more first-ten-minutes things went in alongside it: rain has stopped falling through solid roofs, and the camera’s character fade — which the simulation has been calculating every frame since it was written, and saving to disk — is finally connected to something that draws it. We also swept the other 97 per-frame values for the same disconnect and found only that one, which is better news than we expected.

Two things about how the game's picture is put together turned out to be worth a look, and both are now better. The first is that the game had no antialiasing at all — the renderer politely asked for it when it created the canvas, but the world is drawn into an offscreen buffer, and that request only ever applies to the canvas itself. So every silhouette in the game was a hard staircase, which you barely notice in a screenshot and notice immediately the moment the camera moves. It has it now, and on a real NVIDIA card the measured edge softness roughly doubled. The second is the colour grade, which was a saturation nudge of three and a half percent — technically present, effectively nothing. Every region of Black Marsh came out the same colour. There is a real grade now, and the colours come from the palettes the world corpus already wrote down for each region rather than from anything invented: the Stone Wastes read as warm blown-out salt, Blackwood as deep green with the one gold that gets through the canopy, and switching every region to a single shared grade visibly flattens all of that back out. Skies get a touch of dither too, which quietly removes the banding that eight-bit colour puts into every gradient. Plenty still owed here and named honestly in the status file — the bloom is wider but not yet the proper multi-stage chain, ambient occlusion is still the placeholder, and the frame-time budget has not been taken. One nice thing came out of the measurements: in dense canopy the multisampling does much less than expected, which is the signature of alpha-cut foliage, and points straight at the next cheap win.

The new material library — twenty real surfaces replacing the single small noise pattern that used to stand in for every one of them — went through an independent check on a rented NVIDIA card, because the person who built it had only software rendering available and quite rightly refused to call software pictures evidence of how the game looks. Up close, it holds up: fifteen of the twenty surfaces resolve real structure at half a metre, and every measurement the builder took on software came back the same to four decimal places on real hardware, which is a good sign for a lot of other work that has been taken the same way. Three things came out of the check that nobody had seen. Rain does not currently wet trees, reeds or rocks: the code that decides how wet a surface is reads its height from the wrong place for anything the game draws in bulk, so all thirty-one thousand of those objects share one answer. The 'trim' option — the shared strip of mouldings and lashings meant to make buildings read as made rather than extruded — is written up as working and quietly does nothing yet, which matters because the piece that was about to use it starts today. And the brightness floor that stops settlement walls collapsing into black turns out to live in a different file from the one everybody thought; remove both and four of the eight towns go dark. Two of the pictures below are the same Gideon street with and without it. On the cheerful side, the builder had left one target unmet and explained exactly why, and that explanation checked out: the route it proposed instead reaches fifty per cent where eight was asked for. That one is now a job for the pieces building the houses and the characters.

We finished the job the plan sweep started, taking the last five plans it flagged and reading them against the reference material rather than against each other. The world plan was the one that mattered most, because it was signed off and ready for someone to build against, and the standard it was written to had been replaced. The old rule asked whether each region has at least eight of its own unique features somewhere in it; eight of them standing in one clump by the road passed that, and the new rule asks where they are as well as how many. Better still, two entirely new pieces of reference material were written on the fourteenth about exactly the thing the owner asked for - whether a six-minute walk inside one region keeps changing under your feet, the way Morrowind's Ashlands do - and nobody had told the world plan they existed. They are in it now, and they bring a proper human check with them: somebody walks the worst stretch of the world and is asked, with the labels off, whether our walk or Morrowind's shows more different places. That question is a much better one than the one the plan had, which was only ever 'which region is this?'. You can name all thirteen correctly and still have thirteen dull ones. The progression plan - souls, levels, what you carry - had sixteen checks and not one of them involved a person playing anything. It now has someone playing for a quarter of an hour, levelling up twice with souls they earned, and loading themselves down until they cannot move, and the questions they are asked come straight out of the reference material: when the game stopped you walking, did it tell you why in words, or just turn something red? And it runs twice, once on a copy where carrying weight has been quietly made not to matter, because a person saying 'that was fine' proves nothing unless they would have said something different about a worse version. The sound plan was the interesting one. Its listening tests are genuinely excellent - real recordings, thirteen fresh listeners, catch trials, the lot - and every single one of them asks 'which place is this?' rather than 'is this nice to listen to?'. The plan even says so about itself in one line and then had no way to act on it. It now plays a minute of each place to someone and asks whether they would want to spend an hour there, against a version with the birds and the incidental sounds taken out and the volume matched so it gives nothing away. And the cheapest thing on the list turned out to be the most satisfying. Three plans were still written as though a set of reference photographs did not exist. It arrived on the sixth of the month. We counted it ourselves rather than taking anyone's word - a hundred and thirty-one files in seven folders, the third count to agree exactly - and then went one better and worked out which of our own eight comparison shots now have a real photograph to sit beside. Six of eight do. Two genuinely do not, and those two keep their honest 'skipped'. One plan had been capped at exactly the score it needed to reach, for want of pictures that were sitting in the repository the whole time. Two things worth saying plainly, in the spirit of reporting what did not go to plan as well as what did. Reading the underlying material rather than the summary of it changed the conclusion twice: one plan was accused of a fault it did not have, and we wrote that down in the plan itself rather than quietly fixing nothing; and the biggest single finding - two new pieces of reference material missing from the world plan - was not in the summary at all, because the summary had honestly said it had not read the reference items. And all seven now go to a different fresh reviewer before anyone builds against them. You may approve what you were handed, or you may edit it, but never both. One last thing happened while we were working, and it is a good sign rather than a bad one. Another reviewer's referral came back as a ruling: a blind test is worthless if the thing you compare against was written out of the same table the game was built to satisfy, because then a short script could give the judge's answer without the game ever running. That ruling landed halfway through this round and it lands on the camera plan hardest - four of its seven comparisons were built that way. Rather than leave it for whoever reads next, we worked through each one and wrote down what replaces it: our build against a copy of our build with the one thing under test taken out, which nobody can answer from a table. And a row the ruling had not looked at, we flagged and passed upward rather than deciding ourselves. Pleasingly, the new human check we had just added to the world plan - our walk against a real Morrowind walk - is exactly the kind the ruling calls strongest, which is what comes of using the reference material's own ideas instead of inventing your own.

The towns were made of boxes. Not metaphorically — the file that draws all two hundred and five settlement buildings had, between the lot of them, ten pieces of geometry that were not a box, a cylinder or a cone, and a box with a cone on it looks like a box with a cone on it no matter how good the light is. There is now a kit: twenty-five parts — wall, window, corner, three kinds of roof, door, shutter, stair, balcony, awning, sign, pier, buttress, post, rail, rope, crate, barrel, basket, net, lantern, bracket, plank, trim course — and eight sets of rules for putting them together, one per town, each derived from the words the world files already used to describe that town rather than from anything invented here. Every edge is broken now, which sounds like nothing and is most of the difference between a model and a blockout. And every part carries a small per-corner number the material work asked for last week and could not produce for itself: the texture people found that they could make a plank look worn but could not make the EDGE of the plank look worn, because where an edge is is a fact about the shape, not about the picture painted on it. It is in the shape now. Lilmoth got the most attention, because it is where the game starts and it was the weakest of the eight: it is two cities stacked, the lower one drowned, and it now looks like that — wet colonial stone with a salt line on it below the tide, reed and salvage above, outside stairs to the first floor, and masts and drying racks over the water. Two honest problems. The street furniture — the paving, the courts, the causeways — is still made the old way, about ten thousand pieces of it. And our own offline check of whether the skyline reads cannot tell the new rooflines from flattened ones, which either means the check is blunt or the skyline is timid; only a picture settles that, and that is the next thing to take.

You could see through the player. Orbit the camera in close and there was sky where a shoulder or the small of a back should be, and it had been declared fixed more than once because everyone kept looking for a transparency bug. There isn't one — every surface on the character is fully opaque and always has been. The holes are geometric: the body is built from tubes and spheres welded onto a skeleton, and in five separate places the pieces did not quite meet. So the first thing built this round was an instrument that can actually see the problem. It draws the character and nothing else — no world, no sky — from twenty-four angles at three distances, in eighty different poses taken from the game's own animation data, and counts background pixels that are completely surrounded by body. Five thousand seven hundred and sixty pictures, on the processor, in under three minutes, with no graphics card needed. What it found: a dorsal crest of four spines hovering thirteen centimetres behind the back rather than growing out of it; a tail whose root sat exactly on the surface of the hip instead of inside it, so it peeled away whenever the character bent; joint balls at every elbow, knee and shoulder that were smaller than the limbs they were meant to join, which leaves a notch on the outside of every bend; a belt with three millimetres of clearance; and a helmet floating four centimetres above the skull. All five are closed, the measured hole count is down to about a quarter of what it was, and the worst single frame improved more than sevenfold. The joint rule is now derived from the body's own proportions rather than typed in by hand, so nobody can reopen the gap later by adjusting a radius. The other half of the work is about not doing this forty times. There are now two base bodies on one skeleton, and seventeen named characters that are nothing but a page of numbers each — a build, a set of proportions, a snout length, a crest size, a palette, a kit. Widen the shared body by six per cent and fifteen of the seventeen visibly change, which is the whole point: improving the player improves every Argonian in Black Marsh in the same commit. Every one of them is measurably a different shape, judged on silhouette rather than colour, because two other agents independently found this week that colour alone cannot tell Morrowind's own regions apart. Said plainly: nobody has looked at these characters yet. Everything above is an automatic measurement, and the rule here is that a measurement can fail a build and can never pass one. Faces and hands are better — there is a jaw, a brow, three fingers and a thumb — but they are not finished, and the animation clip set has not been touched at all.

Ten people building parts of the same world will imagine ten different worlds unless somebody writes down what it is supposed to look like — and the last few attempts at that were paragraphs, which nobody can aim at and nobody can check. So this one is numbers. Nothing was drawn and nothing was bought: we measured 313 reference pictures the project already holds and already has permission to use for exactly this, and turned them into ranges a frame either lands in or does not. The most useful single number answers a complaint from earlier today. Someone noticed that every horizon in the game is dead flat, even in the region whose own data says it has four hundred metres of hills. Now there is a figure for how un-flat a horizon should be: measured against the reference set, the skyline wanders up and down by about a sixth of the height of the picture, and a flat one measures zero. Every region gets its own version of that, ordered by how much relief its terrain data claims — so the ridge country is asked for the most and the flat comb country for the least. Two other things came out of it. The reference world is far less colourful than a swamp is usually painted: at the median, almost none of the picture is strongly saturated, and bright colour is nearly always a light source rather than a surface. And a genuinely awkward result we are publishing rather than burying — the reference world's own regions cannot be told apart by colour alone. A machine given only their palettes guesses which region it is looking at slightly worse than chance. So we did not publish a colour-separation target, because a target read off a test the reference itself fails is a number pretending to be a fact. Region identity has to come from the shape of the land, which is the harder thing and the right thing. Twelve of the hundred and four rows are marked unset with the reason written beside them, including one we wanted badly and cannot have: you cannot read a distance in metres out of a screenshot.

A while back we worked out that most of what this project spends goes on agents re-reading their own growing conversation — by the end of a long run, every single step re-sends everything that came before it. The obvious fix is to hand the work over to a fresh agent partway through, and we put a number on what that would save: around a quarter of the bill. But that number quietly assumed the handover itself was free, and of course it is not. Someone picking up half-finished work has to read the notes and find their bearings before they can do anything useful. If that costs more than it saves, the whole idea is a mirage. So we measured it, and we did not have to invent an experiment to do it: this project has already handed work over fifty-two times by accident, whenever an agent hit a usage limit or the container restarted and a replacement was sent in. Those are real handovers, already recorded. It turns out a successor needs about twenty steps to reach the point of writing its first line of code, where a fresh agent needs eleven — and those nine extra steps cost about forty-three cents. The saving they unlock is worth about six dollars and twenty-six cents per handover, so there is roughly fourteen times more room than the handover costs. The lever is real. Two things worth saying plainly. The first measurement we tried gave a lovely answer — it said handovers were not just free but actively cheaper — and it was wrong: it was really measuring the fact that successors tend to get given smaller jobs. One of our own controls caught it, and we have published the wrong answer alongside the right one so anyone can check the working. The second is that we cannot yet tell whether a planned handover goes as smoothly as an accidental one, and the quality check we have is too coarse to prove a split agent does not lose the thread. So this goes in as a trial with three tripwires that will pull it back out, not as a rule. Separately, the machine was down to its last three gigabytes, which had already made one set of screenshots fail silently and look like a clean run. We freed nearly sixteen gigabytes — most of it leftovers from an interrupted housekeeping job eight days ago — and taught the screenshot tool to shout when the disk is full instead of banking an empty file.

When we looked hard at the graphics plan last week we found something uncomfortable: it had dozens of checks asking whether the measuring equipment worked, and almost none asking a person whether the game looked good. You could pass every gate and still ship a prototype. The obvious next question was whether the same thing was true of the other thirty plans, so we read all of them. The answer is better than expected and more interesting than a simple yes or no. Fifteen plans are in good shape and several are genuinely excellent — for wayfinding, a fresh person has to walk across the province with the map closed and find the place; for the first hour, someone who has never seen the game plays a full hour and reports what happened; the interface plan already had six independent judges and scores itself on the worst of the six. Nine plans need another pass, and the common thread is worth saying plainly: they check whether things can be told apart rather than whether they are any good. You can prove thirteen regions sound different from one another without ever asking whether any of them sounds nice. But the real finding was structural. Every one of these plans was signed off between the ninth and the twelfth of the month, and the standard changed on the fourteenth — so this is one instruction that hasn't reached them yet, rather than thirty separate mistakes. We also found three plans still assuming a set of reference images doesn't exist. It arrived on the sixth. There are a hundred and thirty-one of them sitting in the repository, and unblocking those three is about three sentences of work.

Following the sweep of all thirty plans, we took the four whose quality checks could not have told us the work was bad, and fixed them one at a time. The common repair is the same idea in each case: somewhere in every plan, a person has to meet the thing the way a player meets it, and say whether it is any good. So the stealth plan now has someone actually sneaking — one theft, one getaway, about ten minutes each — and the question they are asked is the one the reference material asks: can you tell from the screen alone where it is dark enough to move, without a meter telling you? The enemy plan and the combat plan now both have someone fighting, rather than a judge reading a graph of a fight. And each of those runs twice: once on the real build and once on a copy with the repair taken out, because a person saying 'that was good' proves nothing unless they would have said something different about a worse version. If the two feel the same, the check has told us nothing, and we say so rather than counting it as a pass. The controls plan needed only one sentence, borrowed word for word from its sister plan for phones and gamepads, which had quietly got this right all along: a green scoreboard doesn't count as finished unless the first-time player actually passed. Its scoring would otherwise let a build reach ninety out of a hundred while someone who had never played it could not work out a single control. Two things worth reporting plainly. Reading the underlying reference material rather than only the plans changed two of the four conclusions — the combat plan turned out to be following its own rulebook correctly, and the real gap was simply that nobody was ever going to watch a fight. And all four now go to a different fresh reviewer before anyone builds against them, which is the rule here: you may approve what you were handed, or you may edit it, but never both.

One of the scoreboards for how the game's systems talk to each other had been reading zero for six days, and it turns out it was never a score at all — it was the measuring tool politely reporting that the machine had been too busy to let it start. We rented a quiet GPU box for three minutes and ran it properly. Twelve of the crossings between systems are real and demonstrated: the patrol you meet on a road changes with the hour, wearing a faction's colours changes who bothers you, killing the thing that was eating the village genuinely shifts how nearly four hundred people feel about you, and the ending of the Steward's quest leaves durable marks on the world, the journal and three factions. To be sure the instrument could still say no, we re-ran the whole sweep with the cause removed and it reported zero every time. We also found that the tool's own self-check had a blind spot in exactly the place it had been wrong before, and closed it.
