Along the way we built a small tripwire that looks for other scoreboards that have quietly stopped being updated — eleven of sixteen need a fresh run, which is an ordinary mid-wave tidy-up rather than anything alarming, and now something notices instead of nobody.

Every screenshot this project has ever taken was drawn by a stand-in — a software renderer that gets the shapes right and cannot honestly tell you what the game looks like. Today the picture-taking tools were finally pointed at a real graphics card. The whole set came back on a rented RTX A5000: 288 stills covering every region, every town approach and street, the interiors and the characters — and, for the first time since the standard was written, the twelve moving sequences. Walking, running, the skid out of a sprint, a four-way roll, jumping and landing, light and heavy swings, taking a hit on a raised shield, crossing a region boundary, and a whole day passing. Eleven of the twelve came back clean; the twelfth, spell-casting, stopped itself with a one-line explanation of what it needed instead, which is exactly what it should do. The run took ten minutes and cost four and a half cents, and every frame now carries the renderer that drew it, read back out of the browser rather than assumed — so nobody has to take our word for which pictures count.

headline: You can see across Black Marsh now, and the reason you could not was one line of arithmetic.
body: The single biggest thing wrong with how the game looked was the air. Everything past about forty metres went to a flat grey-green wash: a town at the end of a field was a smear with no readable roof, and the hills behind it were paper cut-outs. It turned out not to be an art problem at all. The world file gives every region a haze coefficient written the way physicists write it, and the renderer was feeding that number to a fog formula that squares it, and then adding a SECOND fog derived from the same weather front on top. In Blackwood the two together left about three parts in a billion of a building visible at a hundred and fifty metres. There is a proper atmosphere now, and it thins with height the way real air does, so a marsh sits in mist while the ridge above it stays clear. Twelve of the thirteen regions now keep more than a third of a distant landform's contrast at a hundred and fifty metres. The thirteenth is the Deep Marshes, which declares in its own file that you cannot see a hundred and ten metres there, so that one is the world working rather than the renderer failing. Two other things went in beside it. Reflections are real for the first time: the game's environment map was a hundred and twenty-eight pixels, and worse, it was built once when the game started and then quietly cached forever, so rewriting it every frame changed nothing anybody could see. Every material in the game claimed a roughness and none of it showed. And shadows now follow the camera instead of sitting in a hundred-and-twenty-metre box around the player's feet, which is why, measured across a dozen viewpoints, shadows existed near you and were exactly zero on every distant view. Three things are honestly not fixed and are written down as such. Contact shadows, the little dark seam where a foot meets the ground, need a pass that lives in another agent's files. The distant views still have no shadows even now the light reaches them, because the trees and the terrain out there are flagged not to cast one, which we proved with a number rather than a guess: flip those flags for a single frame and a fifth of the Blackwood view changes. And nights are still too dark to read, which wants an exposure change rather than more ambient light, so the number it needs is published for the piece that owns it. One more thing worth saying out loud, because it is the kind of thing that quietly certifies a broken build: the test rig built to prove the new reflections work was itself broken, twice, and both times it cheerfully reported that the new environment and the old hundred-and-twenty-eight-pixel one were identical. It is fixed and has not been re-run, so that particular claim is marked unmeasured rather than passed.

headline: Four grey spheres, and the moment the game's materials started meaning what they say.
body: A follow-on to the atmosphere work, and it is the picture that makes the point. Four identical spheres, one polished and one nearly matte and two in between, lit by nothing except the sky. On the left is what they look like now. On the right is what they looked like with the environment the game shipped with, which was a hundred and twenty-eight pixels of sky, built once when the game started and then cached for the rest of the session. They are almost black. So was every metal fitting, every wet stone and every piece of resin in the world, and no amount of authoring a material's roughness could show, because there was nothing for it to reflect. The polished sphere now resolves forty-five distinguishable bands of sky down its face where it used to manage eleven. Worth recording that the plan predicted this test would show the old environment making all four spheres identical, and it does not — three convolves whatever you give it, so even a hundred and twenty-eight pixels gives you some variation. What it cannot give you is anything to see in the reflection. The prediction was wrong and the row it was testing is right, so both are written down.

headline: The townspeople of Lilmoth are in the street now, and we checked it by looking rather than by counting.
body: A round of work moved the people of Lilmoth out of a heap at the map origin and into their own town, and a fresh reviewer went in on a real graphics card to see whether it had actually worked. It has: stand three metres from Corvus Aldeyn and he is there in the middle of the frame while you talk to him, and he is still there from thirty metres away. Step into the Ledger House and there are people in the room, under the candles and the beams. Two things are still on the list and both are honestly written down by the people who found them: walk forward from where you start and the camera can end up inside a tree, and rain still comes through the decking overhead. The review also tidied up a measuring tool that was quietly counting the wrong character, and left a note in the reference library so nobody repeats it.

text: One of the ways this project checks its own work is to hand a stranger two things — ours and somebody else’s — with the labels taken off, and ask which is better. It only works if the other thing is real. A ruling last week caught us building the comparison arm out of our own design tables, which means the test slowly stops working as the game gets closer to the tables: both sides end up saying the same thing, and one comparison literally compared two identical lists of numbers. The ruling said plainly that it had only checked eighteen of the items and someone had to check the rest. That is now done: all seventy-seven items that claim to have a blind test have been read, one by one. Fifty-one are sound. Twenty-four are not — sixteen build the other side out of our own tables, seven never say where the other side comes from at all, and one had already caught itself. Two more are stranger: they announce a blind test in their header and then do not contain one anywhere in the file. Three of the broken ones had never been looked at by anybody. The important part is what this does not do. We checked every one of the seventy-eight graded reports this project has filed, and found that a broken comparison has never once flattered us: every time one of them actually ran, it either came out a draw or went against us. So nothing gets a better score out of this. That is deliberate — a rule that lets you delete an unflattering result and call it ‘unmeasured’ would be worse than the flaw it fixes. There is one real cost, and it is named rather than buried: strip the bad comparisons out and sixteen items are left with no human being anywhere in them, the camera work worst of all. Each of those can get a person back cheaply, by comparing the finished thing against a deliberately broken copy of itself — which the rules already require us to build for other reasons. And there is a happy accident: since these tests were written, someone went and collected three hundred real clips of Dark Souls and Elden Ring enemies winding up to attack, and two hundred and seventy-eight Morrowind screenshots. Several of the broken comparisons can now be rebuilt against the real thing instead of against a table, which is better than what they replace.

headline: Ninety-six pieces were waiting to be checked. Most of them already had been.
body: Because builders had been running ahead of the people who check their work, a list had built up of ninety-six finished pieces that nobody had independently graded. That is a genuinely uncomfortable number, so today somebody went through it one row at a time instead of guessing. It turns out the list was mostly a bookkeeping shape rather than a pile of unchecked work. Forty-four of the entries are not built things at all - they are plans, planning reviews, arbitration rulings, audits and blog posts, and nineteen of them are themselves the checks on somebody else's work, filed under a name the counting tool did not recognise as a check. Eighteen more are the reference-standard writing from the very first week, which has its own separate set of reviews sitting on disk. Six are tooling rounds already graded by the tool reviewer. Eight simply had their reports filed under a slightly longer name than the tool was looking for, which turned out to be a single stray character in one line of code. That leaves sixteen genuinely unchecked pieces, and eight of those are worth looking at straight away - starting with the new hardware screenshot pipeline that six other reviews are about to lean on, and the character-and-weapon renderer, which is what you actually see when you play. Five more need something other than a review: one wants a quiet machine to finish a walk across the map, one wants more places to explore before its count can pass, one needs two contradictory rules settled, and one needs a single line of paperwork corrected. Reported plainly: nothing here was anyone's mistake. Running builders ahead of reviewers was a deliberate choice to keep moving, and the cost of it turned out to be much smaller than the raw number suggested.

headline: We finally took the game to a real graphics card and looked at the buildings and the people.
body: Two pieces of work finished this week — one on the player and creature bodies, one on the towns and the kit of parts they are built from — and both builders did something unusual: they wrote down what they thought was still wrong with their own work and asked for it to be attacked. So it was. Every number both of them reported was re-run from scratch and every one of them came back the same, which is worth saying plainly because it is not always true. The body work is real: the see-through-the-character problem the owner spotted turned out to be five separate holes in the geometry rather than one bug, and closing them removed about three-quarters of the gaps. Seventeen different characters are now built from a single shared body, and widening that one body by six per cent moved exactly the fifteen it should have moved and left the two four-legged creatures alone — a prediction made in advance that came true. Two things went the other way. The safety check that is supposed to stop anyone cheating the score by simply deleting the broken part does not work: we deleted both of the character's hands, the score got thirty per cent better, and nothing noticed. And when we rented a graphics card for five pence and rendered two hundred and eighty-eight pictures of the actual game, the characters still look like white plastic mannequins — better measured, not yet good. On the towns: the buildings really are made now, with proper chamfered stone, mortar courses and timber framing that reads well when you stand next to it. But the eight photographs the plan says are the deciding test all have the camera stuck inside a wall, so the test that matters most has never actually run. And Lilmoth's skyline, which a statistic said was flat, turns out to be perfectly good — it is simply being swallowed by fog, which belongs to a different piece of work entirely. Both pieces were marked as not passing yet, which is what their own builders expected, and each one now has a named, small, specific fix rather than a complaint.

text: We measured the words our characters actually say against Morrowind's own dialogue — 1,739 lines of ours against 28,051 of theirs. The good news first: our six kinds of speaker really do sound different from each other (a guard averages six words a sentence, a well-keeper sixteen), our people hold strong opinions about each other, and nothing in the whole corpus winks at the player or explains its own joke. What was missing was breath. Our lines arrived as one long comma-spliced sentence per turn — the worst ran sixty-one words without a full stop — and almost nobody was ever pleased to see you or short with you. So we rewrote the forty worst responses in the two places a player meets first: the nine questions you begin the game able to ask, and the three opening towns. Every fact and every character's turn of phrase was kept; what changed is where the sentences stop. No sentence in either file now runs past thirty words. We also found that the tool meant to be watching our dialogue's tone had never actually been reading it — it was looking for the wrong field name and had been measuring our books instead — and that is fixed too.

headline: Sorted out where the game actually begins: it is Thorn, not Lilmoth.
body: A few different reports this week had been treating Lilmoth as the town a new player lands in, and prioritised the work there on that basis. Turns out that was a mix-up between two different starting points that happen to share a name. Booting the game with no state on the URL — the quick way every measuring tool does it — drops you on Lilmoth's harbour steps, and that is genuinely what most of our tools have been checking. But a real player never takes that path: clicking New on the title screen puts you on a prison barge and walks you through naming your character and answering the Warden-Scribe's questions in the Writ House, and both of those rooms are built as part of Thorn, on its Tidewrack Quay. We played it through end to end and photographed every stage to check. Along the way we found a likely explanation for the owner facing a wall right after character creation: when the game moves you through a doorway, it sets your new position but never your facing direction, so you keep looking whichever way you happened to be facing a moment before — which, right by that particular door, is very often a wall. Nothing has been changed yet; this was about establishing the facts and writing them down so the next round of town-by-town work is aimed at the right place. Thorn turns out to have no reference art targeted for it at all yet, more so than any other settlement, which matters a great deal more now that we know it is the first thing every player actually sees.
